modules.title: Number: Indices, Surds and Standard Form
modules.standfirst: The quick marks at the front of both papers and the "show that" surd question near the back. Prime factors, HCF and LCM, the index laws (including negative and fractional powers), surds and rationalising, standard form and recurring decimals. Every one of these is a routine you can learn step by step, and every one has a classic slip that costs the A1.

subsections.html: This module is the number toolkit that the rest of the course leans on. Most questions are short, usually 1 to 4 marks, and follow a fixed routine, so each section below gives you the routine as numbered steps plus one worked example laid out the way the mark scheme wants it.

subsections.heading: Prime factor decomposition
subsections.html:
Spec 1.4D · 2014 Edexcel Jan 4H Q8 · 2018 Edexcel May 1H Q8

Every whole number bigger than 1 can be written in exactly one way as a product of prime numbers. The exam wants it as a product of powers of primes, e.g. 360 = 23 × 32 × 5.

  1. Divide by the smallest prime that goes in (2, then 3, then 5, then 7…). A factor tree does the same job.
  2. Keep dividing until you reach 1.
  3. Collect equal primes into powers, in increasing order, joined with × signs.
  4. Check: multiply it back out on the calculator.

Worked example — write 1260 as a product of powers of its prime factors

1260 ÷ 2 = 630, 630 ÷ 2 = 315, 315 ÷ 3 = 105, 105 ÷ 3 = 35, 35 ÷ 5 = 7, 7 ÷ 7 = 1 (M1 for at least two correct divisions or a correct partial tree)

1260 = 22 × 32 × 5 × 7 (A1)

✗ "2, 2, 3, 3, 5, 7" as a list. That is not a product, and the A1 is lost.
✗ "4 × 9 × 35". The factors are not all prime.
✓ 22 × 32 × 5 × 7 (or 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 5 × 7 if the question does not say "powers").

subsections.heading: HCF and LCM from prime factors
subsections.html:
Spec 1.4E · 2018 Edexcel May 1H Q8 · 2016 Edexcel SAM 2H Q1

The HCF takes each shared prime to its lowest power; the LCM takes every prime to its highest power.

  1. Write each number as a product of prime powers.
  2. HCF: use only the primes that appear in every number, each to the lowest power it appears.
  3. LCM: use every prime that appears anywhere, each to the highest power it appears.
  4. Leave it in index form if the numbers were given in index form; otherwise multiply out.

Worked example — HCF and LCM of 84 and 360

84 = 22 × 3 × 7 and 360 = 23 × 32 × 5 (M1 for both decompositions)

HCF: shared primes 2 and 3, lowest powers → 22 × 3 = 12 (A1)

LCM: all primes, highest powers → 23 × 32 × 5 × 7 = 2520 (A1)

Word problems hide the LCM: "one light flashes every 12 seconds, another every 18 seconds, when do they next flash together?" is the LCM (36 seconds). "Largest equal groups" or "largest tile that fits exactly" is the HCF.

2018 1H Q8(b) ran it backwards. If the LCM of A and C contains 24 and A has no factor of 2, then C must contain exactly 24. Reason one prime at a time.

subsections.heading: The index laws
subsections.html:
Spec 1.4C, 2.1A · 2018 Edexcel May 1H Q3 · 2016 Edexcel SAM 2H Q4

Powers of the same base combine by adding, subtracting or multiplying the indices; the numbers in front are dealt with separately.

Index laws — memoriseam × an = am+n  ·  am ÷ an = am−n  ·  (am)n = amn  ·  a0 = 1same base only · a bracket raised to a power raises every factor inside it, numbers included
  1. Deal with the numbers first (multiply, divide, or raise them to the power).
  2. Deal with each letter separately using the laws above.
  3. Write the result as one term, e.g. 27x12y3.

Worked example — simplify (3a4b2)3 and 12x7y2 ÷ 4x3y5

(3a4b2)3: 33 = 27, (a4)3 = a12, (b2)3 = b6 → 27a12b6 (B2; B1 for two of the three parts right)

12 ÷ 4 = 3, x7−3 = x4, y2−5 = y−3 → 3x4y−3 or 3x4/y3 (B2)

✗ (2m3)4 = 2m12. The 2 was not raised to the power.
✗ (2m3)4 = 16m7. The indices were added instead of multiplied.
✓ (2m3)4 = 16m12. That was 2018 1H Q3(b), and the scheme gave B1 for 16m12 with one part wrong.

equations.name: Index laws
equations.formula: am × an = am+n  ·  am ÷ an = am−n  ·  (am)n = amn  ·  a0 = 1

subsections.heading: Negative and fractional indices
subsections.html:
Spec 1.4C (Higher) · 2018 Edexcel May 1H Q15(a) · 2016 Edexcel SAM 2H Q4(d)

A negative index means "one over", the denominator of a fractional index is a root, and the numerator is a power.

Negative and fractional powers — memorisea−n = 1/an  ·  a1/n = n√a  ·  am/n = (n√a)mdo the root first — the numbers stay small
  1. Negative? Flip the base (take the reciprocal) and make the index positive.
  2. Denominator of the index: take that root.
  3. Numerator of the index: raise to that power.

Worked example — evaluate 27−2/3 and (16/81)−3/4

27−2/3 = 1/272/3; ∛27 = 3; 32 = 9 → 1/9

(16/81)−3/4 = (81/16)3/4 (M1 for flipping or for the fourth root); 4√(81/16) = 3/2; (3/2)3 = 27/8 (A1)

The same with letters, like 2018 1H Q15(a): (81x12/y8)−3/4 = (y8/81x12)3/4 = y6/(27x9). Multiply every index by the power, and take the root of the number separately.

✗ 25−1/2 = −5. A negative index never makes the answer negative.
✗ 27−2/3 = 27 × −2/3 = −18. The index is not a multiplier.
✓ 25−1/2 = 1/√25 = 1/5.

subsections.heading: Writing numbers as powers of a prime
subsections.html:
Spec 1.4C · 2018 Edexcel May 2H Q10

To solve 2? = … or compare powers, rewrite every number as a power of the same prime, then the indices must be equal.

  1. Rewrite each number as a power of the common base: 8 = 23, 4 = 22, 1/9 = 3−2, √2 = 21/2.
  2. Combine using the index laws into a single power.
  3. Set the indices equal and solve.

Worked example — 4x × 25 = 83, find x

(22)x × 25 = (23)3 → 22x+5 = 29 (M1)

2x + 5 = 9 → x = 2 (A1)

And 8/27 = 23/27 = 2−4, so n = −4 (the 2018 question).

subsections.heading: Simplifying surds
subsections.html:
Spec 1.4A · 2018 Edexcel May 2H Q21(a)

A surd is simplified by taking out the largest square factor: √(ab) = √a × √b.

Surd rules — memorise√(ab) = √a × √b  ·  √(a/b) = √a/√b  ·  √a × √a = athere is no rule for √(a + b) — it is not √a + √b
  1. Find the largest square number that divides the number under the root (4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49…).
  2. Split: √72 = √36 × √2.
  3. Square-root the square: 6√2.
  4. Only like surds (same number under the root) can be added: 4√3 + 3√3 = 7√3.

Worked example — show that √48 + √27 = 7√3

√48 = √16 × √3 = 4√3 (M1 for one of these)

√27 = √9 × √3 = 3√3

4√3 + 3√3 = 7√3 (A1, with both steps visible)

subsections.heading: Expanding brackets with surds
subsections.html:
Spec 1.4B · 2014 Edexcel Jan 3H Q17

Brackets with surds expand exactly like algebra, with √a × √a = a turning some terms back into whole numbers.

  1. Multiply every term in the first bracket by every term in the second.
  2. Replace √a × √a by a, and √a × √b by √(ab).
  3. Collect the whole numbers and the surds separately: answer in the form p + q√r.

Worked example — expand (3 + √5)2 and (2 + √3)(2 − √3)

(3 + √5)(3 + √5) = 9 + 3√5 + 3√5 + 5 (M1 for 4 terms, at least 3 correct) = 14 + 6√5 (A1)

(2 + √3)(2 − √3) = 4 − 2√3 + 2√3 − 3 = 1. The surds cancel. That is the idea behind rationalising.

✗ (3 + √5)2 = 9 + 5 = 14. The two middle terms are missing.
✓ Always write the bracket out twice and expand all four terms.

subsections.heading: Rationalising the denominator
subsections.html:
Spec 1.4B · 2018 Edexcel May 2H Q21(b) · 2016 Edexcel SAM 2H Q24

Multiplying the top and bottom by the right surd makes the denominator a whole number without changing the value.

  1. Denominator √a: multiply top and bottom by √a.
  2. Denominator a + √b: multiply top and bottom by a − √b (flip the sign). The bottom becomes a2 − b.
  3. Expand the top, simplify the bottom, then cancel any common factor.

Worked example — rationalise 10/√5, then write 4/(3 − √5) in the form a + √b

10/√5 × √5/√5 = 10√5/5 = 2√5

4/(3 − √5) × (3 + √5)/(3 + √5) (M1 for multiplying by (3 + √5)/(3 + √5))

Bottom: 32 − (√5)2 = 9 − 5 = 4. Top: 4(3 + √5)

4(3 + √5)/4 = 3 + √5 (A1)

✗ Multiplying only the denominator by (3 + √5). That changes the value of the fraction.
✗ Multiplying by (3 − √5) again. The surd does not cancel.
✓ Multiply top and bottom by the denominator with the sign flipped.

subsections.heading: Standard form
subsections.html:
Spec 1.9A · 2018 Edexcel May 1H Q5 · 2016 Edexcel SAM 1H Q9

A number in standard form is A × 10n where 1 ≤ A < 10 and n is an integer.

Standard formA × 10n,   1 ≤ A < 10,   n an integerbig numbers: n positive · small numbers (less than 1): n negative
  1. Multiply/divide: multiply/divide the A parts, then use the index laws on the powers of 10.
  2. Add/subtract: make the powers of 10 the same first (or convert to ordinary numbers).
  3. Fix the answer so A is between 1 and 10: 25.2 × 10−4 = 2.52 × 10−3; 0.25 × 104 = 2.5 × 103.

Worked example — (4.2 × 105) × (3 × 10−8) and 3.2 × 105 + 4.5 × 104

4.2 × 3 = 12.6; 105 × 10−8 = 10−3 → 12.6 × 10−3 (M1) = 1.26 × 10−2 (A1)

3.2 × 105 + 0.45 × 105 = 3.65 × 105 (check: 320 000 + 45 000 = 365 000)

On the calculator, use the ×10x key, not "× 10 ^". A display such as 2.52E−03 must be written as 2.52 × 10−3. The E notation is not accepted.

✗ 12.6 × 10−3 left as the final answer. It is not in standard form.
✗ 0.25 × 104 → 2.5 × 105. Making A bigger means making the power smaller.
✓ Check by size: 2.5 × 103 = 2500, and 1.2 × 107 ÷ 4.8 × 103 is about 2500.

subsections.heading: Standard form in context
subsections.html:
Spec 1.9A · 2016 Edexcel SAM 1H Q9(c)–(d)

Context questions are the same calculations, but the answer must be given in the form asked: standard form, a ratio 1 : n, or "how many times bigger".

  1. "How many times bigger" means divide the larger by the smaller.
  2. "Ratio 1 : n" means divide both parts by the first number: 3.5 × 103 : 1.4 × 106 = 1 : 400.
  3. Round only at the very end, to the accuracy asked.

Worked example — the Earth's mass is 5.97 × 1024 kg and the Moon's is 7.35 × 1022 kg

How many times heavier is the Earth? 5.97 × 1024 ÷ 7.35 × 1022 = 81.22… → 81.2 (3 sf) (M1 A1)

Total mass: 5.97 × 1024 + 0.0735 × 1024 = 6.0435 × 1024 → 6.04 × 1024 kg (3 sf)

subsections.heading: Recurring decimals to fractions
subsections.html:
Spec 1.2A (Higher) · 2014 Edexcel Jan 4H Q20

Multiply the decimal by a power of 10 that lines up the repeating block, then subtract so the endless tail cancels.

  1. Let x = the recurring decimal. Write out several repeats: x = 0.454545…
  2. Multiply by 10 for a one-digit repeat, 100 for two digits, 1000 for three.
  3. If the repeat does not start straight after the decimal point, first multiply so it does, and subtract those two.
  4. Subtract, solve for x, and simplify the fraction.

Worked example — show that 0.14 (= 0.1444…) = 13/90

x = 0.1444…

10x = 1.444… and 100x = 14.444… (M1 for two correct recurring decimals that will subtract to a whole number)

100x − 10x = 14.444… − 1.444… → 90x = 13 → x = 13/90 (A1)

Two-digit repeat: 0.3636… → 100x − x = 36 → 99x = 36 → x = 36/99 = 4/11.

✗ Writing "100x = 36.36" with no dots. The recurring tail has to be shown, or the subtraction cannot be seen to cancel.
✗ Using 10x − x for 0.1444… This gives 9x = 1.3, not a whole number, and the method stalls.
✓ Choose the two multiples whose decimal tails are identical, then subtract.

Rules to memorise

HCF: common primes, lowest powers. LCM: all primes, highest powers.

Indices: am × an = am+n · am ÷ an = am−n · (am)n = amn · a0 = 1 · a−n = 1/an · am/n = (n√a)m

Surds: √(ab) = √a√b · √a × √a = a · rationalise 1/(a + √b) with (a − √b), and the bottom becomes a2 − b

Standard form: A × 10n, 1 ≤ A < 10

Recurring: one-digit repeat → 10x − x · two-digit → 100x − x · three-digit → 1000x − x

subsections.heading: Definitions marked to the word
subsections.html:
TermAccepted wording
Prime numberA number with exactly two factors, 1 and itself (so 1 is not prime)
Prime factorA factor of the number that is itself prime
Highest common factor (HCF)The largest number that divides exactly into each of the numbers
Lowest common multiple (LCM)The smallest number that is a multiple of each of the numbers
IntegerA whole number: positive, negative or zero
Rational numberA number that can be written as a fraction a/b of two integers (b ≠ 0); includes all terminating and recurring decimals
SurdA root that is irrational, i.e. it cannot be written exactly as a fraction, e.g. √2, √5
Reciprocal1 divided by the number; a number times its reciprocal is 1
Standard formA × 10n with 1 ≤ A < 10 and n an integer

questions.promptHtml: Why does the HCF use the lowest power of each shared prime, but the LCM the highest?
questions.answerHtml:
A common factor has to fit inside every number. If one number has only 22, no common factor can contain 23, so the biggest you can take is the smallest power available.

A common multiple has to contain every number. If one number needs 23, the multiple must contain at least 23, so you take the biggest power. And any prime in any number must appear.

questions.promptHtml: Why is a0 = 1, not 0?
questions.answerHtml:
Use the division law: a3 ÷ a3 = a3−3 = a0. But anything divided by itself is 1. So a0 must equal 1 (for any a ≠ 0).

The same argument gives negative indices: a2 ÷ a5 = a−3, and it also equals 1/a3.

questions.promptHtml: Why does a power of ½ mean a square root?
questions.answerHtml:
a1/2 × a1/2 = a1/2 + 1/2 = a1 = a. So a1/2 is the number which, multiplied by itself, gives a. That is exactly √a.

In the same way, three lots of a1/3 multiply to a, so a1/3 = ∛a.

questions.promptHtml: A student writes √(9 + 16) = √9 + √16 = 7. What is wrong, and what rule were they thinking of?
questions.answerHtml:
√(9 + 16) = √25 = 5, not 7. Square roots do not split over addition.

They split over multiplication: √(9 × 16) = √9 × √16 = 12. That is why √72 = √36 × √2 works: you must split into a product, never a sum.

questions.promptHtml: Why does multiplying by (3 + √5) get rid of the surd in 1/(3 − √5)?
questions.answerHtml:
(3 − √5)(3 + √5) is a difference of two squares: 32 − (√5)2 = 9 − 5 = 4. The two surd terms, +3√5 and −3√5, cancel.

You multiply the top by the same bracket, so you are really multiplying by (3 + √5)/(3 + √5) = 1. The value does not change, only its form.

questions.promptHtml: Why is 34 × 103 not in standard form, and how do you fix it without changing its value?
questions.answerHtml:
The front number must satisfy 1 ≤ A < 10, and 34 does not.

34 = 3.4 × 10, so 34 × 103 = 3.4 × 10 × 103 = 3.4 × 104. Dividing A by 10 means multiplying the power by 10 (adding 1 to n), so the value is unchanged.

questions.promptHtml: For x = 0.1444…, why do you subtract 10x from 100x rather than x from 10x?
questions.answerHtml:
You need two numbers with identical tails so that the subtraction leaves a whole number. 10x = 1.444… and 100x = 14.444… both end in 444… forever, so 90x = 13 exactly.

x = 0.1444… and 10x = 1.444… have different tails (0.1444 vs 0.444), so 9x = 1.3. That still works if you then multiply by 10, but it is messier. The 1 at the front is not part of the repeat.

questions.promptHtml: A student writes 8−2/3 = −16/3. Explain the two misconceptions and give the right value.
questions.answerHtml:
They treated the index as something to multiply by: 8 × −2/3. An index is not a multiplier. It tells you which root and power to take.

They also treated "negative" as "the answer is negative". A negative index means the reciprocal.

Correctly: 8−2/3 = 1/82/3; ∛8 = 2; 22 = 4 → 1/4.

modules.title: Fractions, Percentages, Ratio and Proportion
modules.standfirst: The money-and-sharing questions that open every paper, plus the proportion question that closes the first half. The whole topic runs on one idea: multipliers. A 4% fall is × 0.96, three years of it is × 0.96³, and undoing a 5% rise is ÷ 1.05. Get that habit and reverse percentages, compound interest and "y is proportional to x²" all become the same calculation.

From the 2018 May 1H mark scheme, on the salary that became HK$252 000 after a 5% rise:

"NB: An answer of 239 400 scores M0 M0 A0"

239 400 is 252 000 minus 5% of 252 000. That takes 5% of the new amount, but the rise was 5% of the old one. The method is wrong, so it scores zero, not "nearly right". Divide by the multiplier: 252 000 ÷ 1.05 = 240 000.

subsections.html: Almost every question here is one of four routines: fraction arithmetic, percentage multipliers, ratio "parts", and proportion "find k". The calculator is allowed on both papers, but fraction "show that" questions still need every line written out, because the answer is printed on the paper.

subsections.heading: Fractions and mixed numbers — "show that"
subsections.html:
Spec 1.2F, 1.2I · 2018 Edexcel May 2H Q4 · 2016 Edexcel SAM 2H Q10

Convert mixed numbers to improper fractions, then add or subtract over a common denominator, or multiply (or flip and multiply to divide).

  1. Change every mixed number to an improper fraction: 3 2/5 = 17/5.
  2. Add/subtract: rewrite both over a common denominator, then combine the numerators.
  3. Divide: multiply by the reciprocal of the second fraction.
  4. Simplify and convert back to a mixed number, matching the form printed in the question.

Worked example — show that 3 2/5 − 1 3/4 = 1 13/20

17/5 − 7/4 (M1 for correct improper fractions)

= 68/20 − 35/20 (M1 for a correct common denominator with correct numerators)

= 33/20 = 1 13/20 (A1 shown, with no calculator decimals)

Division: 2 1/3 ÷ 1 5/9 = 7/3 ÷ 14/9 = 7/3 × 9/14 = 63/42 = 3/2 = 1 1/2.

✗ Writing 3.4 − 1.75 = 1.65 = 1 13/20. Decimal working does not show the fraction method, and in a "show that" it scores nothing.
✓ Improper fractions → common denominator → simplify, with every stage written.

subsections.heading: Percentage change and multipliers
subsections.html:
Spec 1.6B, 1.6D, 1.6E · 2018 Edexcel May 2H Q3 · 2016 Edexcel SAM 2H Q5

Increasing by r% multiplies by (1 + r/100); decreasing by r% multiplies by (1 − r/100).

Percentage change — memorisepercentage change = (change ÷ original) × 100always divide by the ORIGINAL amount · +8% → × 1.08 · −7.5% → × 0.925
  1. Turn the percentage into a multiplier.
  2. New amount = original × multiplier.
  3. For a percentage change: find the change, then divide by the original and × 100.

Worked example — a price rises from $480 to $552. Find the percentage increase.

Change = 552 − 480 = 72 (M1)

72 ÷ 480 × 100 = 15% (A1). Or: 552 ÷ 480 = 1.15, so 15% up.

✗ 72 ÷ 552 × 100 = 13.0%. Dividing by the new amount.
✓ Always divide by the value before the change.

subsections.heading: Reverse percentages
subsections.html:
Spec 1.6F · 2018 Edexcel May 1H Q7(b) · 2016 Edexcel SAM 1H Q8

If you know the amount after a percentage change, divide by the multiplier to get back to the original.

  1. Write the multiplier for the change (a 12% rise is 1.12, a 35% sale is 0.65).
  2. original × multiplier = new amount, so original = new ÷ multiplier.
  3. If you are told the amount of the change instead (SAM 1H Q8: the 15% reduction was $22.50), then 15% = 22.50, 1% = 1.50 and 100% = 150.

Worked example — after a 12% increase a laptop costs $1344. Find the price before the increase.

112% = 1344, or x × 1.12 = 1344 (M1)

1344 ÷ 1.12 (M1) = $1200 (A1)

Check: 1200 × 1.12 = 1344 ✓

✗ 1344 × 0.88 = 1182.72. Taking 12% off the new price.
✓ Divide the new price by 1.12. The 12% was 12% of the unknown original, not of 1344.

subsections.heading: Compound interest and depreciation
subsections.html:
Spec 1.6G, 1.6B (Higher) · 2016 Edexcel SAM 2H Q8 · 2018 Edexcel May 1H Q7(a)

Compound change applies the same multiplier once per year, so n years is the multiplier to the power n.

Compound growth and decayvalue = P × (1 ± r/100)nP = starting amount · r = percentage rate per year · n = number of years · + for interest, − for depreciation
  1. Write the yearly multiplier: 3.5% interest → 1.035; 18% depreciation → 0.82.
  2. Raise it to the number of years and multiply by the starting amount.
  3. Round only at the end, to the accuracy asked (money: 2 dp or the nearest whole unit).
  4. If asked for the interest, subtract the original amount at the end.

Worked example — $25 000 is invested at 3.5% per year compound interest for 4 years

25 000 × 1.0354 (M2; M1 for 25 000 × 1.035 or a correct year-by-year method started)

= 28 688.075… = $28 688.08 (A1)

Interest earned = 28 688.08 − 25 000 = $3688.08

Depreciation: a $15 000 car losing 18% a year is worth 15 000 × 0.825 = $5561.10 after 5 years.

✗ 25 000 × 0.035 × 4 + 25 000. That is simple interest. The 2018 scheme gave only a special case B1 for 160 000 × 0.12 (4% × 3).
✗ 160 000 × 0.96 × 3. Multiplying by 3 instead of cubing.
✓ 160 000 × 0.963 = 141 557.76 → HK$141 558.

subsections.heading: Repeated percentage change and "how many years?"
subsections.html:
Spec 1.6A (Higher)

Successive percentage changes multiply; they do not add.

  1. Multiply the multipliers: +30% then −20% → 1.3 × 0.8 = 1.04.
  2. Read off the overall change: 1.04 means a 4% increase, not 10%.
  3. "After how many years does it first fall below…?" Keep multiplying year by year (or try powers) and state the first whole year that passes the target.

Worked example — a car worth $24 000 loses 12% of its value each year. After how many years is it first worth less than half?

0.885 × 24 000 = $12 665.57 (still above $12 000) (M1 for trying a power of 0.88)

0.886 × 24 000 = $11 145.70 (below $12 000) (M1 for the values either side)

6 years (A1)

✗ "+30% then −20% is +10%". The 20% is taken off a bigger amount.
✓ 1.3 × 0.8 = 1.04 → a 4% increase overall.

subsections.heading: Ratio — simplifying and sharing
subsections.html:
Spec 1.7A, 1.7B · 2018 Edexcel May 2H Q2 · 2016 Edexcel SAM 1H Q2

A ratio splits an amount into equal parts: find the value of one part, then multiply.

  1. Add the ratio numbers to get the total number of parts.
  2. One part = amount ÷ total parts.
  3. Multiply each ratio number by one part.
  4. If you are told a difference (e.g. "A gets $36 more than B"), that difference equals the difference in parts, and you find one part from that instead.
  5. For the form 1 : n, divide both sides by the first number.

Worked example — $2880 is shared in the ratio 3 : 5 : 7. Find the difference between the largest and smallest shares.

3 + 5 + 7 = 15 parts; 2880 ÷ 15 = 192 per part (M1)

(7 − 3) × 192 (M1) = $768 (A1)

Difference version: Amir and Beth share in the ratio 5 : 3, and Amir gets $36 more. 2 parts = 36, so 1 part = 18; Amir gets 90, Beth 54.

✗ 2880 ÷ 3 = 960 for the first share. Dividing by the ratio number, not the total of the parts.
✓ Total parts first, then one part, then multiply.

subsections.heading: Ratio with fractions and combined ratios
subsections.html:
Spec 1.7E · 2018 Edexcel May 1H Q2

A fraction of a whole and a ratio within that fraction chain together: work from the number you know back to the whole.

  1. Turn a ratio into fractions: girls : boys = 2 : 7 means girls are 2/9 of the children.
  2. Use the known number to find the group it belongs to (girls → children).
  3. Use the fraction of the whole to find the whole (children → everyone), then answer the question asked.
  4. To combine a : b and b : c, scale them so the b values match.

Worked example — a : b = 2 : 3 and b : c = 4 : 5. Find a : b : c.

Make b the same: 2 : 3 = 8 : 12 and 4 : 5 = 12 : 15 (M1)

a : b : c = 8 : 12 : 15 (A1)

subsections.heading: Direct proportion
subsections.html:
Spec 2.5A (Higher) · 2018 Edexcel May 2H Q16 · 2014 Edexcel Jan 3H Q14

"y is directly proportional to xn" means y = kxn for some constant k, which you find from one pair of values.

Direct proportiony ∝ xn  ⇒  y = kxnthe spec only uses x, x2, x3 and √x
  1. Write the equation with k: y = kx2 (use the power in the question).
  2. Substitute the given pair and solve for k.
  3. Write the formula with the number for k. This is where the A1 is.
  4. Use the formula for the new value. When you square-root at the end, take the positive root if the context needs one.

Worked example — y is directly proportional to x2. y = 45 when x = 3. Find y when x = 4.

y = kx2 (M1)

45 = k × 32 → k = 5 (M1)

y = 5x2 (A1)

x = 4: y = 5 × 16 = 80 (B1 ft)

✗ y = x2 + k. Proportion means multiply by k.
✗ Finding k = 5 but then writing the formula as y = kx2. The scheme wants y = 5x2 written out.

subsections.heading: Inverse proportion
subsections.html:
Spec 2.5A (Higher) · 2016 Edexcel SAM 2H Q16 · 2012 Edexcel Jan 3H Q15

"y is inversely proportional to xn" means y = k/xn: as x goes up, y goes down.

Inverse proportiony ∝ 1/xn  ⇒  y = k/xn"inversely proportional to the square of d" is F = k/d2
  1. Write y = k/xn.
  2. Substitute the pair and rearrange: k = y × xn.
  3. Write the formula with the number for k.
  4. To find x, rearrange: xn = k/y, then take the root.

Worked example — F is inversely proportional to d2. F = 20 when d = 3. Find d when F = 5.

F = k/d2 (M1); 20 = k/9 → k = 180 (M1); F = 180/d2 (A1)

5 = 180/d2 → d2 = 36 (M1) → d = 6 (A1)

subsections.heading: Scaling in proportion and the graphs
subsections.html:
Spec 2.5A (Higher) · 2018 Edexcel May 2H Q16(b)

Without finding k, you can see what happens: if y ∝ xn and x is multiplied by s, then y is multiplied by sn (or divided by sn for inverse).

  1. Write the scale factor for x (a 25% increase is × 1.25).
  2. Raise it to the power: y ∝ x2 → y is × 1.252 = × 1.5625.
  3. For inverse proportion, divide instead: y ∝ 1/x2 → y is × 1/1.5625 = × 0.64, which is a 36% decrease.
  4. Graph shapes: y ∝ x is a straight line through the origin; y ∝ x2 is a curve through the origin getting steeper; y ∝ 1/x is a curve that never meets the axes.

Worked example — R = 3t2 and R = 12/x. Show that t is inversely proportional to √x.

3t2 = 12/x (M1 for equating)

t2 = 4/x → t = 2/√x, which is of the form k/√x, so t ∝ 1/√x (A1)

subsections.heading: Unitary method and exchange rates
subsections.html:
Spec 1.7C, 1.7D, 1.10C

Find the value of one unit, then multiply to the number you want. Exchange rates are direct proportion with k = the rate.

  1. Write what "1 unit" is worth (1 pen, 1 gram, £1).
  2. Multiply or divide to reach the amount asked.
  3. For comparisons ("which is better value?") convert both to the same currency or the same unit amount, then compare and state which with the figures.

Worked example — £1 = €1.16. A watch costs €348 in Paris and £310 in London. Where is it cheaper, and by how much in pounds?

348 ÷ 1.16 = £300 (M1)

£310 − £300 = £10 (M1)

Paris is cheaper by £10 (A1)

The multipliers behind most of the marks

Up r%: × (1 + r/100) · Down r%: × (1 − r/100) · Reverse: ÷ the multiplier

Compound: P × (multiplier)n · Repeated changes: multiply the multipliers

Percentage change = change ÷ original × 100

Ratio: total parts → one part → multiply · Proportion: y = kxn or y = k/xn, find k, write the formula

subsections.heading: Definitions marked to the word
subsections.html:
TermAccepted wording
PercentageA number of parts per hundred
MultiplierThe number you multiply by to apply a percentage change, e.g. 1.08 for +8%
Compound interestInterest calculated on the original amount plus the interest already added, each year
DepreciationA loss in value over time, usually a fixed percentage of the current value each year
RatioA comparison of quantities in proportion, a : b, telling you how many parts each gets
Directly proportionaly = kx: when one is multiplied by a number, the other is multiplied by the same number
Inversely proportionaly = k/x: when one is multiplied by a number, the other is divided by the same number
Reciprocal1 ÷ the number; dividing by a fraction is multiplying by its reciprocal

questions.promptHtml: A shop raises a price by 20%, then cuts the new price by 20%. Why is it not back where it started?
questions.answerHtml:
The 20% cut is taken from a bigger number than the 20% rise was. As multipliers: 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96.

So the final price is 96% of the original, a 4% fall overall. Percentage changes multiply; they never simply add.

questions.promptHtml: Why do you divide by 1.05, not multiply by 0.95, to undo a 5% increase?
questions.answerHtml:
The rise was original × 1.05 = new. Undoing "× 1.05" means "÷ 1.05".

× 0.95 takes 5% of the new amount, which is bigger than 5% of the original. 252 000 × 0.95 = 239 400, but 240 000 × 1.05 = 252 000. They differ by 600, and the scheme gives zero for the first.

questions.promptHtml: Why is compound interest P × 1.023, not P × 1.06?
questions.answerHtml:
Each year the 2% is added to the current balance, which already includes last year's interest. So the balance is multiplied by 1.02 three times: 1.02 × 1.02 × 1.02 = 1.061208.

× 1.06 is simple interest, 2% of the original three times. The difference, 0.1208%, is the "interest on the interest".

questions.promptHtml: Money is shared in the ratio 3 : 7 : 4, and the second share is $30 more than the third. Why is one part worth $10?
questions.answerHtml:
The second share is 7 parts and the third is 4 parts, so the difference between them is 7 − 4 = 3 parts.

3 parts = $30, so 1 part = $10. Then the first share = 3 × 10 = $30. You never need the total.

questions.promptHtml: y is directly proportional to x2. Without finding k, what happens to y when x is tripled?
questions.answerHtml:
y = kx2. Replace x by 3x: k(3x)2 = 9kx2 = 9y.

So y is multiplied by 9. In general, multiplying x by s multiplies y by sn when y ∝ xn.

questions.promptHtml: F is inversely proportional to d2. Explain why doubling d gives a quarter of F.
questions.answerHtml:
F = k/d2. With 2d: k/(2d)2 = k/(4d2) = F/4.

The square makes the effect bigger than the change in d. Doubling divides by 22 = 4, and tripling divides by 9. This is the inverse square law.

questions.promptHtml: What does a graph of y against x look like if y is directly proportional to x, and why does it have to go through the origin?
questions.answerHtml:
A straight line through (0, 0) with gradient k.

y = kx, so when x = 0, y = k × 0 = 0. A straight line that does not pass through the origin, like y = 2x + 3, is linear but not proportional: doubling x does not double y.

questions.promptHtml: To divide by 14/9 you multiply by 9/14. Why does that work?
questions.answerHtml:
Dividing asks "how many 14/9s fit into this?" Multiplying by the reciprocal gives the same answer because (14/9) × (9/14) = 1.

So a ÷ (14/9) = a × (9/14) × [(14/9) ÷ (14/9)] = a × 9/14. Dividing by a number is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal.

questions.promptHtml: Show that 2 5/6 + 1 3/4 = 4 7/12 (3)
questions.answerHtml:
M1 for correct improper fractions 17/6 and 7/4 (or dealing with the whole numbers separately, 3 + 5/6 + 3/4) 1

M1 for a correct common denominator, e.g. 34/12 + 21/12 1

A1 for 55/12 = 4 7/12 shown 1

markScheme.point: M1 for correct improper fractions 17/6 and 7/4 (or dealing with the whole numbers separately, 3 + 5/6 + 3/4)
M1 for a correct common denominator, e.g. 34/12 + 21/12

modules.title: Accuracy and Bounds
modules.standfirst: Every measurement is rounded, so every calculation with it has a range. The Higher bounds question is worth 2 to 4 marks and always tests the same thing: which end of each range makes the answer biggest or smallest. For subtraction and division it is the opposite end from what you expect. This module also covers rounding, significant figures, estimation and choosing a sensible accuracy, which cost marks on nearly every question in the paper.
modules.appearedIn: every paper here (rounding); bounds in most

subsections.html: A value "correct to" some accuracy could really be anywhere in a range half a unit either side. Bounds questions ask how far that range stretches after a calculation. Everything else here is about writing numbers to the right accuracy and not losing accuracy along the way.

subsections.heading: Rounding to decimal places
subsections.html:
Spec 1.8B · every paper

Look at the digit after the last one you are keeping: 5 or more rounds up, 4 or less leaves it.

  1. Count the decimal places you need and draw a line after that digit.
  2. Look at the next digit only.
  3. Round, and keep trailing zeros that are part of the accuracy: 7.2968 to 2 dp is 7.30, not 7.3.

Worked example — round 7.2968 and 0.0060749 to 2 decimal places

7.29|68: the next digit is 6, so round up. 7.29 → 7.30 → 7.30

0.00|60749: the next digit is 6, so round up → 0.01

subsections.heading: Significant figures
subsections.html:
Spec 1.8B · every paper ("Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures")

Significant figures start at the first non-zero digit; zeros before it are placeholders and don't count.

  1. Find the first non-zero digit and count from there.
  2. Round at the required figure as usual.
  3. For big numbers, fill with zeros to keep the size: 38 472 to 3 sf is 38 500, not 385.
  4. Zeros between non-zero digits count: 4.07 has 3 sf.

Worked example — 0.004076 to 2 sf, 38 472 to 3 sf

0.004076: the first significant digit is the 4. Keep 4, 0; the next digit is 7, so round up → 0.0041

38 472: keep 3, 8, 4; the next digit is 7, so round up → 38 500

✗ 38 472 to 3 sf = 385. The size of the number has changed.
✗ 0.004076 to 2 sf = 0.0. The leading zeros were counted as significant.
✓ Only the first non-zero digit starts the count, and zeros fill back to the right size.

subsections.heading: Estimation
subsections.html:
Spec 1.8D

Estimate by rounding every number to 1 significant figure, then calculating in your head.

  1. Round each number to 1 sf (unless the question says otherwise).
  2. Show the rounded numbers. That is the method mark.
  3. Work out the simpler calculation. Dividing by a small decimal makes the answer bigger.

Worked example — estimate (48.7 × 3.12) ÷ 0.487

(50 × 3) ÷ 0.5 (M1 for at least two numbers correctly rounded)

= 150 ÷ 0.5 = 300 (A1). The exact value is 312, so the estimate is sensible.

subsections.heading: Upper and lower bounds of a measurement
subsections.html:
Spec 1.8C · 2016 Edexcel Jan 3H Q9(b) · 2017 Edexcel Jan 4HR Q9(c)

The bounds are half a unit of the rounding either side of the stated value.

Bounds of a rounded valuebounds = value ± ½ × (the unit it was rounded to)"to 1 dp" → ± 0.05 · "to the nearest 10" → ± 5 · "to 2 sf" for 3400 → ± 50
  1. Identify the unit of rounding: nearest cm (1), 1 dp (0.1), 2 sf of 3400 (100).
  2. Halve it.
  3. Subtract for the lower bound and add for the upper bound.
  4. Error interval: LB ≤ x < UB.

Worked example — bounds of 6.4 cm (1 dp), 3400 g (2 sf) and 70 kg (nearest 5 kg)

6.4 cm: unit 0.1, half 0.05 → 6.35 ≤ l < 6.45

3400 g to 2 sf: the second sf is the hundreds, so the unit is 100 and half is 50 → 3350 and 3450

70 kg to the nearest 5: half of 5 is 2.5 → 67.5 and 72.5

✗ Upper bound of 6.4 = 6.49 or 6.449… The upper bound is written as 6.45, even though 6.45 itself would round up.
✗ 3400 to 2 sf: bounds 3399.5 and 3400.5. That treats it as the nearest whole number.
✓ Work out the unit from the accuracy stated, then halve it.

equations.name: Bounds of a rounded value
equations.formula: bounds = value ± ½ × (the unit it was rounded to)

subsections.heading: Bounds for counted quantities
subsections.html:
Spec 1.8C · 2014 Edexcel Jan 4H Q21

A number of items "to the nearest 100" has bounds 50 either side, and in bounds calculations you use those values just as you would for a measurement.

  1. 1300 sheets to the nearest 100 → 1250 ≤ n < 1350.
  2. In a calculation, use 1250 and 1350 as the bounds (the mark schemes accept them).
  3. Decide which bound you need using the rules in the next sections.

subsections.heading: Bounds in addition and multiplication
subsections.html:
Spec 1.8A (Higher)

For adding and multiplying positive values, the biggest answer comes from the upper bounds and the smallest from the lower bounds.

  1. Write both bounds of every value.
  2. Max: UB + UB, UB × UB. Min: LB + LB, LB × LB.
  3. Round only at the end, and only if asked.

Worked example — a rectangle measures 8.3 cm by 5.6 cm, each to 1 dp

Bounds: 8.25 ≤ l < 8.35 and 5.55 ≤ w < 5.65 (B1 for any correct bound)

Upper bound of perimeter = 2(8.35 + 5.65) = 28 cm

Upper bound of area = 8.35 × 5.65 = 47.1775 cm² (M1 A1); lower bound of area = 8.25 × 5.55 = 45.7875 cm²

subsections.heading: Bounds in subtraction
subsections.html:
Spec 1.8A (Higher) · 2018 Edexcel May 2H Q15

To make a difference as big as possible, take the biggest first number and subtract the smallest second number, and the other way round for the minimum.

Bounds of a difference — memoriseUB(a − b) = UB(a) − LB(b)  ·  LB(a − b) = LB(a) − UB(b)the bounds cross over
  1. Write the four bounds.
  2. Upper bound of a − b: UB of a, minus the LB of b.
  3. Lower bound of a − b: LB of a, minus the UB of b.

Worked example — a = 12.4 and b = 5.7, both to 1 dp. Find the bounds of a − b.

a: 12.35 to 12.45; b: 5.65 to 5.75 (B1)

UB = 12.45 − 5.65 = 6.8 (M1 for the correct combination, A1)

LB = 12.35 − 5.75 = 6.6

✗ UB(a − b) = 12.45 − 5.75 = 6.7. Upper minus upper is not the maximum, because you are taking away more than you need to.
✓ To maximise a − b, make a big and b small.

equations.name: Bounds of a difference
equations.formula: UB(a − b) = UB(a) − LB(b)  ·  LB(a − b) = LB(a) − UB(b)

subsections.heading: Bounds in division
subsections.html:
Spec 1.8A (Higher) · 2014 Edexcel Jan 4H Q21

A fraction is biggest when the top is biggest and the bottom is smallest.

Bounds of a quotient — memoriseUB(a ÷ b) = UB(a) ÷ LB(b)  ·  LB(a ÷ b) = LB(a) ÷ UB(b)speed = distance ÷ time · density = mass ÷ volume · thickness = height ÷ number
  1. Write the bounds of the numerator and the denominator.
  2. For the maximum, divide the upper bound of the top by the lower bound of the bottom.
  3. For the minimum, divide the lower bound of the top by the upper bound of the bottom.

Worked example — a runner covers 200 m (nearest 5 m) in 24.6 s (nearest 0.1 s). Find the upper bound of the average speed.

Distance 197.5 to 202.5; time 24.55 to 24.65 (B1)

UB speed = 202.5 ÷ 24.55 (M1) = 8.2484… = 8.25 m/s (3 sf) (A1)

(LB speed = 197.5 ÷ 24.65 = 8.01 m/s)

equations.name: Bounds of a quotient
equations.formula: UB(a ÷ b) = UB(a) ÷ LB(b)  ·  LB(a ÷ b) = LB(a) ÷ UB(b)

subsections.heading: Bounds in a formula
subsections.html:
Spec 1.8A (Higher) · 2016 Edexcel SAM 1H Q17

Work from the inside out: decide for each part whether it should be as big or as small as possible to push the whole answer the way you want.

  1. Write the bounds of every letter.
  2. Decide what the final answer needs, e.g. maximum.
  3. For each numerator: make it big. For each denominator: make it small. Inside a subtraction, cross over as before.
  4. Substitute in one line, then evaluate. Show the line you substituted. The scheme marks that line.

Worked example — y = (a + b)/c with a = 5.3, b = 2.1, c = 1.8, all to 1 dp

UB of y: top biggest, bottom smallest → (5.35 + 2.15) ÷ 1.75 (M1) = 4.29 (3 sf) (A1)

LB of y: (5.25 + 2.05) ÷ 1.85 = 3.95 (3 sf)

subsections.heading: Bounds as a percentage or ratio
subsections.html:
Spec 1.8A (Higher), spec example

"The smallest possible X as a percentage of the largest possible X" means work out both bounds, then LB ÷ UB × 100.

  1. Find the lower bound of the quantity.
  2. Find the upper bound of the quantity.
  3. LB ÷ UB × 100, rounded as asked.

Worked example — a rectangle is 20 cm by 11 cm, each to the nearest cm. Smallest area as a percentage of largest area, to 3 sf.

Smallest area = 19.5 × 10.5 = 204.75 (M1)

Largest area = 20.5 × 11.5 = 235.75 (M1)

204.75 ÷ 235.75 × 100 (M1) = 86.85… = 86.9% (A1)

subsections.heading: Choosing a suitable degree of accuracy
subsections.html:
Spec 1.8A (Higher)

A value is known to a given accuracy only if its upper and lower bounds both round to the same number at that accuracy.

  1. Work out the upper and lower bounds of the answer.
  2. Round both to 1 sf, 2 sf, 3 sf… and stop at the last level where they agree.
  3. Give that value and say why: "both bounds round to … to 2 sf".

Worked example — P = 23.7 × 8.46, with 23.7 to 1 dp and 8.46 to 2 dp. Give P to a suitable degree of accuracy.

UB = 23.75 × 8.465 = 201.04…; LB = 23.65 × 8.455 = 199.96… (M1 for both)

To 3 sf: 201 and 200, which disagree. To 2 sf: 200 and 200, which agree.

P = 200 (2 sf), because both bounds round to 200 to 2 sf (A1)

subsections.heading: Accuracy in the final answer
subsections.html:
Spec 1.11A · every paper

Keep full calculator values all the way through and round once, at the end, to the accuracy the question asks for.

  1. No instruction? Give an exact answer, or 3 sf for a non-exact decimal (angles to 1 dp).
  2. Money: 2 dp, e.g. $28 688.08, or "to the nearest HK$" if asked.
  3. Context: people and objects are whole numbers. "How many boxes are needed" rounds up; "how many fit" rounds down.
  4. Write the unrounded value first (e.g. 54.361…), then the rounded answer. If the rounding goes wrong, the method mark is still there.

Worked example — volume of a sphere of radius 2.35 cm

V = 4/3 × π × 2.353 = 54.3615… = 54.4 cm³ (3 sf)

Rounding r to 2.4 first gives 57.9. That is wrong by more than 3, and the A1 is lost.

✗ Rounding a middle value, then carrying on with the rounded number.
✓ Use the calculator's ANS or memory, and round once.

The bounds rules

Bounds of a value: ± half the unit of rounding. Error interval LB ≤ x < UB

a + b, a × b: max = UB with UB · min = LB with LB

a − b: max = UB(a) − LB(b) · min = LB(a) − UB(b)

a ÷ b: max = UB(a) ÷ LB(b) · min = LB(a) ÷ UB(b)

Suitable accuracy: the level at which UB and LB round to the same value

subsections.heading: Definitions marked to the word
subsections.html:
TermAccepted wording
Significant figureA digit counted from the first non-zero digit
Decimal placeA digit position after the decimal point
Upper boundThe largest value a rounded number could have had (the boundary; the value itself would round up)
Lower boundThe smallest value that would round to the given number
Error intervalThe range of possible values, written LB ≤ x < UB
EstimateAn approximate answer found by rounding each number (usually to 1 sf) first
Degree of accuracyHow precisely a value is given, e.g. to 3 sf, 2 dp or the nearest 10

questions.promptHtml: A length is 6.4 cm to 1 dp. Why is the upper bound written as 6.45 when 6.45 itself would round to 6.5?
questions.answerHtml:
The true length can be anything up to, but not including, 6.45: 6.449, 6.4499, 6.44999… There is no "largest number below 6.45", so we use the boundary 6.45 and write 6.35 ≤ l < 6.45.

In calculations, using 6.45 gives the limit the answer can approach, which is what the question wants.

questions.promptHtml: Why does the upper bound of a − b use the lower bound of b?
questions.answerHtml:
Subtracting b takes something away. To keep as much as possible, take away as little as possible, which means the smallest b.

So the biggest a minus the smallest b gives the biggest difference. With a = 12.4 and b = 5.7 (1 dp): 12.45 − 5.65 = 6.8, but 12.45 − 5.75 is only 6.7.

questions.promptHtml: Why does the maximum speed use the minimum time?
questions.answerHtml:
Speed = distance ÷ time. Dividing by a smaller number gives a bigger answer: covering the same distance in less time means going faster.

So for the maximum speed use the maximum distance and the minimum time: UB ÷ LB.

questions.promptHtml: 3400 is given "correct to 2 significant figures". Why are its bounds 3350 and 3450, not 3399.5 and 3400.5?
questions.answerHtml:
To 2 sf, the second significant figure is the 4, which is in the hundreds column. So the number was rounded to the nearest 100.

Half of 100 is 50, so the bounds are 3400 ± 50. 3399.5 and 3400.5 would only be right if it had been rounded to the nearest whole number.

questions.promptHtml: P = 23.7 × 8.46 has bounds 199.96 and 201.04. Why can P only be given as 200 to 2 sf, and not as 201?
questions.answerHtml:
To 3 sf the bounds round to 200 and 201, so we cannot tell which is correct. The true value might be either.

To 2 sf both round to 200. That is the most accurate value we can be certain of, so 200 (2 sf) is the suitable degree of accuracy.

questions.promptHtml: Why does rounding the radius to 2.4 before finding the volume of a sphere of radius 2.35 cm give a much worse answer?
questions.answerHtml:
The volume depends on r3, so a small error in r is magnified. 2.4 is about 2% too big, and cubing makes that about 6%.

4/3π(2.35)3 = 54.4 but 4/3π(2.4)3 = 57.9. Rounding early loses the A1, even with a perfect method.

questions.promptHtml: For y = 3a/(b − c), explain which bound of b and which bound of c give the largest possible y.
questions.answerHtml:
For y to be big, the numerator 3a must be big (UB of a) and the denominator b − c must be small.

b − c is smallest when b is small and c is large: LB of b minus UB of c. So UB(y) = 3 × UB(a) ÷ (LB(b) − UB(c)). The subtraction inside the denominator flips the rule twice.

questions.promptHtml: Why do you round up to find the number of 12-egg boxes needed for 100 eggs, but round down to find how many 12-egg boxes you can fill?
questions.answerHtml:
100 ÷ 12 = 8.33… 8 boxes hold only 96 eggs, so to hold every egg you need 9 boxes. Round up.

But you can only fill 8 boxes completely. The ninth would have just 4 eggs. Round down. The context decides, not the "5 or more" rule.

modules.title: Algebraic Manipulation
modules.standfirst: Expanding, factorising, algebraic fractions, rearranging formulae and proof. These are the skills that every later algebra question depends on. On their own they are worth 2 to 4 marks each and appear on every paper. The Higher-only versions to master are triple brackets, quadratics with a ≠ 1, the difference of two squares, fractions over quadratic denominators, and formulae where the subject appears twice.

subsections.html: Expanding and factorising are the same process run in opposite directions, and every section below comes back to that. Algebraic fractions are ordinary fraction rules applied after factorising. Rearranging is solving an equation with letters left in. Proof is expanding until the answer can be seen.

subsections.heading: Expanding single and double brackets
subsections.html:
Spec 2.2C, 2.2E · 2015 Edexcel Jan 4HR Q11(c)

Every term in one bracket multiplies every term in the other; then collect like terms.

  1. Single bracket: multiply the outside term by each inside term, and watch the signs: −2(x − 4) = −2x + 8.
  2. Double bracket: four products (a grid or FOIL), then collect the two middle terms.
  3. A squared bracket is two brackets: (3x − 2)2 = (3x − 2)(3x − 2).

Worked example — expand (2x − 3)(x + 5) and (3x − 2)2

2x × x = 2x2; 2x × 5 = 10x; −3 × x = −3x; −3 × 5 = −15 (M1 for 4 terms, 3 correct)

= 2x2 + 7x − 15 (A1)

(3x − 2)(3x − 2) = 9x2 − 6x − 6x + 4 = 9x2 − 12x + 4

✗ (3x − 2)2 = 9x2 + 4 or 9x2 − 4. The middle terms are missing.
✗ −2(x − 4) = −2x − 8. The sign on the second term is wrong.
✓ Write the squared bracket out twice, and multiply the sign with the number.

subsections.heading: Expanding triple brackets
subsections.html:
Spec 2.2A (Higher) · 2018 Edexcel May 1H Q11(a) · 2016 Edexcel SAM 1H Q11

Multiply two of the brackets first and simplify, then multiply that quadratic by the third bracket.

  1. Choose two brackets and expand them to a simplified quadratic (3 terms).
  2. Multiply each of those 3 terms by each term of the third bracket, giving 6 terms.
  3. Collect like terms: x3, then x2, then x, then the number.
  4. Check: substitute x = 1 into the question and into your answer. They must agree.

Worked example — expand and simplify (x + 2)(x − 3)(x + 4)

(x + 2)(x − 3) = x2 − 3x + 2x − 6 = x2 − x − 6 (M1 for expanding any two brackets, at least 3 of 4 terms correct)

(x2 − x − 6)(x + 4) = x3 + 4x2 − x2 − 4x − 6x − 24 (M1 for 6 terms, at least half correct)

= x3 + 3x2 − 10x − 24 (A1)

Check with x = 1: 3 × (−2) × 5 = −30, and 1 + 3 − 10 − 24 = −30 ✓

subsections.heading: Factorising — common factors
subsections.html:
Spec 2.2D · 2018 Edexcel May 2H Q1(c) · 2016 Edexcel SAM 1H Q6(a)

"Factorise fully" means take out the highest common factor of the numbers and the lowest power of every shared letter.

  1. HCF of the numbers.
  2. For each letter in every term, take the lowest power.
  3. Divide each term by that factor to fill the bracket.
  4. Check the bracket has no common factor left, then expand to check.

Worked example — factorise fully 15a3b − 25a2b2

HCF of 15 and 25 is 5; lowest powers a2 and b → 5a2b

15a3b ÷ 5a2b = 3a; 25a2b2 ÷ 5a2b = 5b

5a2b(3a − 5b) (M1 A1; the 2018 2H scheme gave the M1 for "any correct partially factorised expression with at least 2 terms in the common factor", such as 5a(3a2b − 5ab2) here)

✗ 5a(3a2b − 5ab2). Correct, but not fully factorised, so 1 mark out of 2.
✓ Check the bracket: if every term inside still shares a factor, take it out.

subsections.heading: Factorising quadratics x2 + bx + c
subsections.html:
Spec 2.2F · 2018 Edexcel May 1H Q3(d)

Find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b.

  1. List factor pairs of c, with signs.
  2. Pick the pair that adds to b.
  3. Write (x + p)(x + q) and expand to check.

Worked example — factorise x2 + x − 30

Multiply to −30, add to +1: 6 and −5 (M1 for (x ± 6)(x ± 5))

(x + 6)(x − 5) (A1)

subsections.heading: Factorising quadratics with a ≠ 1
subsections.html:
Spec 2.2B (Higher) · 2015 Edexcel Jan 4HR Q11(d)

Multiply a × c, find two numbers with that product and sum b, split the middle term, then factorise in pairs.

  1. Work out a × c.
  2. Find two numbers that multiply to ac and add to b.
  3. Split bx into those two terms.
  4. Factorise the first pair and the second pair; the same bracket appears in both.
  5. Take out that bracket. Expand to check.

Worked example — factorise 6x2 + x − 12

ac = 6 × −12 = −72; two numbers with product −72 and sum +1: 9 and −8

6x2 + 9x − 8x − 12 = 3x(2x + 3) − 4(2x + 3) (M1 for splitting correctly or for (3x ± 4)(2x ± 3))

= (3x − 4)(2x + 3) (A1)

✗ (6x − 4)(x + 3). This expands to 6x2 + 14x − 12. Always expand to check the middle term.
✓ With a ≠ 1, use the ac method rather than guessing.

subsections.heading: Difference of two squares
subsections.html:
Spec 2.2B (Higher) · 2014 Edexcel Jan 3H Q19 · 2018 Edexcel May 1H Q15(b)

Anything squared minus anything squared factorises into (first − second)(first + second).

Difference of two squares — memorisea2 − b2 = (a − b)(a + b)a and b can be numbers, terms or whole brackets · a2 + b2 does not factorise
  1. Take out any common factor first (2x2 − 50 = 2(x2 − 25)).
  2. Identify what is being squared: 25x2 = (5x)2, 36y2 = (6y)2.
  3. Write (a − b)(a + b). If a and b are brackets, simplify inside each factor.

Worked example — factorise 25x2 − 36y2, 2x2 − 50 and (x + 5)2 − (x − 1)2

25x2 − 36y2 = (5x − 6y)(5x + 6y)

2x2 − 50 = 2(x2 − 25) = 2(x − 5)(x + 5)

[(x + 5) − (x − 1)][(x + 5) + (x − 1)] (M1) = 6(2x + 4) = 12(x + 2) (A1)

✗ (x + 5) − (x − 1) = 4. The bracket sign flips −1 to +1, so it is 6.
✓ Put every bracket in its own bracket before simplifying: (x + 5) − (x − 1) = x + 5 − x + 1 = 6.

subsections.heading: Simplifying algebraic fractions
subsections.html:
Spec 2.2C (Higher)

You can only cancel factors, never individual terms, so factorise the top and the bottom completely first.

  1. Factorise the numerator fully.
  2. Factorise the denominator fully.
  3. Cancel any bracket (or factor) that appears in both.
  4. Leave the answer factorised.

Worked example — simplify fully (3x2 − 6x)/(x2 − 4)

Top: 3x(x − 2) (B1). Bottom: (x − 2)(x + 2) (B1)

Cancel (x − 2): 3x/(x + 2) (B1)

✗ (x2 + 3)/(x2 + 5) = 3/5, "cancelling the x2". Terms joined by + or − cannot be cancelled.
✓ Cancel only whole factors, after factorising.

subsections.heading: Adding and subtracting algebraic fractions
subsections.html:
Spec 2.2C (Higher) · 2018 Edexcel May 1H Q15(b)

Put both fractions over a common denominator, the product of the denominators or, better, their LCM, then combine the numerators.

  1. Factorise each denominator; the common denominator is every factor that appears, used once.
  2. Multiply each numerator by whatever its denominator is missing.
  3. Combine the numerators in a bracket, watching the minus sign, and simplify.
  4. Leave the denominator factorised.

Worked example — write 2/(x + 3) + 5/(x − 1) as a single fraction

Common denominator (x + 3)(x − 1) (M1)

[2(x − 1) + 5(x + 3)] / [(x + 3)(x − 1)] (M1)

= (7x + 13)/((x + 3)(x − 1)) (A1)

With a quadratic denominator, as in 2018: 1/(9x2 − 25) = 1/((3x − 5)(3x + 5)) and 1/(6x + 10) = 1/(2(3x + 5)), so the common denominator is 2(3x − 5)(3x + 5), not the product of the two.

✗ [2(x − 1) − 5(x + 3)] written as 2x − 2 − 5x + 15. The minus must go through the whole bracket, so it is −5x − 15.
✓ Bracket each new numerator before combining.

subsections.heading: Multiplying and dividing algebraic fractions
subsections.html:
Spec 2.2C (Higher) · 2016 Edexcel SAM 1H Q18

Multiply tops and bottoms, or, to divide, flip the second fraction and multiply, factorising everything so you can cancel.

  1. Dividing? Turn the second fraction upside down and change ÷ to ×.
  2. Factorise every numerator and denominator.
  3. Cancel common factors across the whole product.
  4. Multiply what is left.

Worked example — simplify (x2 − 16)/(3x + 12) ÷ (x2 − 3x − 4)/(6x)

= (x2 − 16)/(3x + 12) × 6x/(x2 − 3x − 4) (M1)

= (x − 4)(x + 4)/[3(x + 4)] × 6x/[(x − 4)(x + 1)] (M1 for correct factorising)

Cancel (x − 4), (x + 4) and 3: 2x/(x + 1) (A1)

subsections.heading: Changing the subject — subject appears once
subsections.html:
Spec 2.3F, 2.3A (Higher) · 2018 Edexcel May 2H Q1(a) · 2016 Edexcel SAM 2H Q13

Undo what has been done to the subject, in reverse order, doing the same to both sides.

  1. Clear fractions by multiplying both sides by the denominator.
  2. Get the term containing the subject on its own (add or subtract).
  3. Divide by its coefficient.
  4. Undo any power or root last: square root to undo a square (± or "positive" as stated), square to undo a root, cube root to undo a cube.
  5. Write "subject = …". The A1 depends on it.

Worked example — make r the subject of V = πr2h/3

3V = πr2h (M1 for a correct first step)

r2 = 3V/(πh)

r = √(3V/(πh)) (A1)

✗ Stopping at r2 = 3V/(πh). The subject is r, not r2.
✗ Writing only "√(3V/(πh))". The 2018 scheme required the answer "seen with a =".

subsections.heading: Changing the subject — subject appears twice
subsections.html:
Spec 2.3A (Higher) · 2016 Edexcel Jan 4HR Q19 · 2014 Edexcel Jan 3H Q16

Gather every term containing the subject on one side, then factorise the subject out.

  1. Clear any fraction or root first (multiply up, or square both sides).
  2. Expand brackets.
  3. Collect all terms with the subject on one side and everything else on the other.
  4. Factorise: take the subject out as a common factor.
  5. Divide by the bracket.

Worked example — make q the subject of p = (2q + 1)/(q − 3)

p(q − 3) = 2q + 1 (M1 for clearing the fraction)

pq − 3p = 2q + 1

pq − 2q = 1 + 3p (M1 for collecting q terms on one side)

q(p − 2) = 1 + 3p (M1 for factorising)

q = (1 + 3p)/(p − 2) (A1)

✗ q = (1 + 3p + 2q)/p. q is still on both sides, so it is not the subject.
✓ If the subject appears twice, you must factorise it out. That step is the method mark.

subsections.heading: Algebraic proof
subsections.html:
Spec 2.2E (Higher)

Write the general numbers in algebra, expand and simplify, then show the result has the required form and say so in words.

  1. Choose the representation: any integer n; consecutive n, n + 1; even 2n; odd 2n + 1; consecutive odd 2n + 1, 2n + 3.
  2. Write the expression the question describes and expand it.
  3. Simplify and factorise to show the form: a multiple of 8 is 8 × (an integer); odd is 2 × (integer) + 1.
  4. Finish with a sentence: "8(n + 1) is a multiple of 8 because n + 1 is an integer."

Worked example — prove that (2n + 3)2 − (2n − 3)2 is a multiple of 12 for all integers n

(4n2 + 12n + 9) − (4n2 − 12n + 9) (M1 for expanding both)

= 24n (A1)

= 12 × 2n, and 2n is an integer, so it is a multiple of 12 (A1 for the conclusion)

✗ "n = 1 gives 24, n = 2 gives 48, so it is true." Examples are not a proof.
✗ Using n and n + 1 for two odd numbers. They are not both odd.
✓ Use algebra for the general case, and finish with a sentence.

Routines to know cold

Triple brackets: two first → simplify → × the third → collect. Check with x = 1.

ax2 + bx + c: product ac, sum b → split the middle → factorise in pairs

a2 − b2 = (a − b)(a + b)

Fractions: factorise first; cancel factors only; the common denominator is the LCM of the denominators

Subject twice: clear fractions → expand → collect → factorise → divide

Proof: n, 2n, 2n + 1; expand; factorise to the form; finish with a sentence

subsections.heading: Definitions marked to the word
subsections.html:
TermAccepted wording
ExpandMultiply out the brackets
Factorise fullyWrite as a product, with no common factor left inside any bracket
ExpressionA collection of terms with no equals sign, e.g. 3x + 2
EquationA statement that two expressions are equal, true for particular values
IdentityA statement true for all values of the variable, written ≡
FormulaA rule linking two or more variables, e.g. A = πr2
SubjectThe variable on its own on one side of a formula
CoefficientThe number multiplying a variable, e.g. 7 in 7x

questions.promptHtml: Why does (x + 3)2 not equal x2 + 9? Use a number to show it.
questions.answerHtml:
(x + 3)2 = (x + 3)(x + 3) = x2 + 3x + 3x + 9 = x2 + 6x + 9. The two middle terms come from the "cross" products.

With x = 1: (1 + 3)2 = 16, but 12 + 9 = 10. The missing 6 is the 6x term.

questions.promptHtml: Why does a triple expansion like (x + 2)(x − 3)(x + 4) have to give an x3 term and a constant of −24 before you do any working?
questions.answerHtml:
The x3 term comes only from x × x × x, and the constant comes only from 2 × (−3) × 4 = −24.

So you can check your final answer at a glance: leading term x3, constant −24. If either is wrong, there is a slip in the working.

questions.promptHtml: In the ac method for 6x2 + x − 12, why do you look for two numbers that multiply to −72?
questions.answerHtml:
If 6x2 + x − 12 = (px + q)(rx + s), then expanding gives pr x2 + (ps + qr)x + qs. The two middle products ps and qr multiply to pr × qs = 6 × (−12) = −72, and they add to the middle coefficient, 1.

So the pair with product ac and sum b is exactly the two parts of the middle term, and splitting there lets the grouping work.

questions.promptHtml: Why does x2 − 9 factorise, but x2 + 9 does not?
questions.answerHtml:
(x − 3)(x + 3) = x2 + 3x − 3x − 9 = x2 − 9. The middle terms cancel because the signs differ.

For x2 + 9 you would need two numbers that multiply to +9 and add to 0, which is impossible for real numbers. There is no difference of squares, because it is a sum.

questions.promptHtml: Why can you cancel (x − 2) in 3x(x − 2)/((x − 2)(x + 2)), but not the x in (x + 3)/(x + 5)?
questions.answerHtml:
(x − 2) is a factor of both top and bottom, since everything is multiplied by it. Dividing top and bottom by the same factor leaves the value unchanged.

In (x + 3)/(x + 5), x is a term, added to something else. Check with x = 1: 4/6 = 2/3, but "cancelling x" gives 3/5. Cancelling terms changes the value.

questions.promptHtml: For 1/(9x2 − 25) − 1/(6x + 10), why is the best common denominator 2(3x − 5)(3x + 5) and not (9x2 − 25)(6x + 10)?
questions.answerHtml:
Factorised, the denominators are (3x − 5)(3x + 5) and 2(3x + 5). They share (3x + 5). The lowest common multiple needs each factor only once: 2(3x − 5)(3x + 5).

The product works too, but it contains (3x + 5) twice, so you would have to cancel at the end. That is extra algebra where slips happen, and the "simplest form" mark depends on it.

questions.promptHtml: When the subject appears twice, why must you factorise it out rather than just divide?
questions.answerHtml:
After collecting, you have something like pq − 2q = 1 + 3p. You cannot divide by "p" or by "−2" alone, because each only removes q from one term.

Factorising gives q(p − 2) = 1 + 3p. Now q is multiplied by one thing, (p − 2), so dividing by it leaves q on its own. Without factorising, the subject never ends up alone on one side.

questions.promptHtml: Why is "2n + 1" a good way to write any odd number, and why don't examples count as a proof?
questions.answerHtml:
2n is a multiple of 2, so it is always even when n is an integer, and one more than an even number is odd. Every odd number can be written this way, so working with 2n + 1 covers them all at once.

Examples only check the cases you tried. A statement can hold for the first few numbers and fail later. The algebra shows it holds for every integer n.

modules.title: Equations and Inequalities
modules.standfirst: The engine room of both papers. Every current-spec paper has a linear equation, a quadratic and a pair of simultaneous equations, and most have an inequality or a shaded region. The marks go to people who show each line of algebra: "show clear algebraic working" means a correct answer with no working can score nothing.

The front of the May 2018 1H mark scheme sets the rule for every "show your working" equation:

"Apart from questions 3c, 11b and 20 (where the mark scheme states otherwise) the correct answer, unless clearly obtained from an incorrect method, should be taken to imply a correct method."

Q3c and Q11b were the linear equation and the quadratic formula. On those, a bare correct answer is not enough. Write every line: expand, collect, divide. For the formula, write the substitution out in full.

subsections.html: An equation is a balance. Whatever you do to one side you do to the other, until the letter is on its own. Inequalities follow the same rules, with one extra: multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the sign. Quadratics need one more idea: if two things multiply to give zero, one of them must be zero.

subsections.heading: Linear equations with brackets and unknowns on both sides
subsections.html:
Spec 2.4A · 2018 Edexcel May 1H Q3(c) · 2016 Edexcel SAM 2H Q4(e)

Get rid of brackets, get every x-term on one side and every number on the other, then divide.

  1. Expand any brackets, taking care with a minus sign in front.
  2. Collect the x-terms on the side where there are more of them, so the x-coefficient stays positive.
  3. Collect the numbers on the other side.
  4. Divide by the coefficient of x. Leave the answer as a fraction or exact decimal unless told otherwise.

Worked example: solve 4(x − 2) = 7x + 13

4x − 8 = 7x + 13   (M1: brackets expanded correctly)

−8 − 13 = 7x − 4x   →   −21 = 3x   (M1: x-terms on one side, numbers on the other)

x = −7   (A1)

Check: 4(−7 − 2) = −36 and 7(−7) + 13 = −36. ✓

✗ 3(x − 4) − 2(x − 5) → 3x − 12 − 2x − 10. The second bracket has a −2 in front, so −2 × −5 = +10.
✗ 3x = 12 → x = 36, or x = 12 − 3. Dividing is the only move that undoes "3 times".
✓ 3x − 12 − 2x + 10 = x − 2.

subsections.heading: Equations with fractions, and forming equations
subsections.html:
Spec 2.4A, 2.4B · 2017 Edexcel Jan 3HR Q16(a) (old spec)

Multiply every term, on both sides, by the lowest common denominator. Then the fractions disappear and it is an ordinary linear equation.

  1. Find the LCD of all the denominators.
  2. Multiply every term by it, including any term with no fraction. Put each numerator in a bracket first.
  3. Expand, collect and solve as before.

Worked example: solve (2x + 1)/3 − (x − 2)/4 = 2

LCD = 12.   4(2x + 1) − 3(x − 2) = 24   (M1: all three terms multiplied by 12)

8x + 4 − 3x + 6 = 24   (M1: brackets expanded, sign on the +6 correct)

5x = 14   →   x = 2.8   (A1)

Forming an equation. Turn the words into algebra, then solve. For example, the angles of a triangle are a°, (a + 10)° and (a + 20)°, so a + a + 10 + a + 20 = 180, 3a = 150 and a = 50.

✗ Multiplying only the fractions by 12 and leaving the "= 2" alone. The 2 must become 24.
✗ 4(2x + 1) − 3x − 2. Without the bracket the −3 only hits the x, so the sign of the −2 is wrong.
✓ Bracket every numerator before you multiply out.

subsections.heading: Linear inequalities and the number line
subsections.html:
Spec 2.8 (Foundation A–C) · 2018 Edexcel May 2H Q1(b) · 2013 Edexcel Jan 3H Q7 (old spec)

Solve an inequality exactly like an equation, except that multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the inequality sign.

  1. Treat the inequality sign like an equals sign: add, subtract, multiply and divide both sides.
  2. If you multiply or divide by a negative, flip the sign. Or avoid it by moving the x-term to the other side.
  3. For a double inequality, such as −3 < 2x + 1 ≤ 9, do the same thing to all three parts.
  4. On a number line, use an open circle for < or > and a filled circle for ≤ or ≥.

Worked example: solve −3 < 2x + 1 ≤ 9 and list the integers

Subtract 1 from all three parts: −4 < 2x ≤ 8   (M1)

Divide all three parts by 2: −2 < x ≤ 4   (A1)

Integers: −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. −2 is not included (strict <); 4 is included (≤)   (B1)

Worked example: solve 7 − 3x ≥ 19

−3x ≥ 12. Divide by −3 and flip: x ≤ −4.

Or avoid the negative: 7 − 19 ≥ 3x, so −12 ≥ 3x, so −4 ≥ x, which is the same as x ≤ −4.

✗ −3x ≥ 12 → x ≥ −4. The sign did not flip. Test x = 0: 7 − 0 ≥ 19 is false, so x ≥ −4 cannot be right.
✗ Writing "x = 3" as the answer to an inequality. The answer is a range, with an inequality sign in it.
✓ Test one value from your answer in the original inequality before moving on.

subsections.heading: Simultaneous linear equations by elimination
subsections.html:
Spec 2.6A · 2018 Edexcel May 2H Q9 · 2016 Edexcel SAM 2H Q9

Make the coefficients of one letter the same size, then add or subtract the equations so that letter disappears.

  1. Multiply one or both equations so that x (or y) has the same coefficient in each.
  2. Same signs, subtract. Different signs, add.
  3. Solve the equation in one letter.
  4. Substitute back into an original equation to find the other letter.
  5. Check both values in the other original equation.

Worked example: 3x + 2y = 16 and 5x − 3y = 14

× 3 and × 2:   9x + 6y = 48   and   10x − 6y = 28   (M1: coefficients of y matched)

The y-signs are different, so add: 19x = 76, so x = 4   (M1: correct operation to eliminate y)

3(4) + 2y = 16, so 2y = 4, so y = 2.   x = 4, y = 2   (A1)

Check in the second equation: 5(4) − 3(2) = 14. ✓

If one equation is already "y = …" or "x = …", substitution is quicker. Put that expression into the other equation.

✗ 9x + 6y = 48 and 10x − 6y = 28, subtracted: −x + 12y = 20. That removes nothing.
✗ Multiplying only the left-hand side: 3x + 2y = 16 becomes 9x + 6y = 16.
✓ Multiply every term, including the right-hand side. Add when the signs are different.

subsections.heading: Simultaneous equations as intersecting lines
subsections.html:
Spec 2.6B · 2018 Edexcel May 1H Q12(a)

The solution of two simultaneous equations is the point where their graphs cross.

Every point on a line satisfies that line's equation. The crossing point lies on both lines, so it satisfies both equations at once. In 2018 1H Q12(a) the lines 3y = 2x + 6 and 4x + 3y = 24 crossed at (3, 4), so the answer was x = 3, y = 4, read straight off the grid for 1 mark.

  • Parallel lines never meet, so their equations have no solution.
  • A reading off a graph is an estimate. If the question says "show clear algebraic working", a graphical answer scores nothing.

subsections.heading: Quadratic equations by factorising
subsections.html:
Spec 2.7A · 2018 Edexcel May 1H Q3(d) · 2016 Edexcel SAM 1H Q6(b)

Rearrange to "= 0", factorise, then set each bracket equal to zero. If two numbers multiply to give 0, one of them must be 0.

  1. Rearrange so that one side is 0: ax2 + bx + c = 0.
  2. Factorise. For x2 + bx + c, find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b. For ax2 + bx + c, find two numbers that multiply to ac and add to b, then split the middle term.
  3. Set each bracket = 0 and solve. There are usually two answers.

Worked example: solve 2x2 + 5x − 12 = 0

ac = 2 × −12 = −24. Two numbers that multiply to −24 and add to 5: 8 and −3.

2x2 + 8x − 3x − 12 = 2x(x + 4) − 3(x + 4) = (2x − 3)(x + 4)   (M1: correct factors)

2x − 3 = 0 or x + 4 = 0   →   x = 1.5 or x = −4   (A1)

Special cases: x2 − 25 = 0 is a difference of two squares, (x − 5)(x + 5) = 0, so x = ±5. For x2 = 7x, rearrange to x2 − 7x = 0, so x(x − 7) = 0, giving x = 0 or x = 7.

✗ (x − 4)(x + 6) = 0 → x = −4 or x = 6. The signs flip: x − 4 = 0 gives x = +4.
✗ x2 = 7x → divide by x → x = 7. Dividing by x throws away the solution x = 0.
✓ Always rearrange to "= 0" and factorise. Never divide by x.

subsections.heading: The quadratic formula
subsections.html:
Spec 2.7B · 2018 Edexcel May 1H Q11(b) · 2015 Edexcel Jan 4HR Q14 (old spec)

The formula solves every quadratic, factorisable or not. Use it whenever the question asks for decimals or significant figures.

The quadratic formula — on the formula sheetx = (−b ± √(b2 − 4ac)) ÷ 2asolves ax2 + bx + c = 0 (a ≠ 0) · the whole of −b ± √… is divided by 2a
  1. Rearrange to ax2 + bx + c = 0 and write down a, b and c with their signs.
  2. Substitute in full and write it down. That line is the M marks.
  3. Work out b2 − 4ac first, then the two answers: one with +, one with −.
  4. Round at the end, to the accuracy asked.

Worked example: solve 2x2 − 7x + 2 = 0, giving answers to 3 s.f.

a = 2, b = −7, c = 2

x = (7 ± √((−7)2 − 4 × 2 × 2)) ÷ (2 × 2) = (7 ± √33) ÷ 4   (M1: correct substitution · M1: √33 correctly evaluated)

x = (7 + 5.7445…) ÷ 4 = 3.186…   or   x = (7 − 5.7445…) ÷ 4 = 0.3138…

x = 3.19 or x = 0.314   (A1)

✗ b = 7 when the equation says −7x. Then −b is wrong and so is everything after it.
✗ −72 typed into a calculator gives −49. Type (−7)2 = 49.
✗ 7 ± √33 ÷ 4, where only the root is divided by 4. The whole numerator goes over 2a.
✓ Write the substitution with brackets round every negative number.

equations.name: The quadratic formula — on the formula sheet

subsections.heading: Completing the square and the turning point
subsections.html:
Spec 2.2D, 2.7B · 2016 Edexcel SAM 2H Q22 · 2018 Edexcel May 2H Q21(c)

Halve the coefficient of x to make the bracket, then subtract the square of that half to put the expression back as it was.

Completing the square — memorisex2 + bx + c = (x + b/2)2 − (b/2)2 + cb/2 = half the x-coefficient · the turning point of y = (x + p)2 + q is (−p, q)
  1. If the x2 term has a coefficient a ≠ 1, take a out of the x2 and x terms first: a(x2 + (b/a)x) + c.
  2. Write (x + half)2 and subtract half2.
  3. Tidy the numbers. If you took a out, multiply the subtracted square by a.
  4. To solve: make the bracket the subject, square-root (±), then isolate x.
  5. Turning point of y = a(x + p)2 + q is (−p, q): a minimum if a > 0, a maximum if a < 0.

Worked example: x2 + 6x − 5

Half of 6 is 3: (x + 3)2 − 9 − 5 = (x + 3)2 − 14   (M1: (x + 3)2 seen · A1)

Solve x2 + 6x − 5 = 0: (x + 3)2 = 14, so x + 3 = ±√14, so x = −3 ± √14 (0.742 or −6.74).

Turning point of y = x2 + 6x − 5: the bracket is 0 when x = −3, and then y = −14. Minimum at (−3, −14).

Worked example: 2x2 − 12x + 7 in the form a(x + b)2 + c

2(x2 − 6x) + 7   (M1: 2 taken out of the first two terms)

2[(x − 3)2 − 9] + 7 = 2(x − 3)2 − 18 + 7   (M1)

= 2(x − 3)2 − 11, so a = 2, b = −3, c = −11   (A1)

SAM 2H Q22(b) asked why y = 2x2 − 8x + 9 never meets the x-axis. 2x2 − 8x + 9 = 2(x − 2)2 + 1. A square is never negative, so y ≥ 1: the minimum point (2, 1) is above the x-axis.

✗ 2(x − 3)2 − 9 + 7. The −9 is inside the bracket that is multiplied by 2, so it becomes −18.
✗ Turning point of (x + 3)2 − 14 is (3, −14). The x-coordinate is the value that makes the bracket zero: −3.
✓ Expand your answer back out to check it gives the original expression.

subsections.heading: Forming and solving quadratics from a context
subsections.html:
Spec 2.7C · 2016 Edexcel SAM 1H Q15 · 2018 Edexcel May 2H Q22

Write an expression for the quantity you are given (an area, a total, a product), set it equal to the value, rearrange to "= 0" and solve. Then check which answers make sense.

  1. Write the expression (for example, area = length × width) using the lengths in x.
  2. Set it equal to the given value and expand.
  3. Rearrange to ax2 + bx + c = 0. In a "show that", this line must match the question exactly.
  4. Solve, then reject any answer that gives a negative length, a negative number of people, and so on. Say why.
  5. Answer the question asked. It usually wants an area or a perimeter, not x.

Worked example: a rectangle is (x + 4) cm by (x − 1) cm, with area 36 cm². Find its perimeter.

(x + 4)(x − 1) = 36   →   x2 + 3x − 4 = 36   →   x2 + 3x − 40 = 0   (M1 · A1)

(x + 8)(x − 5) = 0   →   x = 5 or x = −8   (M1)

x = −8 gives a width of −9 cm, which is impossible, so x = 5   (A1)

Rectangle is 9 cm by 4 cm, so the perimeter is 2(9 + 4) = 26 cm   (M1 · A1)

✗ Stopping at "x = 5". The question asked for the perimeter.
✗ Keeping both roots. The SAM 1H Q15 scheme said "Ignore negative root". Reject it and say why.

subsections.heading: Simultaneous equations: one linear, one quadratic
subsections.html:
Spec 2.7D · 2014 Edexcel Jan 4H Q22 · 2013 Edexcel Jan 4H Q26 (old spec)

Rearrange the linear equation to make one letter the subject, substitute it into the quadratic, and solve the resulting quadratic. There are usually two pairs of answers.

  1. Make y (or x) the subject of the linear equation.
  2. Substitute into the quadratic one, using brackets: (2x − 1)2, not 2x − 12.
  3. Expand and simplify to a 3-term quadratic = 0. Divide through by a common factor if there is one.
  4. Solve (factorise or formula).
  5. Put each x into the linear equation to get its partner y. Give the answers as pairs.

Worked example: y = x + 1 and x2 + y2 = 13

x2 + (x + 1)2 = 13   (M1: substitution)

x2 + x2 + 2x + 1 = 13   →   2x2 + 2x − 12 = 0   →   x2 + x − 6 = 0   (M1: 3-term quadratic)

(x + 3)(x − 2) = 0   →   x = −3 or x = 2   (M1 · A1)

y = x + 1:   x = 2, y = 3 and x = −3, y = −2   (A1)

Geometrically, this finds where a straight line crosses a circle (x2 + y2 = 13 is a circle, centre O, radius √13) or a curve. Two points of intersection give two pairs.

✗ (x + 1)2 = x2 + 1. The middle term, 2x, is missing. Write (x + 1)(x + 1) if you need to.
✗ Pairing the answers wrongly: x = 2 with y = −2. Each x gives its own y.
✓ Substitute each pair back into the quadratic equation as a check: 22 + 32 = 13 ✓.

subsections.heading: Quadratic inequalities
subsections.html:
Spec 2.8A · 2016 Edexcel Jan 3H Q16 (old spec) · 2018 Edexcel May 2H Q17(b)

Find the critical values by solving the equation, sketch the parabola, then read off where the graph is below (< 0) or above (> 0) the x-axis.

  1. Rearrange to quadratic < 0 (or > 0, ≤ 0, ≥ 0).
  2. Solve the equation = 0 to get the two critical values.
  3. Sketch the U-shaped curve (for a positive x2 term) through them.
  4. < 0: the part below the axis, which is between the roots, one inequality: p < x < q.
    > 0: the parts above, which are the two tails, written as two inequalities: x < p or x > q.

Worked example: solve x2 − x − 12 < 0

(x − 4)(x + 3) = 0 gives critical values −3 and 4   (M1 · A1)

U-shaped curve, below the axis between the roots: −3 < x < 4   (A1)

Worked example: solve 2x2 + 5x − 3 > 0

(2x − 1)(x + 3) = 0 gives critical values −3 and ½. Above the axis means the tails: x < −3 or x > ½.

Worked example: solve x2 ≥ 25

Critical values ±5. x2 − 25 ≥ 0 means the tails: x ≤ −5 or x ≥ 5.

✗ x2 < 16 → x < ±4, or x < 4. x = −10 satisfies x < 4 but (−10)2 = 100 is not less than 16.
✗ "−3 > x > 5" for the two tails. No number is both less than −3 and greater than 5.
✓ x2 < 16 → −4 < x < 4. The tails need two separate inequalities joined by "or".

subsections.heading: Regions defined by linear inequalities
subsections.html:
Spec 2.8 (Foundation D–E, Higher B) · 2018 Edexcel May 1H Q12(b) · 2016 Edexcel SAM 2H Q14

Draw each boundary line, then use a test point to decide which side of each line is wanted. The region is where every inequality is true at once.

  1. Draw each boundary as a straight line. For x + y = 7, the easy points are (0, 7) and (7, 0).
  2. For each line, test a point not on it, usually (0, 0). If it makes the inequality true, that side is wanted.
  3. Find the region that is on the correct side of every line. Shade it, or shade what is not wanted if the question says so, and label it R.
  4. y > … is above a line, y < … is below it, x > … is to the right, and x < … is to the left.

Worked example: y ≥ 2, y ≤ 2x + 1 and x + y ≤ 7

y ≥ 2: on or above the horizontal line y = 2. y ≤ 2x + 1: test (0, 0): 0 ≤ 1 is true, so the side containing O, below the line. x + y ≤ 7: test (0, 0): 0 ≤ 7 is true, so the side containing O.

The region is the triangle with vertices (0.5, 2), (5, 2) and (2, 5). Each vertex is where two boundary lines cross, for example 2x + 1 = 7 − x gives x = 2.

The spec says "conventions for the inclusion of boundaries are not required", so solid and dashed lines both score. The 2018 1H scheme accepted "May shade wanted or unwanted regions", provided the region is clear and labelled.

✗ Shading below y = 2x + 1 by eye without testing a point. For a steep line, "below" and "to the right" are easy to confuse.
✗ Forgetting to label R, which leaves the examiner guessing which region you meant.
✓ Tick each inequality against one point inside your region before you finish.

Methods and formulae to have ready

Linear: expand → x-terms one side → numbers the other → divide. Fractions: multiply every term by the LCD.

Inequality: as an equation, but × or ÷ by a negative flips the sign.

Simultaneous (linear): match coefficients; same signs subtract, different signs add; substitute back; check.

Quadratic: = 0 first. Factorise, or use x = (−b ± √(b2 − 4ac)) ÷ 2a (on the formula sheet), or complete the square.

Completing the square: x2 + bx + c = (x + b/2)2 − (b/2)2 + c. Turning point of y = a(x + p)2 + q is (−p, q).

Linear + quadratic: substitute the linear into the quadratic, solve, and pair each x with its own y.

Quadratic inequality: critical values, sketch. < 0 → between (p < x < q). > 0 → tails (x < p or x > q).

Regions: draw the lines, test (0, 0) for each, label R.
