questions.promptHtml: A student solves x2 = 6x by dividing both sides by x and gets x = 6. What has gone wrong?
questions.answerHtml:
Dividing by x is only allowed if x ≠ 0, and x = 0 is one of the solutions. 02 = 6 × 0 is true.

The safe method is to rearrange to x2 − 6x = 0, factorise to x(x − 6) = 0, and read off x = 0 or x = 6. A quadratic usually has two solutions. If you only find one, check how you lost the other.

questions.promptHtml: Why does multiplying an inequality by −1 reverse the sign? Use 2 < 5 to explain.
questions.answerHtml:
2 < 5 is true. Multiply both by −1: −2 and −5. On the number line, −2 is to the right of −5, so −2 > −5. The order has swapped.

Multiplying by a negative reflects every number in 0, so the larger one becomes the smaller one. That is why the sign must flip. You can avoid it altogether by moving the x-term to the side where it will be positive.

questions.promptHtml: Why does x2 < 9 give −3 < x < 3, but x2 > 9 give x < −3 or x > 3?
questions.answerHtml:
Sketch y = x2 − 9. It is a U-shape crossing the x-axis at −3 and 3.

x2 − 9 < 0 means the curve is below the axis. That happens only between the roots, so it is one joined-up range.

x2 − 9 > 0 means above the axis, which happens on both outer sides. These are two separate pieces, so there are two inequalities joined by "or". Test x = −10: 100 > 9 is true, so the left-hand tail really is included.

questions.promptHtml: How can you tell quickly whether a quadratic will factorise, and what does the formula do when b2 − 4ac is negative?
questions.answerHtml:
Work out b2 − 4ac. If it is a perfect square (0, 1, 4, 9, 16, …), the roots are rational and the quadratic factorises. If not (e.g. 33), the roots involve a surd, so use the formula or complete the square.

If b2 − 4ac is negative, there is no real square root, so the equation has no real solutions. The graph of y = ax2 + bx + c does not cross the x-axis.

questions.promptHtml: Why does writing y = (x − 2)2 + 5 tell you straight away that the minimum point is (2, 5)?
questions.answerHtml:
(x − 2)2 is a square, so it is never negative. Its smallest possible value is 0, when x = 2.

So the smallest y can be is 0 + 5 = 5, when x = 2. Every other x adds something positive. That is the minimum point: (2, 5). If there is a negative multiplier in front, −(x − 2)2 + 5, the square is subtracted, so (2, 5) becomes a maximum.

questions.promptHtml: In linear-with-quadratic simultaneous equations, why do you substitute the linear equation into the quadratic, and not the other way round? Why must you find y from the linear equation afterwards?
questions.answerHtml:
The linear equation is easy to rearrange to "y = …" with no square roots. Rearranging x2 + y2 = 13 would give y = ±√(13 − x2), which is messy and loses solutions.

Afterwards, each x must be paired with the correct y. If you put x into the quadratic, you get two y-values for each x (±), and only one of them is on the line. The linear equation gives exactly one y, the right one.

questions.promptHtml: In the SAM lawn question, solving 6x2 + 7x − 98 = 0 gave x = 3.5 or x = −14/3. Why is only one answer used?
questions.answerHtml:
x was a length (the lawn was 3x by 2x metres). A negative x would give negative lengths, which cannot happen. The algebra does not know that. It solves the equation for every number.

So you reject x = −14/3, and say why in words, then use x = 3.5: the lawn is 10.5 m by 7 m, area 73.5 m².

questions.promptHtml: Two lines are drawn accurately and cross at about (1.4, 2.7). Why is that only an estimate, and when would the exam refuse to accept it?
questions.answerHtml:
The crossing point satisfies both equations, but reading it off a grid is limited by the drawing: a line drawn slightly thick, or a point read to the nearest small square. The exact answer might be (1.375, 2.75).

If the question says "Show clear algebraic working", you must solve algebraically. A graphical answer scores nothing there. Graphs are for "use the graph" questions, and to check an algebraic answer is sensible.

modules.title: Sequences and Arithmetic Series
modules.standfirst: A small topic that earns a lot of marks. There is an easy nth-term question near the start of a paper, and a 5-mark arithmetic-series question near the end. Both are pure method: one formula to memorise, one on the formula sheet, and a pair of simultaneous equations.

intel.html:
PaperWhat was asked
2016 Edexcel SAM 2H Q2 (2)The nth term of the arithmetic sequence 2, 9, 16, 23, …
2016 Edexcel SAM 1H Q23 (5)The 4th term is 17 and the 10th term is 35: find the sum of the first 50 terms
2018 Edexcel May 2H Q23 (5)The sum of the first 48 terms is 4 times the sum of the first 36: find the sum of the first 30 terms (the answer is 0)
2015 Edexcel Jan 4HR Q5 (3)A number pattern of rows 1 × 3 + 1, 4, 2²: which row has 676, and expressions in n for the columns (old spec)

Arithmetic series were added in the 4MA1 spec, so no old-spec paper asks for Sn. The same SAM 1H question was reused, word for word, as Q22 of the school's Practice Paper 5.

From the SAM 2H mark scheme, on the nth term of 2, 9, 16, 23:

"M1 for 7n + k (k may be zero)"

So "7n" on its own scores 1 mark out of 2. The second mark needs the right constant: 7n − 5. Check it with n = 1: 7 − 5 = 2. ✓

subsections.html: A sequence is a list of numbers that follow a rule. The rule can link each term to the one before (term-to-term) or give any term directly from its position (the nth term). An arithmetic sequence adds the same amount each time. That constant step is what makes a clean nth-term formula and a clean sum formula possible.

subsections.heading: Term-to-term rules
subsections.html:
Spec 3.1A, 3.1B (Foundation)

A term-to-term rule tells you how to get from one term to the next.

  1. Work out the differences between consecutive terms. If they are all the same, the rule is "add d".
  2. If not, try the ratio: does each term multiply by the same number?
  3. If neither works, look for special patterns: squares, cubes, powers, or adding the previous two terms.
SequenceRuleNext two terms
5, 9, 13, 17, …add 421, 25
20, 14, 8, 2, …subtract 6−4, −10
1, 2, 4, 8, …multiply by 2 (powers of 2)16, 32
1, 4, 9, 16, …square numbers (n2)25, 36
1, 1, 2, 3, 5, …add the previous two terms8, 13

✗ "The rule is +4" for 5, 9, 13, 17 when the question asks for the nth term. That is the term-to-term rule, and it scores nothing there.
✓ Read which one is asked for. "Rule for the next term" means term-to-term. "Expression in terms of n" means the nth term.

subsections.heading: Position-to-term rules: generating terms from the nth term
subsections.html:
Spec 3.1A (Foundation) · 2015 Edexcel Jan 4HR Q5 (old spec)

An nth-term rule gives any term directly: replace n with the position number.

  1. Substitute n = 1, 2, 3, … in turn.
  2. Use brackets for anything squared: for n = 3 in 2n2 − 1, 2 × 32 − 1 = 17, not (2 × 3)2 − 1.

Worked examples

4n + 3: n = 1, 2, 3 gives 7, 11, 15. The differences are all 4, the number in front of n.

n2 + 3: n = 1 to 5 gives 4, 7, 12, 19, 28. The differences are 3, 5, 7, 9, which are not constant, so this is not arithmetic.

The 2015 pattern: row n was n × (n + 2) + 1 = (n + 1)2. Column 2 held 4, 9, 16, … so 676 = 262 is in row 25.

subsections.heading: The nth term of a linear sequence
subsections.html:
Spec 3.1C · 2016 Edexcel SAM 2H Q2

The nth term of a sequence that goes up by d each time is dn + (first term − d).

  1. Find the common difference d. That is the number in front of n.
  2. Write out the d times table underneath the sequence and see what you must add or subtract to get each term. That is the constant.
  3. Write dn + constant, then check it with n = 1 and n = 2.

Worked example: 5, 8, 11, 14, …

Difference = +3, so compare with 3n: 3, 6, 9, 12. Each term is 2 more.   nth term = 3n + 2   (M1 for 3n + k · A1)

Check: n = 1 gives 5 ✓, n = 4 gives 14 ✓.

Worked example: 20, 14, 8, 2, … (decreasing)

Difference = −6, so compare with −6n: −6, −12, −18, −24. Each term is 26 more.   nth term = 26 − 6n

✗ n + 3 for 5, 8, 11, 14. That adds 1 each time, not 3.
✗ 6n + 26 for 20, 14, 8, 2. A decreasing sequence needs a negative coefficient of n.
✓ The coefficient of n is always the common difference, sign included.

subsections.heading: Using the nth term: is a number in the sequence?
subsections.html:
Spec 3.1C · 2015 Edexcel Jan 4HR Q5(a) (old spec)

Set the nth term equal to the number and solve for n. The number is in the sequence only if n comes out as a positive whole number.

  1. Write nth term = the number.
  2. Solve for n.
  3. If n is a positive integer, the number is term n. If not, it is not in the sequence. Say so, and give the reason.
  4. For "the first term greater than 200", solve as an inequality and round n up.

Worked example: is 100 a term of 3n + 2?

3n + 2 = 100, so 3n = 98, so n = 32.67 (to 2 d.p.). Not a whole number, so 100 is not in the sequence. It falls between term 32 (98) and term 33 (101).

Worked example: the first term of 8n − 3 that is greater than 200

8n − 3 > 200, so n > 25.375, so n = 26. The term is 8 × 26 − 3 = 205.

subsections.heading: Arithmetic sequences: a, d and the nth term
subsections.html:
Spec 3.1A, 3.1B (Higher)

In an arithmetic sequence the first term is a and each step adds d, so the nth term has had (n − 1) steps added.

nth term of an arithmetic sequence — memoriseun = a + (n − 1)da = first term · d = common difference · n = position · NOT on the formula sheet

It is the same rule as dn + (a − d), just written a different way: a + (n − 1)d = dn + (a − d). For 5, 8, 11, … it gives 5 + 3(n − 1) = 3n + 2.

d can be negative (a decreasing sequence) or a fraction. The 20th term of 7, 4.5, 2, … is 7 + 19 × (−2.5) = −40.5.

✗ u20 = a + 20d. To get from term 1 to term 20 you take 19 steps.
✓ u20 = a + 19d.

equations.name: nth term of an arithmetic sequence

subsections.heading: Finding a and d from two terms
subsections.html:
Spec 3.1A (Higher) · 2016 Edexcel SAM 1H Q23

Each term you are given makes one equation in a and d. Two terms give a pair of simultaneous equations.

  1. Write each given term as a + (n − 1)d = its value.
  2. Subtract the equations: the a's cancel and leave a multiple of d.
  3. Find d, then substitute back to find a.

Worked example: the 2nd term is 7 and the 5th term is 19

a + d = 7 and a + 4d = 19   (M1)

Subtract: 3d = 12, so d = 4   (A1). Then a = 7 − 4 = 3   (A1)

The sequence is 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, … ✓

Shortcut: from the 2nd term to the 5th is 3 steps, and the value rises by 12, so d = 12 ÷ 3. In SAM 1H Q23, the 4th term is 17 and the 10th is 35: 6 steps, a rise of 18, so d = 3 and a = 17 − 3 × 3 = 8.

subsections.heading: The sum of an arithmetic series
subsections.html:
Spec 3.1C (Higher) · 2016 Edexcel SAM 1H Q23 · 2018 Edexcel May 2H Q23

A series is the terms of a sequence added together. For an arithmetic series there is a formula for the sum of the first n terms, and it is on the formula sheet.

Sum of an arithmetic series — on the formula sheetSn = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d]Sn = sum of the first n terms · a = first term · d = common difference
Sum using the last term — memoriseSn = n/2 (a + l)l = the last term added · useful when you know where the series ends
  1. Identify a, d and n (the number of terms, not the last term).
  2. Substitute and write the substitution down: that line is the method mark.
  3. Work out the square bracket first, then multiply by n/2.

Worked example: the sum of the first 50 terms of 4 + 7 + 10 + 13 + …

a = 4, d = 3, n = 50

S50 = 50/2 [2 × 4 + 49 × 3] = 25 × [8 + 147] = 25 × 155 = 3875   (M1 · A1)

Worked example: SAM 1H Q23 finished

a = 8, d = 3:   S50 = 25 × [16 + 49 × 3] = 25 × 163 = 4075

Or: the 50th term is 8 + 49 × 3 = 155, so S50 = 25 × (8 + 155) = 4075.

✗ Putting the last term in as n. n is how many terms there are.
✗ n/2 × 2a + (n − 1)d, with the bracket missing, so only 2a gets multiplied by n/2.
✓ Brackets exactly as on the formula sheet, and the square bracket worked out first.

equations.name: Sum of an arithmetic series — on the formula sheet

subsections.heading: Sums of multiples, and sums between two limits
subsections.html:
Spec 3.1C (Higher)

To add up a run of terms, first find how many there are, then use Sn = n/2 (a + l).

  1. Find the first and last terms in the range.
  2. Number of terms n = (last − first) ÷ d + 1. The "+ 1" counts the first term.
  3. S = n/2 × (first + last).

Worked example: the sum of all the multiples of 7 between 100 and 300

First multiple: 105 (7 × 15). Last: 294 (7 × 42).

n = (294 − 105) ÷ 7 + 1 = 27 + 1 = 28 terms

S = 28/2 × (105 + 294) = 14 × 399 = 5586

✗ n = (294 − 105) ÷ 7 = 27. That counts the gaps, not the terms, and loses one.
✓ Check with a small case: from 7 to 21 in 7s is (21 − 7) ÷ 7 + 1 = 3 terms: 7, 14, 21.

subsections.heading: Finding n when the sum is given
subsections.html:
Spec 3.1C (Higher), with 2.7C

If Sn is known and n is not, the formula becomes a quadratic in n. Solve it, and keep only the positive whole-number answer.

  1. Substitute a and d into Sn = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d], leaving n as a letter.
  2. Set it equal to the given sum, multiply out and rearrange to = 0.
  3. Solve the quadratic (factorise or use the formula).
  4. Reject a negative or fractional n. For "how many terms before the sum first exceeds …", round up.

Worked example: how many terms of 3 + 7 + 11 + … add up to 210?

n/2 [6 + 4(n − 1)] = n/2 (4n + 2) = n(2n + 1) = 2n2 + n   (M1)

2n2 + n = 210, so 2n2 + n − 210 = 0   (A1)

(2n + 21)(n − 10) = 0, so n = 10 or n = −10.5   (M1)

n must be a positive whole number, so n = 10   (A1). Check: S10 = 5 × (6 + 36) = 210 ✓

subsections.heading: Harder problems: when a and d are both unknown
subsections.html:
Spec 3.1 (Higher) · 2018 Edexcel May 2H Q23

Turn each piece of information into an equation in a and d, then solve them together, exactly as with any simultaneous equations.

  1. A term gives a + (n − 1)d = value. A sum gives n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d] = value.
  2. Simplify each equation: divide out common factors.
  3. Solve simultaneously, then answer the actual question, which is often a different sum.

Worked example: the 5th term is 14 and the sum of the first 10 terms is 155

a + 4d = 14   and   10/2 [2a + 9d] = 155, so 2a + 9d = 31

Double the first: 2a + 8d = 28. Subtract: d = 3, then a = 14 − 12 = 2.

How 2018 2H Q23 worked: S48 = 4 × S36, find S30

24(2a + 47d) = 4 × 18(2a + 35d) = 72(2a + 35d)

48a + 1128d = 144a + 2520d, so 96a + 1392d = 0, so 2a + 29d = 0 (÷ 48)

S30 = 15(2a + 29d) = 15 × 0 = 0. You never need a and d separately. The positive and negative terms cancel.

✗ Giving up because there are "two unknowns and one equation". Look at what is asked. S30 needed only the combination 2a + 29d.
✓ Write S30 = 15(2a + 29d) early, and look for that bracket in your working.

subsections.heading: Sequences in context
subsections.html:
Spec 3.1C, 3.1B (Higher)

A pattern that grows by the same amount each time is an arithmetic sequence. Decide what a, d and n mean in the story before you use a formula.

  • "How many in pattern/row/week n?" That is a term: un = a + (n − 1)d.
  • "How many altogether in the first n?" That is a sum: Sn.

Worked example: a theatre has 20 seats in row 1, and each row has 2 more seats than the row in front. There are 25 rows.

Row 25: 20 + 24 × 2 = 68 seats (a term)

Total: S25 = 25/2 × (20 + 68) = 12.5 × 88 = 1100 seats (a sum)

subsections.heading: Sequences that are not arithmetic
subsections.html:
Spec 3.1A (Foundation): odd, even, squares, multiples and powers

If the differences are not constant, the sequence is not arithmetic, so neither a + (n − 1)d nor Sn applies.

  • Squares 1, 4, 9, 16, … have nth term n2. Anything like n2 + 3 or (n + 1)2 is a square pattern shifted.
  • Powers such as 2, 4, 8, 16, … (nth term 2n) multiply by the same number each time.
  • Odd numbers are 2n − 1, even numbers are 2n, and multiples of k are kn.

4MA1 asks you to generate terms from rules like these and to recognise them. It does not ask you to find the nth term of a quadratic sequence, or to sum a geometric series. Those belong to other courses.

✗ Using Sn = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d] to add up 1 + 4 + 9 + 16 + …. The formula only works when the differences are constant.
✓ Check the differences before you reach for a formula.

What to write down

Linear nth term: dn + (first term − d). Check with n = 1.

Arithmetic nth term (memorise): un = a + (n − 1)d

Sum (formula sheet): Sn = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d]   or   Sn = n/2 (a + l)

Two terms given: two equations in a and d, then subtract.

Is x a term? nth term = x. It is a term only if n is a positive integer.

Number of terms from first to last: (last − first) ÷ d + 1

Sum given, n unknown: quadratic in n; keep the positive whole number.

subsections.heading: Definitions marked to the word
subsections.html:
TermAccepted wording
SequenceAn ordered list of numbers that follow a rule
Term-to-term ruleThe rule that gives each term from the previous term
nth termA position-to-term rule: an expression in n that gives the term in position n
Arithmetic sequenceA sequence with a constant difference between consecutive terms
Common difference, dThe amount added each time. It is negative for a decreasing sequence
SeriesThe sum of the terms of a sequence
SnThe sum of the first n terms

questions.promptHtml: Why is the number in front of n in a linear nth term always the common difference?
questions.answerHtml:
Each time n goes up by 1, dn goes up by exactly d, and the constant stays the same. So consecutive terms differ by d.

That is why you can read d straight off the sequence, and why a decreasing sequence must have a negative coefficient: 26 − 6n drops by 6 each time.

questions.promptHtml: Why is the formula un = a + (n − 1)d and not a + nd?
questions.answerHtml:
The first term is a itself, with no steps added. The 2nd term has 1 step, the 3rd has 2, and so the nth has (n − 1) steps.

A quick check: n = 1 must give a. a + (1 − 1)d = a ✓, but a + 1d would already be the 2nd term.

questions.promptHtml: The nth term is 5n − 3. Explain how you know that 72 is a term but 75 is not.
questions.answerHtml:
5n − 3 = 72 gives 5n = 75, so n = 15, a whole number. So 72 is the 15th term.

5n − 3 = 75 gives 5n = 78, so n = 15.6. There is no "15.6th term", so 75 is not in the sequence. Every term is 3 less than a multiple of 5, so ends in 2 or 7, and 75 does not.

questions.promptHtml: Why does Sn = n/2 (a + l) work? Use 1 + 2 + 3 + … + 100.
questions.answerHtml:
Pair the first and last terms: 1 + 100 = 101. The second and second-last: 2 + 99 = 101. Every pair adds to the same total, a + l, because as one term goes up by d the other goes down by d.

There are 100 terms, so 50 pairs: 50 × 101 = 5050. In general, n/2 pairs, each worth (a + l). The formula-sheet version is the same thing with l = a + (n − 1)d put in.

questions.promptHtml: Why does "find n when Sn is given" always lead to a quadratic, and why do you throw one answer away?
questions.answerHtml:
Sn = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d] has n outside the bracket and n inside it. Multiplying out gives an n2 term, so it is a quadratic.

The algebra gives two roots, but n counts terms, so it must be a positive whole number. A negative or fractional root has no meaning and is rejected, with a reason.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between an arithmetic sequence and an arithmetic series? Give an example of each.
questions.answerHtml:
A sequence is the list: 4, 7, 10, 13, …. Questions about it ask for a term, or the nth term.

A series is the terms added: 4 + 7 + 10 + 13 + …. Questions about it ask for a sum, Sn. If a question says "series", expect to use the formula-sheet sum.

questions.promptHtml: A student says the nth term of 4, 7, 12, 19, 28 is 3n + 1, because it "starts by going up in 3". What is wrong?
questions.answerHtml:
The differences are 3, 5, 7, 9. They are not constant, so it is not an arithmetic sequence and no rule of the form dn + c can fit it. 3n + 1 gives 4, 7, 10, and the third term is already wrong.

It is n2 + 3. Always look at more than one difference. On 4MA1 you would be given this rule and asked to use it, not to find it.

questions.promptHtml: In 2018 2H Q23 the sum of the first 30 terms was 0. How can a sum of 30 terms be zero?
questions.answerHtml:
The terms can be negative. 2a + 29d = 0 means a = −14.5d, so if d = 1 the series is −14.5 − 13.5 − … + 13.5 + 14.5. The first term and the 30th cancel, as do the 2nd and 29th, and so on.

In the pairing picture, a + l = 0, so every pair adds to zero, and n/2 × (a + l) = 0.

questions.answerHtml: B1 for 19 and 23 1; B1 for "add 4" 1

modules.title: Functions and Graphs
modules.standfirst: The widest algebra topic on the course, and one of the best-paying. There is a function question (f(3), fg, f−1, the excluded value) on almost every Higher paper, plus a straight-line or perpendicular-line question, a graph to read or draw, and a transformation. Most of it is a handful of routines, done carefully.

subsections.html: A function is a machine: put x in, get f(x) out. Its graph plots every input against its output. Most of this module is reading that idea both ways. Algebra about f turns into a picture, and a picture turns into algebra: a crossing point is a solution, a gradient is a rate, and a shifted curve is a changed formula.

subsections.heading: Function notation
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2A, 3.2B · 2018 Edexcel May 1H Q14(a) · 2016 Edexcel SAM 2H Q17(a)

f(x) = … is a rule. f(a) means "put a in place of every x". f : x ↦ 3x2 − 2 is the same function written another way.

  1. For f(number): substitute, with brackets round negatives, and evaluate.
  2. For "solve f(x) = k": set the expression equal to k and solve the equation.
  3. For f(expression), such as f(2x) or f(x + 1): replace every x with the whole expression, in brackets.

Worked example: f(x) = 3x2 − 2

f(−2) = 3(−2)2 − 2 = 12 − 2 = 10

Solve f(x) = 25: 3x2 − 2 = 25, so x2 = 9, so x = 3 or x = −3

f(x + 1) = 3(x + 1)2 − 2 = 3x2 + 6x + 1

✗ f(−2) = 3 × −22 − 2 = −14. On a calculator, −22 is −4. Use (−2)2.
✗ f(x + 1) = 3x2 − 2 + 1. That is f(x) + 1, a different thing.

subsections.heading: Domain, range and excluded values
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2C · 2018 Edexcel May 1H Q14(d) · 2016 Edexcel SAM 2H Q17(b) · 2016 Edexcel Jan 3HR Q16 (old spec)

The domain is the set of inputs allowed. The range is the set of outputs produced. An input must be excluded if it would make you divide by zero or take the square root of a negative number.

  1. Fraction: set the denominator = 0 and solve. That x is excluded.
  2. Square root: the expression under the root must be ≥ 0. Solve the inequality. The values that break it are excluded.
  3. Range: think about which outputs are possible. x2 is never negative, and a fraction like 2x/(x − 1) never equals its "long-run" value.

Worked examples

f(x) = 3/(x − 2): x − 2 = 0, so x = 2 is excluded (SAM 2H Q17(b)).

g(x) = √(19 − x): need 19 − x ≥ 0, so x ≤ 19. The values that cannot be in any domain are x > 19 (2018 1H Q14(d)).

f(x) = x2 + 3: every output is at least 3, so the range is f(x) ≥ 3.

f(x) = 2x/(x − 1): x = 1 is excluded. Its inverse is x/(x − 2), which has 2 excluded, so 2 cannot be in the range of f (2016 Jan 3HR Q16(d)).

✗ "x = 19 is excluded" for √(19 − x). √0 = 0 is fine. It is x greater than 19 that fails.
✗ "x = −2 is excluded" for 3/(x − 2). Solve x − 2 = 0: x = +2.

subsections.heading: Composite functions: fg(x)
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2D · 2018 Edexcel May 1H Q14(c) · 2016 Edexcel SAM 2H Q17(c) · 2014 Edexcel Jan 3H Q20 (old spec)

fg(x) means f(g(x)): do g first, then put the answer into f. The function nearest the x acts first.

  1. For fg(number): work out g(number), then put that value into f.
  2. For fg(x): write f( … ) with the whole of g(x) inside, in brackets, wherever f has an x.
  3. Simplify: expand and collect.

Worked example: f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x2

fg(3) = f(9) = 19.   gf(3) = g(7) = 49. The order matters.

fg(x) = f(x2) = 2x2 + 1.   gf(x) = g(2x + 1) = (2x + 1)2 = 4x2 + 4x + 1

2018 1H Q14(c): f(x) = (3x − 5)/4 and g(x) = √(19 − x). Find fg(3).

g(3) = √16 = 4   (M1). f(4) = (12 − 5)/4 = 1.75   (A1)

✗ fg(3) worked out as g(f(3)). Read fg from the right: g is next to the x, so it goes first.
✗ fg(x) = f(x) × g(x). fg is a function of a function, not a product.

subsections.heading: Inverse functions: f−1(x)
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2D · 2018 Edexcel May 1H Q14(b) · 2016 Edexcel Jan 3HR Q16(c) (old spec)

The inverse function undoes f: if f turns 3 into 1, f−1 turns 1 back into 3. To find it, write y = f(x) and rearrange to make x the subject.

  1. Write y = f(x).
  2. Rearrange to make x the subject.
  3. Swap the letters: replace y with x and write f−1(x) = ….
  4. Check: put a number through f, then through f−1. You should get your number back.

Worked example: f(x) = (3x − 5)/4 (2018 1H Q14(b))

y = (3x − 5)/4 → 4y = 3x − 5 → 4y + 5 = 3x → x = (4y + 5)/3   (M1: correct first two steps)

f−1(x) = (4x + 5)/3   (A1)

Check: f(5) = 2.5 and f−1(2.5) = (10 + 5)/3 = 5 ✓

Worked example: f(x) = 2x/(x − 1), where x appears twice

y(x − 1) = 2x → xy − y = 2x → xy − 2x = y → x(y − 2) = y → x = y/(y − 2)

f−1(x) = x/(x − 2). Collect the x-terms on one side and factorise x out.

✗ f−1(x) = 4/(3x − 5), the reciprocal. f−1 is the inverse, not 1 ÷ f.
✗ Reversing the operations but not their order. For "× 3, then − 5, then ÷ 4", the inverse is "× 4, then + 5, then ÷ 3".

subsections.heading: Straight lines: gradient, y = mx + c, midpoint and length
subsections.html:
Spec 3.3 (Foundation E, G, H; Higher F) · 2016 Edexcel SAM 1H Q13(a) · 2013 Edexcel Jan 3H Q10 (old spec)

In y = mx + c, m is the gradient (the rise for each 1 across) and c is where the line crosses the y-axis. Two points fix a line.

Gradient between two points — memorisem = (y2 − y1) ÷ (x2 − x1)change in y ÷ change in x · keep the points in the same order top and bottom
Midpoint of a line segment — memoriseM = ((x1 + x2)/2, (y1 + y2)/2)the mean of the x-coordinates and the mean of the y-coordinates
Length of a line segment — memorised = √((x2 − x1)2 + (y2 − y1)2)Pythagoras on the horizontal and vertical steps
  1. Gradient from the two points.
  2. Find c: substitute one point into y = mx + c and solve. Or use y − y1 = m(x − x1).
  3. Rearrange to the form asked, e.g. ax + by = c with integers. Multiply through to clear fractions.
  4. To read m and c off an equation like 4x + 3y = 12, first rearrange to y = −(4/3)x + 4.

Worked example: SAM 1H Q13(a), the line through (−3, 5) and (1, 2), as ax + by = c

m = (2 − 5) ÷ (1 − (−3)) = −3/4   (M1)

2 = −¾(1) + c, so c = 11/4   (M1). y = −¾x + 11/4   (M1)

× 4: 4y = −3x + 11, so 3x + 4y = 11   (A1)

Worked example: A(2, −1) and B(8, 7)

Midpoint: ((2 + 8)/2, (−1 + 7)/2) = (5, 3). Gradient: 8/6 = 4/3. Length: √(62 + 82) = √100 = 10.

✗ Gradient = change in x ÷ change in y. It is up over across: change in y on top.
✗ For 2y = 6x + 5, "the gradient is 6". Divide by 2 first: y = 3x + 2.5, so m = 3.

subsections.heading: Parallel and perpendicular lines
subsections.html:
Spec 3.3G (Higher) · 2018 Edexcel May 1H Q20 · 2016 Edexcel SAM 1H Q13(b) · 2016 Edexcel Jan 4H Q12 (old spec)

Parallel lines have equal gradients. Perpendicular gradients multiply to −1: flip the fraction and change the sign.

Perpendicular gradients — memorisem1 × m2 = −1m2 = −1/m1 · e.g. 2/3 → −3/2 · parallel lines: m1 = m2
  1. Get the given line into y = mx + c form and read off m.
  2. Parallel: same m. Perpendicular: −1/m.
  3. Substitute the given point to find c.
  4. To show two lines are perpendicular, find both gradients and show that their product is −1.

Worked example: 2018 1H Q20, the line through (4, 37) perpendicular to 3y = 2x + 12

y = (2/3)x + 4, so the gradient is 2/3   (M1). Perpendicular gradient: −3/2   (M1)

37 = −3/2 × 4 + c, so c = 43   (M1). y = −(3/2)x + 43   (A1)

× 2: 3x + 2y = 86   (A1: integer coefficients, as asked)

SAM 1H Q13(b): show that y = 3x + 5 and 6y + 2x = 1 are perpendicular

6y = 1 − 2x, so y = 1/6 − (1/3)x, and the gradient is −1/3.   3 × (−1/3) = −1, so the lines are perpendicular. ✓

✗ Perpendicular to gradient 2/3 is −2/3, or 3/2. You need both steps: flip and change the sign, giving −3/2.
✗ Using the gradient of 3y = 2x + 12 as 2. Divide by 3 first.

subsections.heading: Recognising the shapes of graphs
subsections.html:
Spec 3.3A (Higher), 3.3I (Foundation) · 2016 Edexcel SAM 2H Q19

Each family of equation has a characteristic shape, and the sign of the leading term tells you which way round it goes.

EquationShapeTell-tale features
y = mx + cStraight linem > 0 goes up to the right; m < 0 goes down
y = ax2 + bx + cParabolaa > 0: U-shape (minimum); a < 0: ∩-shape (maximum); crosses the y-axis at c
y = ax3 + …Cubic: an S-shapea > 0: rises from bottom-left to top-right; up to two turning points
y = k/xReciprocal: two separate branchesNever touches either axis; k > 0 in the 1st and 3rd quadrants
y = sin x, y = cos xWave between −1 and 1Repeats every 360°; sin starts at 0, cos starts at 1
y = tan xRepeating branchesRepeats every 180°; undefined at 90°, 270°, …

To match an equation to a sketch, check three things: the shape family, the direction (sign of the leading term) and the y-intercept (put x = 0). In SAM 2H Q19, y = x2 + x − 6 was the U-shape crossing the y-axis at −6. (Exponential graphs such as y = 2x are not in the 4MA1 list.)

subsections.heading: Plotting a curve from a table of values
subsections.html:
Spec 3.3A (Higher) · 2018 Edexcel May 2H Q14(a), (b)

Complete the table by substituting each x, plot every point accurately, then join them with a smooth curve, not with straight segments.

  1. Substitute each x into the equation, with brackets for negatives. Use the given values as a check on your method.
  2. Plot each point to within half a small square.
  3. Join the points with a smooth curve through all of them. Turning points are rounded, not pointed.
  4. For y = k/x, do not join across x = 0. The two branches are separate.

Worked example: 2018 2H Q14(a), y = x3 − 2x2 − 3x + 4

x = −2: (−8) − 2(4) − 3(−2) + 4 = −8 − 8 + 6 + 4 = −6

x = −1: −1 − 2 + 3 + 4 = 4 · x = 1: 1 − 2 − 3 + 4 = 0 · x = 2: 8 − 8 − 6 + 4 = −2 · x = 3: 27 − 18 − 9 + 4 = 4

The scheme gave B2 for all five, or B1 for 2, 3 or 4 correct.

✗ −2x2 at x = −2 worked out as +8. The square is done first: −2 × 4 = −8.
✗ Joining the points with a ruler. The curve is marked on being smooth and passing through the points.

subsections.heading: Solving equations with graphs
subsections.html:
Spec 3.3E (Higher) · 2018 Edexcel May 2H Q14(c) · 2017 Edexcel Jan 4HR Q18 (old spec)

Where two graphs cross, their y-values are equal, so the x-coordinates of the crossing points solve "one equation = the other".

  1. Write the drawn graph's equation = the equation you must solve, and subtract to see what is left over.
  2. That leftover is the straight line to draw: drawn curve = new equation + leftover.
  3. Draw the line and read off the x-coordinates of every intersection.
  4. For "f(x) = k": draw the horizontal line y = k and count or read the crossings.

Worked example: 2018 2H Q14(c). The graph of y = x3 − 2x2 − 3x + 4 is drawn. Solve x3 − 2x2 − x + 1 = 0.

x3 − 2x2 − 3x + 4 = (x3 − 2x2 − x + 1) − 2x + 3

So when x3 − 2x2 − x + 1 = 0, the curve's y equals −2x + 3. Draw y = −2x + 3   (M1)

It crosses the curve at x ≈ −0.8, 0.6 and 2.2   (A1 A1: the scheme accepted −0.9 to −0.7, 0.4 to 0.7 and 2.1 to 2.4)

✗ Reading the y-coordinates of the crossings. The solutions are the x-values.
✗ Drawing y = 0 because the equation "equals 0". That solves the equation of the drawn curve, not the new one.

subsections.heading: Trigonometric graphs
subsections.html:
Spec 3.3A (Higher) · 2018 Edexcel May 1H Q18(b) · 2016 Edexcel SAM 2H Q19

sin and cos are waves of height 1 that repeat every 360°. tan repeats every 180° and has no maximum. Symmetry gives the second solution your calculator will not show you.

x0°90°180°270°360°
sin x010−10
cos x10−101
tan x0undefined0undefined0
  1. Use the calculator (sin−1, cos−1, tan−1) for the first solution.
  2. sin: the second solution is 180° − first. cos: 360° − first. tan: first + 180°.
  3. Add or subtract 360° to find any more in the range asked.

Worked examples, for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°

sin x = 0.5: 30° and 180° − 30° = 30°, 150°

cos x = −0.5: 120° and 360° − 120° = 120°, 240°

tan x = 1: 45° and 45° + 180° = 45°, 225°

2018 1H Q18(b): read a, b, c from y = a sin(x − b)° + c

The graph ran from a minimum of −1 to a maximum of 3. The centre line is y = 1, so c = 1. The height from the centre is 2, so a = 2.

A normal sine wave rises through its centre line at 0°. This one does so at 90°, so it has been shifted 90° right: b = 90.

subsections.heading: Transformations of graphs
subsections.html:
Spec 3.3B, 3.3C (Higher) · 2018 Edexcel May 1H Q18(a) · 2016 Edexcel SAM 1H Q20

A change outside the brackets acts on y and does what you expect. A change inside the brackets acts on x and does the opposite.

New graphTransformationPoint (p, q) moves to
y = f(x) + aTranslation by (0, a): up a(p, q + a)
y = f(x + a)Translation by (−a, 0): left a(p − a, q)
y = af(x)Stretch parallel to the y-axis, scale factor a(p, aq)
y = f(ax)Stretch parallel to the x-axis, scale factor 1/a(p/a, q)

With a = −1: y = −f(x) reflects in the x-axis, and y = f(−x) reflects in the y-axis.

  1. Decide whether the change is outside (y-direction) or inside (x-direction, opposite way).
  2. Move the given point: change only the coordinate that is affected.
  3. When describing, use the full wording: "translation by the vector (0, −4)", or "stretch parallel to the y-axis, scale factor 2".

Worked example: SAM 1H Q20, maximum at (3, 5)

f(x + 3): inside, so left 3 → (0, 5).   2f(x): outside, so y doubles → (3, 10).

f(3x): inside, so x is divided by 3 → (1, 5).   f(x) − 4: translation by (0, −4).

2018 1H Q18(a): minimum at (−2, −1)

f(x − 5): right 5 → (3, −1).   ½f(x): y halves → (−2, −0.5).

✗ f(x + 3) moves the graph 3 to the right. It moves it left: the old x = 3 now happens when x + 3 = 3, i.e. at x = 0.
✗ "It moves down 4" for f(x) − 4. Describe it as a translation with a vector.

subsections.heading: Gradients of curves: drawing a tangent
subsections.html:
Spec 3.3D (Higher) · 2016 Edexcel Jan 3H Q15(c) (old spec)

A curve's gradient changes from point to point. The gradient at a point is the gradient of the tangent there: a straight line that just touches the curve without crossing it.

  1. Lay a ruler against the curve at the point so that it touches but does not cut across, with equal gaps either side.
  2. Draw the tangent long: a longer line gives a more accurate gradient.
  3. Pick two points far apart on the tangent and use rise ÷ run.
  4. Check the sign: the curve going down to the right means a negative gradient.

Worked example: y = x2 at x = 2

The tangent at (2, 4) passes through (1, 0) and (3, 8). Gradient = (8 − 0) ÷ (3 − 1) = 4.

A drawn answer is an estimate, so the scheme accepts a range. Module 8 shows how differentiation gives the exact value.

✗ Using the chord between two points on the curve instead of a tangent. That gives the average gradient between the points, not the gradient at one of them.

subsections.heading: Distance–time and speed–time graphs
subsections.html:
Spec 3.3A (Foundation: "to include speed/time and distance/time graphs")

On a distance–time graph the gradient is the speed. On a speed–time graph the gradient is the acceleration and the area underneath is the distance travelled.

GraphGradient meansArea under it meansFlat line means
Distance–timeSpeed(nothing useful)Stationary
Speed–timeAcceleration (negative = deceleration)Distance travelledConstant speed
  1. Gradient = change in vertical ÷ change in horizontal, with units: m/s from a distance–time graph, m/s² from a speed–time graph.
  2. Area under a speed–time graph: split it into triangles, rectangles and trapezia and add them.
  3. Average speed = total distance ÷ total time, including any time spent stopped.

Worked example: 0 to 20 m/s in 10 s, 20 m/s for 30 s, then to rest in 5 s

Acceleration = 20 ÷ 10 = 2 m/s². Deceleration = 20 ÷ 5 = 4 m/s².

Distance = ½ × 10 × 20 + 30 × 20 + ½ × 5 × 20 = 100 + 600 + 50 = 750 m

Average speed = 750 ÷ 45 = 16.7 m/s (3 s.f.)

✗ Reading distance off the vertical axis of a speed–time graph. The vertical axis is speed. Distance is the area.
✗ Average speed = (0 + 20 + 0) ÷ 3. Use total distance ÷ total time.

The routines

fg(x): g first, then f. f−1: y = f(x), make x the subject, swap the letters, check.

Excluded values: denominator = 0; expression under √ < 0.

Lines: m = Δy ÷ Δx; y = mx + c; midpoint is the mean of the coordinates; length = √(Δx2 + Δy2).

Parallel: same m. Perpendicular: m1m2 = −1 (flip and change the sign).

Graphical solutions: x-values of the crossings; the line to draw = drawn curve − new equation.

Trig: sin → 180 − x; cos → 360 − x; tan → x + 180.

Transformations: outside acts on y, as expected. Inside acts on x, the opposite way (f(x + a) goes left; f(ax) multiplies x by 1/a).

Speed–time: gradient = acceleration, area = distance.

questions.promptHtml: f(x) = x + 5 and g(x) = 2x. Show that fg(x) ≠ gf(x), and explain why the order matters.
questions.answerHtml:
fg(x) = f(2x) = 2x + 5.   gf(x) = g(x + 5) = 2x + 10.

"Double then add 5" is a different process from "add 5 then double". In gf, the 5 gets doubled too. The function written next to the x acts first, just as in f(g(x)).

questions.promptHtml: Why do you swap x and y at the end when finding an inverse, and how is the graph of f−1 related to the graph of f?
questions.answerHtml:
The inverse takes f's outputs as its inputs. Making x the subject gives x in terms of y, the output. We then rename the input "x" so it can be written as a normal function, f−1(x).

Swapping x and y on a graph is a reflection in the line y = x. If (2, 7) is on y = f(x), then (7, 2) is on y = f−1(x).

questions.promptHtml: Why must x = 2 be excluded from the domain of f(x) = 3/(x − 2), but no value is excluded for f(x) = 3/(x2 + 1)?
questions.answerHtml:
At x = 2 the first denominator is 0, and dividing by zero has no answer, so f(2) does not exist.

x2 + 1 is always at least 1, because x2 is never negative. The second denominator can never be 0, so every real x is allowed.

questions.promptHtml: Why do the gradients of perpendicular lines multiply to −1? Use a line of gradient 2.
questions.answerHtml:
A line of gradient 2 goes 1 across and 2 up. Rotating that step by 90° turns "1 across, 2 up" into "2 across, 1 down", a gradient of −1/2.

The rotation swaps rise and run (flip the fraction) and reverses one direction (change the sign). 2 × (−1/2) = −1. The same happens for any gradient m, giving −1/m.

questions.promptHtml: Why does y = f(x − 5) move the graph 5 to the right, even though there is a minus sign?
questions.answerHtml:
Whatever f did at x = 0, the new graph does when x − 5 = 0, i.e. at x = 5. Every feature now happens 5 later along the x-axis, so the graph has moved right.

That is why the 2018 minimum at (−2, −1) moved to (3, −1) for f(x − 5). Changes inside the bracket act on x in the opposite way to how they look.

questions.promptHtml: The graph of y = x2 is drawn. Why does drawing y = x + 6 on the same axes solve x2 − x − 6 = 0?
questions.answerHtml:
At a crossing point both graphs have the same y, so x2 = x + 6, which rearranges to x2 − x − 6 = 0.

So the x-coordinates of the crossings are exactly the solutions: x = −2 and x = 3, which you can check by factorising (x − 3)(x + 2). The y-coordinates, 4 and 9, are not the answer.

questions.promptHtml: Why does the area under a speed–time graph give the distance travelled?
questions.answerHtml:
At constant speed, distance = speed × time. On a speed–time graph that is a rectangle: height (speed) × width (time).

When the speed changes steadily, the shape becomes a triangle or trapezium, and its area is the average speed × time. Either way, the area measures distance, in m if the axes are in m/s and s.

questions.promptHtml: A calculator gives sin−1(0.5) = 30°. Why is 150° also a solution of sin x = 0.5, and how would you find all the solutions from 0° to 720°?
questions.answerHtml:
The sine graph is symmetrical about 90°, so the height at 30° is repeated at 180° − 30° = 150°. The calculator only returns one value.

The wave repeats every 360°, so add 360° to each: 30°, 150°, 390°, 510°.

questions.promptHtml:
The function f is such that f(x) = (2x + 7)/3

(a) Find f(4) (1)

(b) Express the inverse function f−1 in the form f−1(x) = … (2)

modules.title: Differentiation
modules.standfirst: The calculus at the end of the course, and a reliable 4–8 marks near the back of a paper. The exam uses one rule, for axn, and applies it in four ways: a gradient, a stationary point, a maximum or minimum in a practical problem, and velocity and acceleration from displacement. Once the rule is secure, every question is a routine.

subsections.html: A straight line has one gradient everywhere. A curve's gradient changes as you move along it. Differentiating gives a formula, dy/dx, for the gradient at any x, which is exact where a drawn tangent is only an estimate. Where the gradient is zero the curve is momentarily flat: a peak or a trough. That single fact is behind every maximum, minimum and "at rest" question.

subsections.heading: Rates of change and what dy/dx means
subsections.html:
Spec 3.4A

dy/dx is the gradient of the curve, the rate at which y changes as x changes, and it has its own value at every point.

  • On y = x2 the tangent at x = 1 has gradient 2, at x = 2 gradient 4 and at x = 3 gradient 6. The gradient is 2x, so dy/dx = 2x.
  • dy/dx is read "dee y by dee x". If the letters change, so does the notation: dA/dx, dV/dr, ds/dt.
  • Positive dy/dx means y is increasing, negative means decreasing, and zero means the curve is momentarily flat.

subsections.heading: Differentiating axn
subsections.html:
Spec 3.4B · 2018 Edexcel May 2H Q17(a) · 2016 Edexcel Jan 4H Q16(a) (old spec)

Multiply by the power, then take one off the power. Do it to each term separately. A number on its own disappears.

Differentiating a power of x — memorisey = axn   →   dy/dx = naxn−1n is any integer, including negative · kx → k · a constant → 0 · NOT on the formula sheet
  1. Write every term as a number × a power of x.
  2. For each term: bring the power down and multiply, then reduce the power by 1.
  3. A term in x (x1) becomes just its number. A constant (x0) becomes 0.

Worked example: y = 4x3 − 5x2 + 7x − 2

4x3 → 3 × 4x2 = 12x2 · −5x2 → −10x · 7x → 7 · −2 → 0

dy/dx = 12x2 − 10x + 7   (B2: B1 for any two terms correct)

2018 2H Q17(a): y = x3 − 2x2 − 15x + 5 gives dy/dx = 3x2 − 4x − 15. The scheme's note was "Award B1 for any 2 or 3 of the 4 terms differentiated correctly", so the constant disappearing counts as one of the four.

✗ 4x3 → 12x3. The power must come down by 1: 12x2.
✗ 7x → 7x0 = 0, or −2 → −2. x becomes 1, so 7x → 7. A constant → 0.
✗ 4x3 → 4 × 3 = 12x. Keep the x with its new power.

subsections.heading: Rewrite before you differentiate
subsections.html:
Spec 3.4B · 2016 Edexcel SAM 1H Q21 · 2013 Edexcel Jan 3H Q18(a) (old spec)

The rule only works on separate terms of the form axn, so fractions, brackets and quotients must be turned into powers of x first.

  1. x in the denominator: use a negative power. 2/x = 2x−1, and 3/x2 = 3x−2.
  2. Brackets: expand first. (2x + 1)(x − 3) = 2x2 − 5x − 3.
  3. Divided by x: split into separate fractions. (x3 + 4x)/x = x2 + 4.
  4. Differentiate. With a negative power, "take one off" makes it more negative: −1 → −2.

Worked examples

y = 2/x = 2x−1 → dy/dx = −1 × 2x−2 = −2x−2 = −2/x2

y = 3/x2 = 3x−2 → dy/dx = −6x−3 = −6/x3

y = 8x2 + 2/x (SAM 1H Q21) → dy/dx = 16x − 2x−2

y = (2x + 1)(x − 3) = 2x2 − 5x − 3 → dy/dx = 4x − 5

✗ 2/x → 2/1 = 2, by "differentiating the bottom". Rewrite as 2x−1 first.
✗ 2x−1 → −2x0. The power goes down by 1: −1 − 1 = −2.
✗ Differentiating each bracket separately and multiplying. Expand first.

subsections.heading: The gradient at a point
subsections.html:
Spec 3.4C

Differentiate first, then substitute the x-value into dy/dx, not into y.

  1. Find dy/dx.
  2. Substitute the given x into dy/dx. The result is the gradient of the curve (and of the tangent) at that point.

Worked example: the gradient of y = x3 − 4x + 1 at the point where x = 2

dy/dx = 3x2 − 4.   At x = 2: 3(4) − 4 = 8

Compare module 7: drawing a tangent would only have given an estimate close to 8.

✗ Putting x = 2 into y: 8 − 8 + 1 = 1. That is the y-coordinate, not the gradient.

subsections.heading: Where does the gradient take a given value?
subsections.html:
Spec 3.4C · 2016 Edexcel Jan 4H Q16(b) · 2017 Edexcel Jan 3HR Q20(b) (old spec)

Set dy/dx equal to the value, solve for x, then put each x into the original equation to get y.

  1. dy/dx = the given gradient.
  2. Solve: linear for a quadratic curve, quadratic for a cubic curve.
  3. Substitute each x into y (the original equation) for the coordinates.

Worked example: the point on y = 2x2 − 8x + 3 where the gradient is 12

dy/dx = 4x − 8 = 12, so x = 5   (M1 · A1)

y = 2(25) − 40 + 3 = 13, so the point is (5, 13)   (A1)

For a cubic you get a quadratic. In 2017 3HR Q20, y = x3 − 4x2 + 5x + 4 with gradient 1 gave 3x2 − 8x + 4 = 0, so (3x − 2)(x − 2) = 0 and x = 2/3 or x = 2: two points.

subsections.heading: Stationary points
subsections.html:
Spec 3.4C · 2016 Edexcel SAM 1H Q21 · 2013 Edexcel Jan 3H Q18(b) (old spec)

At a stationary (turning) point the gradient is zero, so solve dy/dx = 0.

  1. Differentiate.
  2. Set dy/dx = 0 and solve for x.
  3. Substitute each x into the original equation to get y.
  4. Give the answer as coordinates (x, y).

Worked example: SAM 1H Q21, the stationary point of y = 8x2 + 2/x

y = 8x2 + 2x−1, so dy/dx = 16x − 2x−2   (M2: M1 for one term correct)

16x − 2/x2 = 0   (M1). Multiply by x2: 16x3 = 2, so x3 = 1/8, so x = 0.5   (M1)

y = 8(0.25) + 2/0.5 = 2 + 4 = 6, so the point is (0.5, 6)   (A1)

Worked example: y = x3 − 3x2 − 9x + 5

dy/dx = 3x2 − 6x − 9 = 3(x2 − 2x − 3) = 3(x − 3)(x + 1) = 0, so x = 3 or x = −1

x = −1: y = −1 − 3 + 9 + 5 = 10.   x = 3: y = 27 − 27 − 27 + 5 = −22

Stationary points: (−1, 10) and (3, −22)

✗ Stopping at "x = 3 or x = −1". The question asks for the coordinates, so find each y.
✗ Substituting x back into dy/dx to get y. That always gives 0. Use the original equation.

subsections.heading: Maximum or minimum? Use the shape
subsections.html:
Spec 3.4D: "by considering the general shape of the graph only"

You decide whether a stationary point is a maximum or a minimum from the shape of the graph, which the equation tells you.

  1. Quadratic, x2 term positive: U-shape, so its one stationary point is a minimum. x2 term negative: ∩-shape, so a maximum.
  2. Cubic, x3 term positive: it rises, dips, then rises. The left-hand (smaller x) stationary point is the maximum and the right-hand one is the minimum. For a negative x3 term, it is the other way round.
  3. In a practical problem, such as A = 120x − 2x2, the leading term is negative, so ∩-shaped, so the stationary point is the maximum the question wants.
  4. To confirm, you can check the sign of dy/dx just either side: + then − is a maximum, − then + is a minimum.

Worked example: y = x3 − 3x2 − 9x + 5, continued

A positive x3 term means the curve rises, falls, then rises again. So (−1, 10) is the maximum and (3, −22) is the minimum.

Check: dy/dx at x = −2 is 15 (going up), at x = 0 is −9 (going down), at x = 4 is 15 (going up). ✓

subsections.heading: Increasing and decreasing: where is the gradient negative?
subsections.html:
Spec 3.4C, with 2.8A · 2018 Edexcel May 2H Q17(b)

"Negative gradient" means dy/dx < 0. That is a quadratic inequality, solved with critical values and a sketch.

  1. Write dy/dx < 0 (or > 0 for a positive gradient).
  2. Solve dy/dx = 0 for the critical values.
  3. dy/dx is a U-shaped quadratic, so < 0 is between the critical values.
  4. Write the answer with inequality signs.

Worked example: 2018 2H Q17(b), y = x3 − 2x2 − 15x + 5

3x2 − 4x − 15 < 0   (M1)

(3x + 5)(x − 3) = 0, so x = −5/3 or x = 3   (M1 · A1)

−5/3 < x < 3   (A1): the curve goes downhill between its maximum and its minimum.

subsections.heading: Maximum and minimum problems
subsections.html:
Spec 3.4C, 3.4E · 2014 Edexcel Jan 4H Q15 · 2015 Edexcel Jan 3HR Q17 · 2016 Edexcel Jan 3HR Q15(c) (old spec)

Write the quantity to be maximised as a formula in one variable, differentiate, set the derivative to zero, then substitute back to get the maximum value.

  1. "Show that": use the constraint (fixed perimeter, fixed volume) to write the other length in terms of x, then substitute it into the area or volume formula.
  2. Differentiate with respect to the variable (dA/dx, dV/dr).
  3. Set it = 0 and solve. Reject values that make a length zero or negative.
  4. Substitute into the original formula for the maximum value, with units.
  5. Justify max or min from the shape: a negative leading term gives a maximum.

Worked example: 120 m of fencing makes three sides of a rectangular pen against a wall. Find the largest possible area.

Two sides are x m, so the side parallel to the wall is (120 − 2x) m.   A = x(120 − 2x) = 120x − 2x2

dA/dx = 120 − 4x = 0, so x = 30   (M1 · A1)

A = 120(30) − 2(900) = 3600 − 1800 = 1800 m²   (A1). The −2x2 term makes it ∩-shaped, so this is a maximum.

✗ Giving x = 30 as "the maximum area". x is a length. Substitute it back into A.
✗ Substituting x = 30 into dA/dx. That gives 0 every time.

subsections.heading: Kinematics: displacement, velocity and acceleration
subsections.html:
Spec 3.4E · 2016 Edexcel SAM 2H Q25

Velocity is the rate of change of displacement, and acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. Differentiate s to get v, then differentiate v to get a.

Velocity from displacement — memorisev = ds/dts = displacement from O (m) · t = time (s) · v = velocity (m/s)
Acceleration from velocity — memorisea = dv/dta = acceleration (m/s²) · differentiate s twice to reach a
Question saysMeans
"initially", "at the start"t = 0
"instantaneously at rest", "changes direction"v = 0
"maximum (or minimum) velocity"a = 0
"returns to O"s = 0

Worked example: SAM 2H Q25, s = t3 − 5t2 − 8t + 3. When is the particle instantaneously at rest?

v = 3t2 − 10t − 8   (M1: 2 of 3 terms correct)

3t2 − 10t − 8 = 0   (A1)

(3t + 2)(t − 4) = 0   (M1)

t = 4 only: t = −2/3 is rejected because time cannot be negative   (A1)

✗ Setting s = 0 for "at rest". At rest means not moving, so the velocity is zero. s = 0 means "back at O".
✗ Keeping t = −2/3. The scheme said "t = 4 only".

subsections.heading: Kinematics: harder questions
subsections.html:
Spec 3.4E (the specification's own example)

Keep s, v and a separate and labelled, and substitute each time into the right one.

  1. Write out s, v and a as three separate lines before answering anything.
  2. Translate the words into a condition (the table above) and solve.
  3. Put the time into whichever of s, v or a the question asks for, with units.

Worked example: s = 24t2 − t3, 0 ≤ t ≤ 20 (the spec example)

v = ds/dt = 48t − 3t2  ·  a = dv/dt = 48 − 6t

Maximum velocity: a = 0, so 48 − 6t = 0, so t = 8. v = 48(8) − 3(64) = 384 − 192 = 192 m/s

Worked example: s = t3 − 6t2 + 9t + 2

v = 3t2 − 12t + 9 = 3(t − 1)(t − 3), so the particle is at rest at t = 1 and t = 3.

Initial velocity: v(0) = 9 m/s.   a = 6t − 12, so a = 0 when t = 2.

Displacement at t = 3: 27 − 54 + 27 + 2 = 2 m from O.

✗ Using v = s/t, "distance over time". That only works at constant velocity. Here velocity changes, so differentiate.

One rule, four uses

Rule: axn → naxn−1. kx → k. A constant → 0. Rewrite 1/x as x−1 and expand brackets first.

Gradient at a point: put x into dy/dx.

Stationary point: dy/dx = 0, solve for x, then put x into y for the coordinates.

Max or min: from the shape. Positive cubic: left point max, right point min. −x2 gives a max.

Negative gradient: dy/dx < 0, a quadratic inequality, answered with inequality signs.

Optimisation: formula in one variable → derivative = 0 → substitute back into the formula.

Kinematics: v = ds/dt, a = dv/dt. At rest: v = 0. Maximum velocity: a = 0. Initially: t = 0.

subsections.heading: Definitions marked to the word
subsections.html:
TermAccepted wording
dy/dxThe gradient of the curve, the rate of change of y with respect to x
Stationary pointA point where the gradient is zero: dy/dx = 0
Maximum pointA stationary point where the curve changes from going up to going down
Minimum pointA stationary point where the curve changes from going down to going up
DisplacementThe distance from a fixed point O, in a stated direction
VelocityThe rate of change of displacement: v = ds/dt
AccelerationThe rate of change of velocity: a = dv/dt
Instantaneously at restVelocity = 0 at that moment

questions.promptHtml: Why does a constant term disappear when you differentiate, and why does 7x become 7?
questions.answerHtml:
dy/dx measures how steep the graph is. Adding a constant (+5) slides the whole graph up without changing its steepness anywhere, so it contributes 0 to the gradient.

y = 7x is a straight line with gradient 7 everywhere, so its derivative is 7. The rule agrees: 7x1 → 1 × 7x0 = 7.

questions.promptHtml: Why must you rewrite 4/x as 4x−1 before differentiating, and what is its derivative?
questions.answerHtml:
The rule works only on terms of the form axn. In 4/x the x is in the denominator, so it is not yet in that form. 4/x = 4x−1 is.

Then −1 × 4x−2 = −4/x2. The derivative is always negative, which matches the graph of y = 4/x: it slopes downhill on both branches.

questions.promptHtml: Why is dy/dx = 0 at a maximum or minimum point?
questions.answerHtml:
Just before a maximum the curve goes up (positive gradient). Just after, it goes down (negative gradient). To change from positive to negative smoothly, the gradient must pass through zero, and it does so exactly at the peak, where the tangent is horizontal.

A minimum is the same in reverse. So solving dy/dx = 0 finds every turning point.

questions.promptHtml: A cubic with a positive x3 term has stationary points at x = −1 and x = 3. Without any more calculation, which is the maximum? Why?
questions.answerHtml:
A positive cubic comes up from the bottom-left and ends at the top-right. To have two turning points, it must rise, turn down, then turn back up.

So the first turning point you meet (smaller x, x = −1) is the maximum, and x = 3 is the minimum. The spec says this "general shape" reasoning is all you need.

questions.promptHtml: In an optimisation question, why do you substitute the x from dA/dx = 0 back into A, and not into dA/dx?
questions.answerHtml:
dA/dx = 0 only tells you where the maximum is: the value of x. It is zero there by definition, so substituting into dA/dx just gives 0.

The maximum value is the area itself, so x goes into the formula for A.

questions.promptHtml: Why is "instantaneously at rest" v = 0, and not s = 0?
questions.answerHtml:
s is where the particle is; v is how fast it is moving. At rest means not moving, so v = 0, even if it is far from O.

"Instantaneously" means it is only stopped for an instant: typically it is turning round, like a ball at the top of its flight. s = 0 would mean it is passing through O, possibly at full speed.

questions.promptHtml: Why does the maximum velocity happen when the acceleration is zero?
questions.answerHtml:
Acceleration is the gradient of the velocity: a = dv/dt. Velocity is at a maximum when its graph is at a peak, which is where its gradient is zero.

It is the same idea as dy/dx = 0 at a stationary point, one level up: v is to a what y is to dy/dx.

questions.promptHtml: Why does a question like 2018 2H Q17(b), "the range of values of x for which C has a negative gradient", lead to a quadratic inequality?
questions.answerHtml:
"Negative gradient" means dy/dx < 0. Differentiating a cubic gives a quadratic, so the condition is a quadratic inequality, solved exactly as in module 5.

dy/dx is a U-shaped quadratic, so it is negative between its roots. Those roots are the x-coordinates of the maximum and minimum. The curve goes downhill between them.

modules.title: Angles, Polygons and Circle Theorems
modules.standfirst: Angle chasing with reasons. Every dated 4MA1 paper here has a polygon or circle question, and three of the four have a circle theorem with "give a reason for each stage". The numbers are usually easy. The marks are lost on the reasons, so this module teaches the exact wording the mark schemes underline.

intel.html:

From the 2018 May 1H mark scheme, Q13. The answer for the reason was "angle at centre is twice angle at circumference", with the key words underlined, and the note said:

"B1 dep on B1 in (a)(i) accept alternative reasons eg. angle at circumference is half the angle at the centre"

Two lessons. The reason mark is dependent: a wrong angle scores nothing for a right reason. And the reason must contain the key words. "Because of the circle theorem" scores zero.

subsections.html: Every question in this module is angle chasing: find one angle, write down why, use it to find the next. The facts come in three layers. Lines and triangles come first, then polygons, then circles. The exam wants a reason at each step, so learn each fact with its sentence.

subsections.heading: Angle facts and parallel lines
subsections.html:
Spec 4.1A–D · 2016 Edexcel Jan 4HR Q2 (old spec)

Angles on a straight line add up to 180°, angles at a point add up to 360°, and parallel lines make pairs of equal or supplementary angles.

FactReason to write
Two angles making a straight lineAngles on a straight line add up to 180°
Angles all the way round a pointAngles at a point add up to 360°
The X shape: opposite anglesVertically opposite angles are equal
The Z shape between parallel linesAlternate angles are equal
The F shape: same position at each crossingCorresponding angles are equal
The C (or U) shape between parallel linesCo-interior angles add up to 180° (also called allied angles)
  1. Mark every angle you find on the diagram as you go.
  2. Write each step as a line: angle = value (reason).
  3. Use the full reason. The letter shapes (Z, F, C) are for you, not the examiner.

Worked example: parallel lines

AB is parallel to CD. A straight line crosses AB at P and CD at Q. Angle BPQ = 118°. Find angle PQD and angle CQP.

Angle PQD = 180° − 118° = 62° (co-interior angles add up to 180°)   (B1 for the angle, B1 for the reason)

Angle CQP = 118° (alternate angles are equal), or 180° − 62° (angles on a straight line add up to 180°).

✗ "Z angles", "F angles", "C angles". These are not accepted as reasons.
✗ "Alternate angles add up to 180°". Alternate angles are equal. Co-interior angles add up to 180°.
✓ "Alternate angles are equal" and "co-interior angles add up to 180°".

subsections.heading: Triangles and quadrilaterals
subsections.html:
Spec 4.1C–D, 4.2A–C

The angles in a triangle add up to 180°, the angles in a quadrilateral add up to 360°, and an exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles.

An isosceles triangle has two equal sides and two equal base angles. An equilateral triangle has all sides equal and all angles 60°. The exterior angle fact saves a step: the angle outside the triangle at one corner equals the two inside angles at the other corners added together.

ShapeSidesAnglesDiagonals
ParallelogramOpposite sides equal and parallelOpposite angles equalBisect each other
RectangleOpposite sides equal and parallelAll 90°Equal, bisect each other
RhombusAll four equal, opposite sides parallelOpposite angles equalBisect each other at 90°
SquareAll four equal, opposite sides parallelAll 90°Equal, bisect each other at 90°
TrapeziumOne pair of parallel sidesCo-interior pairs add up to 180°No special property
KiteTwo pairs of equal adjacent sidesOne pair of opposite angles equalCross at 90°, one bisects the other

Worked example: the four angles of a quadrilateral are 90°, (x + 15)°, (x + 25)° and (x + 35)°. Find x.

90 + x + 15 + x + 25 + x + 35 = 360   (M1: angles in a quadrilateral add up to 360°)

3x + 165 = 360, so 3x = 195 and x = 65   (A1)

Check: 90 + 80 + 90 + 100 = 360. This example is from the spec's own notes.

subsections.heading: Polygons: interior and exterior angles
subsections.html:
Spec 4.2D–E · 2018 Edexcel May 2H Q12 · 2016 Edexcel SAM 2H Q11 · 2015 Edexcel Jan 3HR Q14 (old spec)

A polygon with n sides splits into n − 2 triangles, so its interior angles add up to (n − 2) × 180°, and its exterior angles always add up to 360°.

Sum of interior angles — memoriseS = (n − 2) × 180°n = number of sides · pentagon 540° · hexagon 720° · octagon 1080° · the spec writes it as (2n − 4) right angles
Exterior angle of a regular polygon — memoriseexterior angle = 360° ÷ n  ·  interior angle = 180° − exterior angleinterior + exterior = 180° at every vertex, because together they make a straight line
  1. Irregular polygon: work out the angle sum, add the known angles, subtract.
  2. Regular polygon, given n: exterior = 360 ÷ n, then interior = 180 − exterior.
  3. Regular polygon, given an angle: go through the exterior angle. n = 360 ÷ exterior.

Worked example 1: a hexagon has angles 118°, 132°, 95°, 127°, y° and y°. Find y.

Sum = (6 − 2) × 180 = 720°   (M1)

720 − (118 + 132 + 95 + 127) = 720 − 472 = 248   (M1)

y = 248 ÷ 2 = 124   (M1, A1)

Worked example 2: each interior angle of a regular polygon with n sides is 144°. Find the interior angle of a regular polygon with 2n sides.

Exterior angle = 180 − 144 = 36°   (M1)

n = 360 ÷ 36 = 10, so 2n = 20   (M1)

Exterior angle of the 20-sided polygon = 360 ÷ 20 = 18°   (M1)

Interior angle = 180 − 18 = 162°   (A1)

The 2018 2H Q12 scheme warned: "splitting the shape incorrectly (FDC and DEA are not straight lines) gains no marks for angles calculated from false information."

✗ Assuming lines meet in a straight line because they look as if they do.
✗ Using 360 ÷ n for the interior angle. That is the exterior angle.
✓ Only use a straight line, a parallel pair or an equal length if the question or the diagram's markings say so.

equations.name: Exterior angle of a regular polygon
equations.formula: exterior angle = 360° ÷ n  ·  interior angle = 180° − exterior angle

subsections.heading: Bearings
subsections.html:
Spec 4.4D · 2015 Edexcel Jan 3HR Q11 (old spec)

A bearing is an angle measured clockwise from north, written with three figures.

  1. "The bearing of B from A": stand at A, face north, turn clockwise until you face B.
  2. Draw a north line at the point you are measuring from.
  3. Always write three figures: 064°, not 64°.
  4. Back bearing (A from B): add 180° to the bearing of B from A. If that goes over 360°, subtract 180° instead.

Worked example: the bearing of B from A is 064°. The bearing of C from A is 150°.

Bearing of A from B = 064 + 180 = 244°.

Angle BAC = 150 − 64 = 86°, the angle between the two directions at A.

Bearing of A from C = 150 + 180 = 330°.

North lines are parallel, so alternate and co-interior angles appear at every bearing question. Bearings that need trigonometry or the sine and cosine rules are in module 11.

subsections.heading: Constructions with ruler and compasses
subsections.html:
Spec 4.5A–D · 2016 Edexcel SAM 1H Q5 · 2016 Edexcel Jan 3H Q6 (old spec)

Every construction works by drawing arcs of equal radius, because all the points that are the same distance from two fixed points lie on one straight line: the perpendicular bisector.

Perpendicular bisector of AB:

  1. Open the compasses to more than half of AB.
  2. With the point on A, draw an arc above and below the line.
  3. Keep the same radius. With the point on B, draw arcs crossing the first two.
  4. Join the two crossing points with a straight line.

Bisector of angle ABC:

  1. With the point on B, draw an arc crossing both arms BA and BC.
  2. From each of those two crossing points, draw arcs of equal radius that cross each other.
  3. Draw a straight line from B through that crossing point.

Triangle with three given sides: draw one side with a ruler, then arcs of the other two lengths from each end. Where the arcs cross is the third vertex.

SAM 1H Q5 scheme: M1 for "Circular arc, centre B, to intersect both lines AB and BC", then A1 "dep on M1. Full construction shown."

✗ Rubbing out the arcs, or using a protractor. Without the arcs there is no evidence, so no marks.
✓ Leave every arc visible and draw the final line with a ruler.

Loci are not in the 4MA1 content list, so they are not taught here. Scale drawings (spec 4.5C) are measuring with a ruler and a scale such as 1 cm to 5 km.

subsections.heading: Congruent shapes
subsections.html:
Spec 4.2F–G

Congruent shapes are exactly the same shape and size, so every corresponding side and every corresponding angle is equal.

The spec only asks you to understand the word. The four ways to tell that two triangles are congruent are still worth knowing, because they are how you justify that two lengths or angles in a diagram must be equal:

ConditionWhat must match
SSSAll three sides
SASTwo sides and the angle between them
ASA (or AAS)Two angles and a corresponding side
RHSA right angle, the hypotenuse and one other side

Worked example: ABC is isosceles with AB = AC. M is the midpoint of BC. Show that triangles ABM and ACM are congruent.

AB = AC (given). BM = CM (M is the midpoint). AM is common to both triangles.

So the triangles are congruent (SSS). It follows that angle AMB = angle AMC, and since they make a straight line, each is 90°.

This is beyond what 4MA1 papers have asked, which is why there is no drill question on it. A full congruence proof is a UK GCSE question. On 4MA1 you only need to recognise congruent shapes, for example "two congruent regular pentagons" in a polygon question.

✗ "AAA" as a condition. Three equal angles prove the triangles are similar, not congruent, because one can be an enlargement of the other.
✗ Two sides and an angle that is not between them. Except for RHS, this does not fix the triangle.

subsections.heading: Circle vocabulary, chords and tangents
subsections.html:
Spec 4.6A–B (Foundation) · 2018 Edexcel May 2H Q5

Three facts about chords and tangents need no angle at the circumference, only the centre and the radius.

  1. The angle between a tangent and a radius is 90°.
  2. Two tangents from the same point to a circle are equal in length.
  3. The perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord (and the line from the centre to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to it).

A chord joins two points on the circle. An arc is part of the circumference. A sector is the slice between two radii and an arc. A segment is the region between a chord and an arc. A tangent touches the circle at exactly one point.

Two radii from the centre make an isosceles triangle with any chord. Look for that triangle in every circle question: it gives two equal base angles.

Worked example 1: a chord of length 24 cm is in a circle of radius 13 cm. How far is the chord from the centre?

The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, so it meets the chord 12 cm from each end.

Right-angled triangle with hypotenuse 13 (a radius) and one side 12: distance = √(132 − 122) = √25 = 5 cm.

Worked example 2: PA and PB are tangents from P to a circle, centre O. Angle APB = 50°. Find angle AOB.

Angle OAP = angle OBP = 90° (the angle between a tangent and a radius is 90°).

Angle AOB = 360 − 90 − 90 − 50 = 130° (angles in a quadrilateral add up to 360°).

subsections.heading: The angle at the centre, and the angle in a semicircle
subsections.html:
Spec 4.6C(i)–(ii) · 2018 Edexcel May 1H Q13(a) · 2016 Edexcel Jan 3H Q17(a) (old spec)

The angle an arc makes at the centre is twice the angle it makes at any point on the rest of the circumference.

The two angles must stand on the same arc. Trace the two lines from each end of the arc: to the centre for one angle, to the point on the circumference for the other. The shape they make is an arrowhead or, for a large angle, a reflex angle at the centre.

The angle in a semicircle is the special case where the arc is half the circle. The angle at the centre is then 180°, so the angle at the circumference is 90°. Any triangle drawn on a diameter has a right angle opposite the diameter.

Worked example: L, M and N are on a circle, centre O. Angle MLN = 31°, and L is on the major arc MN. Find angle MON.

Angle MON = 2 × 31 = 62°   (B1)

Reason: the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference   (B1, dependent on the first B1)

2018 1H Q6 used the semicircle fact without saying so: MON was a diameter, so angle MPN = 90° and Pythagoras gave the diameter. That question is worked in module 10.

subsections.heading: Angles in the same segment, and cyclic quadrilaterals
subsections.html:
Spec 4.6B–C(iii)–(iv) · 2016 Edexcel SAM 1H Q16

Angles at the circumference standing on the same arc are equal, and the opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180°.

A cyclic quadrilateral has all four vertices on the circle. The centre does not have to be inside it.

  1. Same segment: look for a "bow tie": two triangles on the same chord, with their third vertices on the same side of the chord. The angles at those vertices are equal.
  2. Cyclic quadrilateral: if the two vertices are on opposite sides of the chord, the angles add up to 180°.

Worked example: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral. Angle ABC = 104° and angle BAC = 38°.

Angle ADC = 180 − 104 = 76° (opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180°).

Angle BDC = angle BAC = 38° (angles in the same segment are equal: both stand on the chord BC, and A and D are on the same side of it).

✗ "Opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral are equal". They add up to 180°. Equal opposite angles is a parallelogram fact.
✗ Calling a quadrilateral cyclic when one corner is the centre O. O is not on the circumference.

subsections.heading: The alternate segment theorem
subsections.html:
Spec 4.6C(v) · 2018 Edexcel May 1H Q13(b) · 2016 Edexcel SAM 1H Q16

The angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment.

At the point where the tangent touches, the chord splits the circle into two segments. The angle between the tangent and the chord equals any angle at the circumference that stands on that chord in the other segment, the one on the far side of the chord from the angle.

  1. Find the tangent and the point of contact.
  2. Pick the chord from that point that makes the given angle with the tangent.
  3. Look at the triangle on that chord whose third vertex is on the far side of the chord. The angle at that vertex is equal.

Worked example: A, B, C and D are on a circle. PA is a tangent at A. Angle PAD = 41° and angle BCD = 98°. Calculate angle ADB, giving reasons.

Angle ABD = 41° (alternate segment theorem)   (B1 for the reason)

Angle BAD = 180 − 98 = 82° (opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180°)   (B1 for the reason)

Angle ADB = 180 − 82 − 41 = 57° (angles in a triangle add up to 180°)   (M2, A1)

This is the SAM 1H Q16 structure with the numbers changed: the scheme gave B1 for each circle reason and M2 A1 for the calculation.

subsections.heading: Intersecting chords
subsections.html:
Spec 4.6A (Higher) · 2018 Edexcel May 2H Q22 · 2015 Edexcel Jan 3HR Q19 (old spec)

When two chords cross, the two parts of one chord multiply to the same number as the two parts of the other.

Intersecting chords, inside the circle — memoriseAP × PB = CP × PDchords AB and CD cross at P inside the circle · multiply the two pieces of each chord
Intersecting chords, outside the circle — memorisePA × PB = PC × PDlines from P outside the circle cut it at A, B and at C, D · each is a distance from P: the near part times the WHOLE line
  1. Decide whether the chords meet inside or outside the circle.
  2. Inside: piece × piece = piece × piece.
  3. Outside: (distance to the near point) × (distance to the far point), both measured from the outside point.
  4. If a line passes through the centre, the part inside the circle is a diameter, 2r.

Worked example (2018 2H Q22, numbers changed)

A, D, B and E are on a circle, centre O. AFBC, OEC and OFD are straight lines. AF = 5 cm, FB = 8 cm, BC = 8 cm, FD = 2 cm and CE = x cm. Find x.

The line OFD runs from the centre to the circle, so extended backwards through O it is a diameter. The part on the far side of F is 2r − 2.

5 × 8 = 2 × (2r − 2)   (M1)

40 = 4r − 4, so r = 11   (A1)

From C: CB × CA = CE × (CE + 2r), so 8 × (8 + 8 + 5) = x(x + 22)   (M1)

168 = x2 + 22x, so x2 + 22x − 168 = 0   (A1)

(x − 6)(x + 28) = 0   (M1)

x = 6. The negative root is a length, so reject it.   (A1)

2018 2H Q22 scheme: "Incorrect working giving the radius as 16 cm gains M0A0". 16 was the diameter.

✗ Outside the circle: 8 × 13, using the chord AB instead of the whole line CA.
✓ Both distances start at the outside point: CB × CA.

subsections.heading: Giving reasons: the wording that scores
subsections.html:
Spec 4.7A · 2018 Edexcel May 2H Q5 · 2016 Edexcel SAM 1H Q16

A reason is a named fact written as a full sentence, and the mark scheme underlines the words it needs.

FactSentence that scores
Centre and circumferenceThe angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference
SemicircleThe angle in a semicircle is 90°
Same segmentAngles in the same segment are equal
Cyclic quadrilateralOpposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180°
Tangent and radiusThe angle between a tangent and a radius is 90°
Tangents from a pointTangents from an external point are equal in length
Chord bisectorThe perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord
Tangent and chordAlternate segment theorem
Isosceles triangleBase angles of an isosceles triangle are equal (OA = OB, radii)
  1. One reason per step. If the question says "give a reason for each stage", every line needs one.
  2. Write the angle with three letters (angle ABD) so there is no doubt which angle you mean.
  3. The reason mark usually depends on the angle being right, so get the angle right first.

2018 2H Q5 (angle PQT) gave B1 for "Angle between tangent and radius(or diameter) is 90 degrees", and accepted the alternate segment theorem instead if that was the route used.

subsections.heading: Why the circle theorems are true
subsections.html:
Spec 4.6C · the spec says "formal proof of these theorems is not required" · the school's "Proof of Circle Theorems" worksheet asks for all five

Every circle theorem comes from one idea: two radii make an isosceles triangle.

4MA1 will not ask you to prove these. The school worksheet does, and knowing the proofs is the best protection against misusing the theorems.

Proof: the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference

A, B and C are on a circle, centre O. Join C to O and extend the line to D.

OA = OC (radii), so triangle AOC is isosceles: angle OAC = angle OCA = x.

Angle AOD is an exterior angle of triangle AOC, so angle AOD = x + x = 2x.

In the same way OB = OC, angle OBC = angle OCB = y, and angle BOD = 2y.

Angle AOB = 2x + 2y = 2(x + y) = 2 × angle ACB.

The rest follow from it:

  1. Semicircle: if AB is a diameter, angle AOB = 180°, so the angle at the circumference is 90°.
  2. Same segment: two angles on the same arc are each half of the same angle at the centre, so they are equal.
  3. Cyclic quadrilateral: opposite angles stand on the two arcs, whose angles at the centre add up to 360°. Halving gives 180°.
  4. Alternate segment: draw the diameter from the point of contact. It meets the tangent at 90° and makes a 90° angle in the semicircle. Subtracting from 90° twice gives the result.

The facts, each with its reason

Lines: straight line 180° · point 360° · vertically opposite equal · alternate equal · corresponding equal · co-interior add up to 180°.

Shapes: triangle 180° · quadrilateral 360° · exterior angle of a triangle = sum of the two interior opposite angles.

Polygons: interior sum (n − 2) × 180° · exterior sum 360° · regular: exterior = 360 ÷ n, interior = 180 − exterior.

Bearings: from north, clockwise, three figures · back bearing ± 180°.

Circles: tangent ⟂ radius · tangents from a point are equal · perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord · angle at centre = 2 × angle at circumference · semicircle 90° · same segment equal · cyclic quadrilateral opposite angles add up to 180° · alternate segment theorem.

Chords: inside AP × PB = CP × PD · outside PA × PB = PC × PD, both measured from P.
