questions.promptHtml: Why do the interior angles of an n-sided polygon add up to (n − 2) × 180°? Why n − 2 and not n?
questions.answerHtml:
Pick one vertex and draw a diagonal to every other vertex you can. The diagonals split the polygon into triangles, and each triangle's angles add up to 180°.

A diagonal cannot go to the vertex itself or to its two neighbours, so from one vertex you draw n − 3 diagonals, which make n − 2 triangles. A pentagon makes 3 triangles: 540°.

The triangles' angles together fill exactly the polygon's interior angles, no more and no less.

questions.promptHtml: Why do the exterior angles of any polygon add up to 360°, and why is that the quickest route for a regular polygon?
questions.answerHtml:
Walk round the edge of the polygon. At each corner you turn through the exterior angle. When you get back to the start you face the way you began, so you have turned through one full turn: 360°.

For a regular polygon all the turns are equal, so each is 360 ÷ n. That is one division. Going through the interior sum takes three steps: (n − 2) × 180, then ÷ n. It also gives you n directly from an angle: n = 360 ÷ exterior.

questions.promptHtml: A student writes "angle ACB = angle ADB, angles in the same segment", but C and D are on opposite sides of the chord AB. What has gone wrong?
questions.answerHtml:
C and D are in different segments. ACBD is then a cyclic quadrilateral with C and D as opposite vertices, so the angles add up to 180°. They are not equal.

They are only equal when both points are on the same arc, on the same side of the chord. Check this before you use the theorem: trace both angles back to the ends of the chord and see which side each vertex is on.

questions.promptHtml: Why must a tangent be perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact?
questions.answerHtml:
The shortest distance from the centre to a straight line is along the perpendicular. If the tangent were not perpendicular to the radius, some other point of the line would be closer to the centre than the radius.

That point would be inside the circle, so the line would cross the circle and meet it twice. A tangent meets it only once, so the radius must be the perpendicular: 90°.

questions.promptHtml: In the proof that the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference, where exactly is the isosceles triangle used, and why is that enough?
questions.answerHtml:
Joining the circumference point C to the centre O makes triangles AOC and BOC. OA, OB and OC are all radii, so both triangles are isosceles, with base angles x and y at C.

The exterior angle of each triangle at O is then 2x and 2y. Added together they make the angle at the centre, 2(x + y), while the angle at C is x + y.

Nothing else was assumed, so the result is true wherever C is on the major arc.

questions.promptHtml: Explain why the alternate segment theorem is true, using a diameter from the point of contact.
questions.answerHtml:
Let the tangent touch at A, and let the chord be AB, with angle x between the tangent and AB. Draw the diameter AC.

The angle between the tangent and the radius AC is 90°, so angle BAC = 90 − x. Angle ABC = 90° (angle in a semicircle). In triangle ABC, angle ACB = 180 − 90 − (90 − x) = x.

Any other angle on chord AB in that segment equals angle ACB (same segment), so it is x too.

questions.promptHtml: Chords AB and CD cross at P. Why does AP × PB = CP × PD?
questions.answerHtml:
Join A to C and D to B. Angle CAP = angle BDP (angles in the same segment, both on chord CB), and angle APC = angle DPB (vertically opposite). So triangles APC and DPB are similar.

Corresponding sides are in the same ratio: AP/DP = CP/BP. Cross-multiplying gives AP × PB = CP × PD.

questions.promptHtml: Why do three equal angles not prove two triangles are congruent, while RHS does?
questions.answerHtml:
Three equal angles fix the shape but not the size. A triangle with angles 50°, 60° and 70° can be drawn with any side length, so AAA only proves the triangles are similar.

In RHS, the right angle, the hypotenuse and one side fix the third side by Pythagoras. All three sides are then equal, which is SSS, so the triangles are congruent.

modules.title: Mensuration and Similarity
modules.standfirst: Area, volume, surface area, similar shapes and compound measures. Every dated 4MA1 paper here has at least two of these, often as a first step in a longer question: a volume becomes a mass, an area ratio becomes a length ratio. The formula sheet gives you the cone, sphere, cylinder and prism, so the marks go on choosing the right one and on units.

subsections.html: Mensuration means measuring: lengths, areas and volumes. Area is length × length, so it is measured in square units. Volume is length × length × length, in cubic units. Similarity builds on exactly that idea: if every length is multiplied by k, areas are multiplied by k2 and volumes by k3. Compound measures (speed, density, pressure) are one quantity divided by another.

subsections.heading: Units of length, area and volume
subsections.html:
Spec 4.9A, 4.10F

An area conversion squares the length conversion, and a volume conversion cubes it.

1 m = 100 cm, so 1 m2 = 100 × 100 = 10 000 cm2 and 1 m3 = 100 × 100 × 100 = 1 000 000 cm3.

ConversionLengthAreaVolume
m to cm× 100× 10 000× 1 000 000
cm to mm× 10× 100× 1000
km to m× 1000× 1 000 000not used
Capacity — memorise1 litre = 1000 cm3  ·  1 m3 = 1000 litres1 ml = 1 cm3

Worked examples

3.5 m2 = 3.5 × 10 000 = 35 000 cm2

2 400 000 cm3 = 2 400 000 ÷ 1 000 000 = 2.4 m3 = 2.4 × 1000 = 2400 litres

✗ 3.5 m2 = 350 cm2, using the length factor for an area.
✓ Convert the lengths first if you are unsure: a 1 m by 1 m square is 100 cm by 100 cm, which is 10 000 cm2.

subsections.heading: Areas of flat shapes
subsections.html:
Spec 4.9B–D · 2016 Edexcel SAM 1H Q10

Every area formula comes from the rectangle: base × perpendicular height.

Triangle and parallelogram — memorisetriangle = ½ × base × height  ·  parallelogram = base × heightthe height is perpendicular to the base, never the slanted side
Area of a trapezium — on the formula sheetA = ½(a + b)ha and b are the parallel sides · h is the perpendicular distance between them
  1. Compound shape: split it into rectangles, triangles, trapezia and parts of circles, or take a small shape away from a large one.
  2. Find any missing length first, often with Pythagoras.
  3. Add or subtract the areas. Keep full calculator values until the end.

Worked example: trapezium with parallel sides 7 cm and 11 cm, 5 cm apart

A = ½ × (7 + 11) × 5 = 45 cm2

SAM 1H Q10 is the classic compound shape: find BC by Pythagoras, then add the right-angled triangle (½ × base × height) and the semicircle on BC. The scheme gave M1 for each of the three parts, dependent on the first. Drill D4 is the same question with new numbers.

equations.name: Triangle and parallelogram
equations.formula: triangle = ½ × base × height  ·  parallelogram = base × height

equations.name: Area of a trapezium — on the formula sheet

subsections.heading: Circles and semicircles
subsections.html:
Spec 4.9E · 2018 Edexcel May 1H Q6

The circumference is π × diameter and the area is π × radius squared.

Circle — memoriseC = πd = 2πr  ·  A = πr2not on the formula sheet · halve the diameter before squaring

A semicircle's perimeter is half the circumference plus the diameter, because the straight edge is part of the boundary.

Worked example (2018 1H Q6, numbers changed): MON is a diameter of a circle, P is on the circle, MP = 4.5 cm, PN = 8.8 cm and angle MPN = 90°. Work out the circumference.

MN2 = 4.52 + 8.82 = 97.69   (M1)

MN = √97.69 = 9.8838…   (M1)

Circumference = π × 9.8838…   (M1, dependent)

= 31.050… = 31.1 cm (3 s.f.)   (A1)

Worked example: perimeter of a semicircle of diameter 12 cm

½ × π × 12 + 12 = 6π + 12 = 30.8 cm (3 s.f.)

subsections.heading: Arcs and sectors
subsections.html:
Spec 4.9A (Higher) · 2016 Edexcel Jan 4H Q24 · 2017 Edexcel Jan 3HR Q21 (old spec)

A sector with angle θ is the fraction θ/360 of the whole circle, so its arc and area are that fraction of the circumference and the area.

Arc length — memorisearc = (θ/360) × 2πrθ in degrees · radians are not in the spec · not on the formula sheet
Sector area — memorisesector area = (θ/360) × πr2perimeter of a sector = arc + 2r
  1. Write down θ/360 as a fraction.
  2. Arc: fraction × 2πr. Area: fraction × πr2.
  3. Perimeter: add the two radii to the arc.
  4. Working backwards from an area: set the formula equal to the area and solve for r2, then r.

Worked example 1: sector with radius 9 cm and angle 80°

Arc = (80/360) × 2π × 9 = 4π = 12.57 cm

Area = (80/360) × π × 81 = 18π = 56.5 cm2

Perimeter = 4π + 9 + 9 = 30.6 cm

Worked example 2: a sector has angle 72° and area 45π cm2. Work out its perimeter.

(72/360) × πr2 = 45π, so r2 = 45 × 360 ÷ 72 = 225   (M1)

r = 15   (A1)

Arc = (72/360) × 2π × 15 = 6π   (M1)

Perimeter = 6π + 15 + 15   (M1) = 48.849… = 48.8 cm   (A1)

✗ Giving the arc length when the question asks for the perimeter. The two radii are part of the boundary.
✗ Using 2πr for the area, or πr2 for the arc. Area has r2 because it is measured in square units.

subsections.heading: Prisms and cylinders
subsections.html:
Spec 4.10C–E · 2016 Edexcel SAM 2H Q3 · 2018 Edexcel May 2H Q6(a)

A prism has the same cross-section all the way through, so its volume is the area of that cross-section times its length.

Volume of a prism — on the formula sheetV = area of cross-section × lengthcuboid, triangular prism, trapezium prism, cylinder
Cylinder — on the formula sheetV = πr2h  ·  curved surface area = 2πrhtotal surface area = 2πrh + 2πr2, adding the two circular ends
  1. Find the shape that is the same all the way through: the cross-section.
  2. Work out its area.
  3. Multiply by the length (the distance between the two end faces).
  4. Surface area: add the area of every face. For a cylinder, the curved surface unrolls into a rectangle 2πr long and h high.

Worked example: cylinder of radius 4 cm and height 10 cm

V = π × 42 × 10 = 160π = 503 cm3 (3 s.f.)

Curved surface = 2π × 4 × 10 = 80π · two ends = 2 × π × 16 = 32π

Total surface area = 112π = 352 cm2 (3 s.f.)

equations.name: Volume of a prism — on the formula sheet

subsections.heading: Pyramids and cones
subsections.html:
Spec 4.10A (Higher), 4.10E · 2017 Edexcel Jan 4HR Q19 (old spec) · 2016 Edexcel SAM 1H Q19

A pyramid or cone holds exactly one third of the prism with the same base and height.

Volume of a pyramid — memoriseV = ⅓ × base area × perpendicular heightNOT on the formula sheet · the height is from the apex straight down to the base
Cone — on the formula sheetV = ⅓πr2h  ·  curved surface area = πrll = slant height · h = vertical height · l2 = r2 + h2
  1. Sketch the right-angled triangle inside the cone: radius r, height h, slant height l.
  2. Use Pythagoras to get whichever of r, h and l is missing.
  3. Volume uses the vertical height h. Curved surface uses the slant height l.
  4. Total surface area of a solid cone = πrl + πr2 (curved surface plus the base).

Worked example: cone with base radius 5 cm and height 12 cm

l = √(52 + 122) = √169 = 13 cm

V = ⅓ × π × 25 × 12 = 100π = 314 cm3

Curved surface = π × 5 × 13 = 65π · total = 65π + 25π = 90π cm2

A square-based pyramid with base 6 cm and height 10 cm: V = ⅓ × 36 × 10 = 120 cm3.

✗ Using the slant height in ⅓πr2h. The volume needs the vertical height.
✗ Forgetting the ⅓ for a pyramid: that gives the volume of a prism.
✗ Total surface area = πrl only. That is the curved part. A solid cone has a circular base too.

equations.name: Volume of a pyramid
equations.formula: V = ⅓ × base area × perpendicular height

equations.name: Cone — on the formula sheet
equations.formula: V = ⅓πr2h  ·  curved surface area = πrl

subsections.heading: Spheres and hemispheres
subsections.html:
Spec 4.10A (Higher) · 2018 Edexcel May 2H Q11 · 2015 Edexcel Jan 3HR Q18 (old spec)

A sphere's volume depends on r3 and its surface area on r2; a hemisphere is half of each, plus a flat circle if it is solid.

Sphere — on the formula sheetV = (4/3)πr3  ·  surface area = 4πr2hemisphere: V = (2/3)πr3 · curved surface 2πr2 · solid hemisphere total 3πr2

Worked examples

Sphere, radius 6 cm: V = (4/3) × π × 216 = 288π = 905 cm3 · SA = 4π × 36 = 144π = 452 cm2

Solid hemisphere, radius 5 cm: V = (2/3) × π × 125 = 262 cm3 · total SA = 2π × 25 + π × 25 = 75π = 236 cm2

✗ Putting the diameter into the formula. 2015 3HR Q18 gave a diameter of 18.6 cm: r = 9.3.
✗ Hemisphere surface = 2πr2 for a solid hemisphere. Add the flat circle: 3πr2.

subsections.heading: Frustums and composite solids
subsections.html:
Spec 4.10 · 2018 Edexcel May 1H Q16

A frustum is a large cone with a similar small cone cut off the top, so its volume is the large cone minus the small cone.

  1. Find the small cone's dimensions from the similar triangles (or the scale factor).
  2. Volume of frustum = volume of large cone − volume of small cone.
  3. Composite solids (a cone on a hemisphere, a cylinder with a hemisphere on top): add the volumes. For surface area, only count faces on the outside.

Worked example: a cone of radius 6 cm and height 16 cm has the top 8 cm cut off

The small cone is similar with scale factor 8/16 = ½, so its radius is 3 cm.

V = ⅓π(62 × 16) − ⅓π(32 × 8) = ⅓π(576 − 72) = 168π = 528 cm3 (3 s.f.)

Check with the volume scale factor: the small cone is (½)3 = ⅛ of the large one, so the frustum is ⅞ of 192π = 168π.

subsections.heading: Exact answers and algebraic volumes
subsections.html:
Spec 4.10 · 2017 Edexcel Jan 4HR Q19 · 2016 Edexcel Jan 3H Q19 (old spec)

"Give your answer as a multiple of π" or "in terms of π" means leave π as a symbol and do not use the π button.

  1. Write every formula with π in it.
  2. If both sides of an equation contain π, divide it out.
  3. Solve for the unknown, then write the answer as a number × π.

Worked example: a cylinder has height equal to twice its radius and volume 54π cm3. Find the radius.

πr2(2r) = 54π, so 2r3 = 54 and r3 = 27

r = 3 cm

Jan 16 3H Q19 is the algebraic version: a sphere and a cone of equal volume. Write both volumes, cancel π and the common powers of r, and rearrange for r. Drill D8 is one.

subsections.heading: Similar shapes: lengths
subsections.html:
Spec 4.11A (Foundation) · 2018 Edexcel May 2H Q6(b) · 2017 Edexcel Jan 4HR Q14 (old spec)

Similar shapes have equal angles and every length multiplied by the same scale factor k.

Length scale factor — memorisek = new length ÷ corresponding old lengthuse one pair of matching sides to find k, then multiply or divide every other length by it
  1. Match the corresponding sides. Redraw the two shapes the same way round if they are nested or flipped.
  2. Find k from a pair of lengths you know in both shapes.
  3. Big from small: × k. Small from big: ÷ k.
  4. For nested triangles (a line parallel to one side), use the whole side of the big triangle, not the extra piece.

Worked example: in triangle ABC, D is on AB and E is on AC with DE parallel to BC. AD = 4 cm, AB = 10 cm, DE = 6 cm. Find BC.

Triangles ADE and ABC are similar (corresponding angles are equal). k = 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5

BC = 6 × 2.5 = 15 cm

✗ Using DB = 6 as the big side. The big triangle's side is AB, the whole length.
✗ Adding instead of multiplying: "AB is 6 more than AD, so BC is 6 more than DE". Similar means multiply.

equations.name: Length scale factor
equations.formula: k = new length ÷ corresponding old length

subsections.heading: Similar shapes: area and volume
subsections.html:
Spec 4.11A–C (Higher) · 2016 Edexcel SAM 2H Q18 · 2018 Edexcel May 1H Q16

If lengths are multiplied by k, areas are multiplied by k2 and volumes by k3.

Area and volume scale factors — memoriselength × k  ·  area × k2  ·  volume × k3surface area and cross-section are areas · mass and capacity scale like volume
  1. Find the scale factor you are given (length, area or volume).
  2. Turn it into the length scale factor: square root an area ratio, cube root a volume ratio.
  3. Turn the length factor into the one you need: square it for area, cube it for volume.

Worked example 1: two similar bottles are 10 cm and 15 cm tall. The small one holds 400 cm3.

k = 15 ÷ 10 = 1.5 · volume factor = 1.53 = 3.375

Large bottle = 400 × 3.375 = 1350 cm3

Worked example 2: solids A and B are similar with surface areas 50 cm2 and 72 cm2. A has volume 250 cm3. Find the volume of B.

Area factor = 72/50 = 36/25, so length factor k = √(36/25) = 6/5   (M1)

Volume of B = 250 × (6/5)3 = 250 × 216/125   (M1) = 432 cm3   (A1)

Worked example 3 (2018 1H Q16, numbers changed): volume of frustum ÷ volume of large cone = 26/27. The large cone has height h. Find the height of the frustum.

Small cone ÷ large cone = 1 − 26/27 = 1/27   (M1)

Length scale factor = ∛(1/27) = 1/3   (M1)

Height of frustum = h − ⅓h   (M1) = ⅔h   (A1)

✗ Multiplying the volume by the area ratio 72/50. Areas and volumes scale differently: go through the length factor.
✗ Taking the cube root of 98/125 in the 2018 question. That ratio compared the frustum with the large cone. The frustum is not similar to anything: first find the small cone, 1 − 98/125 = 27/125.

equations.name: Area and volume scale factors
equations.formula: length × k  ·  area × k2  ·  volume × k3

subsections.heading: Compound measures: speed, density and pressure
subsections.html:
Spec 4.4F–G · 2016 Edexcel SAM 1H Q1 · 2018 Edexcel May 2H Q11 · 2016 Edexcel SAM 2H Q3

A compound measure is one quantity per unit of another, so it is always a division, and its units say which.

Speed — memorisespeed = distance ÷ timekm/h: kilometres per hour · time in hours as a decimal: 45 minutes = 0.75 h
Density — memorisedensity = mass ÷ volumeg/cm3 · mass = density × volume
Pressurepressure = force ÷ areaN/m2 · the spec says the pressure formula will be given
  1. Write the formula in words first.
  2. Convert the units so they match the answer's units: minutes to hours, cm3 or m3, and so on.
  3. Substitute and calculate. Rearrange if you need mass, time or force.

Worked examples

Speed: 420 km in 5 hours 36 minutes. 36 minutes = 36/60 = 0.6 h. Speed = 420 ÷ 5.6 = 75 km/h.

Converting: 72 km/h = 72 000 m ÷ 3600 s = 20 m/s.

Density: gold has density 19.3 g/cm3. A 12 cm3 bar has mass 19.3 × 12 = 231.6 g.

Pressure: a force of 800 N on 0.5 m2 gives 800 ÷ 0.5 = 1600 N/m2.

SAM 1H Q1 (7800 km in 9 h 45 min) gave M1 for "7800 ÷ 9.45", but only as a lesser method mark: the answer 800 needed 9.75 hours.

✗ 9 hours 45 minutes = 9.45 hours.
✓ 45 minutes = 45/60 = 0.75 hours, so 9.75 hours.

What you must memorise (not on the formula sheet)

Circle: C = πd · A = πr2 · arc = (θ/360) × 2πr · sector = (θ/360) × πr2 · sector perimeter = arc + 2r.

Triangle ½bh · parallelogram bh · pyramid ⅓ × base × height.

Similarity: length × k, area × k2, volume × k3. Always go through k.

Units: 1 m2 = 10 000 cm2 · 1 m3 = 1 000 000 cm3 · 1 litre = 1000 cm3.

Compound: speed = distance ÷ time · density = mass ÷ volume · pressure = force ÷ area.

On the formula sheet: trapezium ½(a + b)h · prism · cylinder πr2h and 2πrh · cone ⅓πr2h and πrl · sphere (4/3)πr3 and 4πr2.

questions.promptHtml: A shape is enlarged by scale factor 3. Why does its area become 9 times as big, not 3 times?
questions.answerHtml:
Area is a length times a length. Both lengths are multiplied by 3, so the area is multiplied by 3 × 3 = 9.

You can see it with squares: a 1 cm square enlarged by 3 becomes a 3 cm square, which holds nine of the original squares. Volume has three lengths, so it goes up by 33 = 27.

questions.promptHtml: Why is 1 m3 equal to 1 000 000 cm3 and not 100 cm3?
questions.answerHtml:
A 1 m cube is 100 cm long, 100 cm wide and 100 cm high. Its volume in cm3 is 100 × 100 × 100 = 1 000 000.

The conversion factor is applied once for each dimension: once for length, twice for area, three times for volume. It is the same idea as the scale factors in U1.

questions.promptHtml: Why does the arc length formula have 2πr, while the sector area formula has πr2?
questions.answerHtml:
The arc is a fraction of the circumference, which is a length: 2πr. The sector is a fraction of the whole circle's area: πr2.

In both, the fraction is θ/360, because a sector of angle θ is θ/360 of a full turn. A quick check: r2 only appears in things measured in square units.

questions.promptHtml: What goes wrong if you use the slant height in the cone volume formula, and why?
questions.answerHtml:
The volume is ⅓ × base area × perpendicular height, the distance straight up from the base to the apex. The slant height is longer (it is the hypotenuse of the triangle r, h, l), so the answer comes out too big.

The curved surface formula πrl uses l because the surface unrolls into a sector whose radius is the slant height.

questions.promptHtml: In the 2018 frustum question, why can you not take the cube root of 98/125 to get a scale factor?
questions.answerHtml:
Scale factors only exist between similar shapes. The frustum is not similar to the large cone: it has a flat top, the cone has a point.

The similar pair is the small cone and the large cone. The small cone is 1 − 98/125 = 27/125 of the large one, so k = ∛(27/125) = 3/5. The small cone's height is (3/5)h, and the frustum's is h − (3/5)h = (2/5)h.

questions.promptHtml: A solid hemisphere has total surface area 3πr2. Explain where the 3 comes from.
questions.answerHtml:
The curved part is half of a sphere's surface: ½ × 4πr2 = 2πr2.

The flat face is a circle of radius r: πr2. Together: 2πr2 + πr2 = 3πr2. A hollow bowl has only the 2πr2.

questions.promptHtml: A car travels 60 km at 30 km/h, then 60 km at 60 km/h. Why is its average speed not 45 km/h?
questions.answerHtml:
Average speed = total distance ÷ total time. The first 60 km takes 2 hours and the second takes 1 hour, so it is 120 km in 3 hours: 40 km/h.

The car spends longer at the slower speed, so the slow speed counts for more. Averaging the two speeds ignores that.

questions.promptHtml: Two similar jugs have heights in the ratio 2 : 3. A student says the larger jug holds 1.5 times as much. What is the correct factor, and why?
questions.answerHtml:
The length scale factor is 3/2 = 1.5. Capacity is a volume, so it scales by k3 = 1.53 = 3.375.

The jug is 1.5 times as tall, 1.5 times as wide and 1.5 times as deep, and all three multiply.

modules.title: Pythagoras and Trigonometry
modules.standfirst: Finding lengths and angles in triangles: right-angled ones with Pythagoras and SOHCAHTOA, any triangle with the sine rule, the cosine rule and ½ab sin C, and triangles hidden inside 3D solids. Every dated 4MA1 paper here has at least one of these, worth 3 to 6 marks. The skill that matters is picking the right rule, and not rounding until the end.

subsections.html: Every question here is a triangle with some sides and angles known. If it has a right angle, use Pythagoras (three sides) or SOHCAHTOA (sides and an angle). If it does not, use the sine rule or the cosine rule. In 3D, find a flat right-angled triangle inside the solid and do the same. Keep every value in your calculator until the final answer.

subsections.heading: Pythagoras' theorem
subsections.html:
Spec 4.8A · 2018 Edexcel May 1H Q6 · 2016 Edexcel SAM 1H Q10

In a right-angled triangle, the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides.

Pythagoras' theorem — memorisea2 + b2 = c2c = the hypotenuse, the longest side, opposite the right angle · not on the formula sheet
  1. Find the hypotenuse: the side opposite the right angle.
  2. Finding the hypotenuse: square both sides, add, square root.
  3. Finding a shorter side: square both, subtract the smaller from the hypotenuse, square root.
  4. Check: the hypotenuse must be the longest side.

Worked examples

Shorter sides 6.2 cm and 8.5 cm: c = √(6.22 + 8.52) = √110.69 = 10.5 cm (3 s.f.)   (M1 squares added, M1 square root, A1)

Hypotenuse 14 cm, one side 9.6 cm: a = √(142 − 9.62) = √103.84 = 10.2 cm (3 s.f.)

Pythagoras hides in other shapes: the diagonal of a rectangle, the height of an isosceles triangle (split it in half), the distance between two points, the diameter opposite a right angle in a semicircle.

✗ Adding the squares when you want a shorter side: the answer comes out longer than the hypotenuse.
✗ √(6.2 + 8.5). Square first, add, then root.

subsections.heading: SOHCAHTOA: sides and angles in right-angled triangles
subsections.html:
Spec 4.8B–C · 2018 Edexcel May 2H Q8 · 2016 Edexcel SAM 1H Q7 · 2018 Edexcel May 1H Q9

In a right-angled triangle, each trig ratio is one side divided by another, and it depends only on the angle.

Trigonometric ratios — memorisesin θ = O/H  ·  cos θ = A/H  ·  tan θ = O/AO = opposite the angle · A = adjacent (next to the angle, not the hypotenuse) · H = hypotenuse · "SOH CAH TOA"
  1. Label the sides O, A and H from the angle you are using.
  2. Tick the two sides involved: the one you know and the one you want (or both, for an angle).
  3. Pick the ratio with those two letters.
  4. Write the equation, e.g. cos 52 = 12.6/x, then rearrange.
  5. Angle: use the inverse: θ = sin−1(O/H), and so on.

Worked examples

Opposite from the hypotenuse: H = 18 cm, angle 40°. O = 18 × sin 40 = 11.6 cm   (M1 for sin 40 = O/18, M1 for 18 × sin 40, A1)

Hypotenuse from the adjacent: A = 7.5 cm, angle 28°. cos 28 = 7.5/H, so H = 7.5 ÷ cos 28 = 8.49 cm.

Angle: O = 5 cm, A = 8 cm. tan θ = 5/8, so θ = tan−1(0.625) = 32.0°.

2018 2H Q8 (x = 12.6 ÷ cos 52) accepted "20.4 – 20.5", so full accuracy mattered.

✗ x = 12.6 × cos 52. When the unknown is on the bottom, divide.
✗ Calculator in radians. Check that sin 30 = 0.5 before the exam starts.
✗ Rounding the first side to 4.2 in 2018 1H Q9, then using it for the second side. Keep 4.1589… in the calculator.

equations.name: Trigonometric ratios
equations.formula: sin θ = O/H  ·  cos θ = A/H  ·  tan θ = O/A

subsections.heading: Angles of elevation and depression
subsections.html:
Spec 4.8B (Higher) · 2013 Edexcel Jan 4H Q25 (old spec)

Angles of elevation and depression are both measured from the horizontal: up for elevation, down for depression.

  1. Draw the horizontal line from the observer's eye.
  2. Elevation is the angle up from it to the object. Depression is the angle down from it.
  3. The angle of depression from A to B equals the angle of elevation from B to A (alternate angles, since horizontals are parallel).
  4. Complete the right-angled triangle with the vertical and use SOHCAHTOA.

Worked example: from the top of a 30 m cliff, the angle of depression of a boat is 24°. How far is the boat from the foot of the cliff?

The angle of elevation of the cliff top from the boat is also 24°. The cliff is opposite that angle and the distance is adjacent.

tan 24 = 30/d, so d = 30 ÷ tan 24 = 67.4 m (3 s.f.)

Jan 13 4H Q25 had two angles from the same point: set up tan for each (both with the same horizontal distance), and use the difference of the two heights. Drill D6 is one.

✗ Measuring the angle of depression from the vertical cliff face. It is always from the horizontal.

subsections.heading: Bearings with trigonometry
subsections.html:
Spec 4.4D, 4.8C · 2017 Edexcel Jan 4HR Q9 · 2015 Edexcel Jan 3HR Q11 (old spec)

A bearing problem is a triangle problem with a north line drawn at each point: find the angle in the triangle, then convert it to a bearing.

  1. Draw a north line at every point named in the question.
  2. Put the distances on the diagram. East–west and north–south distances make a right angle.
  3. Find the angle inside the triangle with trig.
  4. Convert: the bearing is measured clockwise from north at the "from" point. Use 180° and 360° and alternate angles between parallel north lines.

Worked example: B is 30 km east and 50 km north of A. Work out the bearing of B from A, and of A from B.

At A, the angle between north and AB: tan θ = 30/50, so θ = tan−1(0.6) = 30.96…°   (M1, A1)

Bearing of B from A = 031° (nearest degree)   (A1)

Bearing of A from B = 031 + 180 = 211° (to the nearest degree, 30.96 + 180 = 210.96)

✗ Working out the angle from the east line and calling it the bearing. tan−1(50/30) = 59° is measured from east, not north.
✓ Always check which angle you found against the north line on your sketch.

subsections.heading: Sine, cosine and tangent of obtuse angles
subsections.html:
Spec 4.8A (Higher) · 2016 Edexcel SAM 2H Q21

For an obtuse angle, sin is positive and equals sin of its supplement, cos is negative, and tan is negative.

Supplementary angles — memorisesin(180° − x) = sin x  ·  cos(180° − x) = −cos xsin 150° = sin 30° = 0.5 · cos 120° = −cos 60° = −0.5

This matters in two places:

  1. Cosine rule for an angle: a negative cosine means the angle is obtuse, and cos−1 gives it correctly. Nothing extra to do.
  2. Sine rule for an angle: sin−1 only ever gives an acute angle. If the angle could be obtuse, the other answer is 180° minus the calculator's.

Worked example: in triangle ABC, a = 11 cm, b = 8 cm, angle B = 40°. Find angle A.

sin A / 11 = sin 40 / 8, so sin A = 11 × sin 40 ÷ 8 = 0.8838…

A = sin−1(0.8838…) = 62.1° or 180 − 62.1 = 117.9°. Both give a valid triangle, since 40 + 117.9 < 180.

The question will tell you which: "angle A is obtuse", or a diagram. In SAM 2H Q21 the question said angle LMN is obtuse, so the angle found by the sine rule (at L) had to be acute.

equations.name: Supplementary angles
equations.formula: sin(180° − x) = sin x  ·  cos(180° − x) = −cos x

subsections.heading: The sine rule
subsections.html:
Spec 4.8C (Higher) · 2016 Edexcel SAM 2H Q21

In any triangle, each side divided by the sine of its opposite angle gives the same number.

The sine rule — on the formula sheeta/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin Cside a is opposite angle A · for an angle, flip it: sin A/a = sin B/b
  1. Use it when you have a side and its opposite angle, plus one more side or angle.
  2. Label: each side takes the letter of the angle opposite it.
  3. Side: a/sin A = b/sin B, so b = a × sin B ÷ sin A.
  4. Angle: sin B = b × sin A ÷ a, then sin−1. Think about the obtuse alternative.

Worked example: angle A = 42°, angle B = 71°, a = 8 cm. Find b.

b/sin 71 = 8/sin 42   (M1)

b = 8 × sin 71 ÷ sin 42 = 11.3 cm (3 s.f.)   (A1)

equations.name: The sine rule — on the formula sheet
equations.formula: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C

subsections.heading: The cosine rule
subsections.html:
Spec 4.8C (Higher) · 2018 Edexcel May 2H Q18 · 2016 Edexcel Jan 4HR Q21 (old spec)

The cosine rule is Pythagoras with a correction term for angles that are not 90°.

The cosine rule — on the formula sheeta2 = b2 + c2 − 2bc cos AA is the angle BETWEEN sides b and c, opposite side a · if A = 90°, cos A = 0 and it is Pythagoras
Cosine rule for an angle — memorisecos A = (b2 + c2 − a2) ÷ 2bca is the side OPPOSITE the angle you want · it is the one subtracted
  1. Side: use it when you know two sides and the angle between them.
  2. Angle: use it when you know all three sides.
  3. Type the whole of b2 + c2 − 2bc cos A in one go, then square root.

Worked example 1: b = 7 cm, c = 10 cm, angle A = 52°. Find a.

a2 = 72 + 102 − 2 × 7 × 10 × cos 52 = 62.81…   (M1)

a = 7.93 cm (3 s.f.)   (A1)

Worked example 2: a triangle has sides 5 cm, 7 cm and 9 cm. Find its largest angle.

The largest angle is opposite the longest side, 9 cm.

cos θ = (52 + 72 − 92) ÷ (2 × 5 × 7) = −7/70 = −0.1   (M1)

θ = cos−1(−0.1)   (M1) = 95.7°   (A1). The negative cosine is why it is obtuse.

✗ Working 49 + 100 − 140 = 9, then × cos 52. The calculator must do 2bc cos A before subtracting: type it all in one line.
✗ Putting the longest side in the b2 + c2 part when you want the largest angle. It is the one you subtract.

equations.name: The cosine rule — on the formula sheet

subsections.heading: Area of a triangle: ½ab sin C
subsections.html:
Spec 4.8E (Higher) · 2016 Edexcel SAM 2H Q21 · 2016 Edexcel Jan 3H Q20 (old spec)

The area of any triangle is half the product of two sides times the sine of the angle between them.

Area of a triangle — on the formula sheetArea = ½ab sin CC is the angle BETWEEN sides a and b · ½ × base × height with height = b sin C

Worked example: two sides 9 cm and 13 cm with an angle of 58° between them

Area = ½ × 9 × 13 × sin 58 = 49.6 cm2 (3 s.f.)

If the angle you have is not between the two sides (as in SAM 2H Q21 and Jan 16 3H Q20), use the sine rule to find another angle, then 180° minus the two angles gives the included one. That is a 6-mark question: M1 sine rule, M1 sin−1, A1 the angle, M1 the included angle, M1 ½ab sin C, A1.

equations.name: Area of a triangle — on the formula sheet

subsections.heading: Choosing the rule
subsections.html:
Spec 4.8C

The information you have, not the question, decides the rule.

You knowYou wantUse
Right angle, two sidesThird sidePythagoras
Right angle, a side and an angleAnother sideSOHCAHTOA
Right angle, two sidesAn angleSOHCAHTOA, inverse
A side, its opposite angle, and one moreSide or angleSine rule
Two sides and the angle between themThe third sideCosine rule
Three sidesAn angleCosine rule, rearranged
Two sides and the angle between themArea½ab sin C

If none of these fit, find another angle first (angles in a triangle add up to 180°), then look again.

subsections.heading: Pythagoras in three dimensions
subsections.html:
Spec 4.8D (Higher) · 2018 Edexcel May 2H Q19 · 2013 Edexcel Jan 3H Q21 (old spec)

A length in 3D is found by using Pythagoras twice, once across a flat face and once up to the point.

Diagonal of a cuboid — memorised = √(a2 + b2 + c2)a, b, c = length, width, height · the space diagonal from one corner to the opposite corner
  1. Find a right-angled triangle that contains the length you want. Sketch it flat.
  2. One of its sides is usually a diagonal across the base. Find that first with Pythagoras.
  3. Use Pythagoras again in the upright triangle.

Worked example: cuboid 4 cm by 3 cm by 12 cm. Find the space diagonal.

Base diagonal = √(42 + 32) = 5 cm. Space diagonal = √(52 + 122) = 13 cm.

In one step: √(16 + 9 + 144) = √169 = 13.

subsections.heading: The angle between a line and a plane
subsections.html:
Spec 4.8F (Higher) · 2018 Edexcel May 2H Q19 · 2016 Edexcel SAM 1H Q19 · 2013 Edexcel Jan 3H Q21 (old spec)

The angle between a line and a plane is the angle between the line and its shadow on the plane, directly underneath it.

  1. From the top end of the line, drop a perpendicular to the plane. Where it lands is the foot.
  2. Join the foot to the point where the line meets the plane. That is the shadow (the projection).
  3. The line, its shadow and the perpendicular make a right-angled triangle, with the right angle at the foot.
  4. Find two of its sides (usually with Pythagoras), then use SOHCAHTOA for the angle at the point where the line meets the plane.

Worked example (2018 2H Q19, numbers changed): triangular prism with AF = 6 cm vertical, AB = 15 cm, BC = 8 cm. E is vertically above D. Angle FAB = angle ADC = angle BCD = 90°. Find the angle between BE and the plane ABCD.

E is above D, so the shadow of BE on the base is BD, and DE = AF = 6 cm.

BD2 = 152 + 82 = 289, so BD = 17 cm   (M1 for a complete method for BD or BE)

tan θ = DE/BD = 6/17   (M1)

θ = 19.4° (1 d.p.)   (A1)

SAM 1H Q19 is the same idea on a cone: the slant height from the curved surface area (πrl = 130), then sin(AVO) = 4.5 ÷ l, and angle AVB is double AVO. The spec says the angle between two planes is not required.

✗ Using the angle at the wrong end: the angle is at the point where the line meets the plane, not at the top.
✗ Using a side edge (BC or AB) as the shadow. The shadow goes to the point directly below the top of the line.

subsections.heading: Problems with more than one triangle
subsections.html:
Spec 4.8C, 4.4D · 2016 Edexcel SAM 2H Q21 · 2017 Edexcel Jan 4HR Q9 (old spec)

In a long problem, each triangle gives you one new length or angle that unlocks the next triangle.

  1. Draw the diagram. For journeys, draw north lines at every turning point.
  2. Find the angle inside the triangle at each turn, using bearings and 180°.
  3. Pick the rule for that triangle (see the table above). Keep full calculator values.
  4. Convert back to a bearing at the end if asked.

Worked example: a ship sails 8 km from S on a bearing of 040° to T, then 11 km on a bearing of 115° to F. Find the distance SF and the bearing of F from S.

At T, the bearing back to S is 040 + 180 = 220°. The angle STF = 220 − 115 = 105°.

SF2 = 82 + 112 − 2 × 8 × 11 × cos 105 = 230.55…   (M1)

SF = 15.2 km (3 s.f.)   (A1)

Sine rule: sin(TSF) = 11 × sin 105 ÷ 15.18… so angle TSF = 44.4°   (M1)

Bearing of F from S = 040 + 44.4 = 084° (nearest degree)   (A1)

The rules and when to use them

Pythagoras (memorise): a2 + b2 = c2, c the hypotenuse. Add for the hypotenuse, subtract for a shorter side.

SOHCAHTOA (memorise): sin = O/H · cos = A/H · tan = O/A. Unknown on the bottom: divide.

Sine rule (formula sheet): a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C. Needs a side with its opposite angle.

Cosine rule (formula sheet): a2 = b2 + c2 − 2bc cos A. Angle version cos A = (b2 + c2 − a2)/2bc is not on the sheet.

Area (formula sheet): ½ab sin C, C between a and b.

Obtuse: sin(180 − x) = sin x · a negative cos means an obtuse angle.

3D: d = √(a2 + b2 + c2) · line and plane: the angle between the line and its shadow.

Bearings: north lines at every point · clockwise from north · three figures · back bearing ± 180.

subsections.heading: Definitions marked to the word
subsections.html:
TermAccepted wording
HypotenuseThe longest side of a right-angled triangle, opposite the right angle
Opposite sideThe side across from the angle being used
Adjacent sideThe side next to the angle being used that is not the hypotenuse
Angle of elevationThe angle up from the horizontal to an object
Angle of depressionThe angle down from the horizontal to an object
Included angleThe angle between two given sides
Projection of a line on a planeThe line's shadow: from where it meets the plane to the foot of the perpendicular from its other end
Angle between a line and a planeThe angle between the line and its projection on the plane

questions.promptHtml: Why does sin 40° have the same value in every right-angled triangle with a 40° angle, however big the triangle?
questions.answerHtml:
All right-angled triangles with a 40° angle have the same three angles (90°, 40°, 50°), so they are similar. Every side is multiplied by the same scale factor.

A ratio of two sides, like opposite ÷ hypotenuse, has the scale factor on the top and the bottom, so it cancels. The ratio depends only on the angle. That is what makes trigonometry possible.

questions.promptHtml: Show that the cosine rule turns into Pythagoras' theorem when the angle is 90°. What does that tell you about the sign of the correction term?
questions.answerHtml:
a2 = b2 + c2 − 2bc cos A. When A = 90°, cos 90° = 0, so a2 = b2 + c2: Pythagoras.

When A is acute, cos A is positive, so a2 is less than b2 + c2: the opposite side is shorter than for a right angle. When A is obtuse, cos A is negative, so the term is added and the side is longer. Both match what you would expect from opening or closing the angle.

questions.promptHtml: Why does the sine rule sometimes give two possible angles, while the cosine rule never does?
questions.answerHtml:
sin x = sin(180° − x), so an acute angle and its obtuse partner have the same sine. Knowing sin B does not tell you which. The calculator's sin−1 always gives the acute one.

Cosines of acute angles are positive and of obtuse angles negative, so every value of cos between −1 and 1 belongs to exactly one angle between 0° and 180°. cos−1 picks the right one.

questions.promptHtml: Where does Area = ½ab sin C come from?
questions.answerHtml:
Take side a as the base. Drop a perpendicular from the opposite vertex to the base. It makes a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse b and angle C, so the height is b sin C (SOHCAHTOA: opposite = hypotenuse × sin).

Area = ½ × base × height = ½ × a × b sin C. That is also why C must be the angle between a and b.

questions.promptHtml: A student rounds the first side in a two-step trig problem to 3 s.f. and gets a final answer that is 0.1 out. Why, and how is it avoided?
questions.answerHtml:
The rounding error in the first value is carried into the second calculation and can grow, especially after multiplying by a large number or dividing by a small sine. The final answer lands outside the mark scheme's range, and the A1 is lost.

Store the unrounded value in the calculator's memory (or use the ANS key), write the rounded value in your working with "…" after it, and round only the final answer.

questions.promptHtml: In the angle between a line and a plane, why must you use the line's shadow, and not any other line in the plane?
questions.answerHtml:
A line meets a plane at one point, and makes different angles with the different lines through that point in the plane. The angle "between the line and the plane" means the smallest of these angles.

The smallest is with the line directly under it: its projection. That is the only choice that makes a right-angled triangle with the perpendicular, so SOHCAHTOA applies.

questions.promptHtml: Why is the bearing of A from B always 180° different from the bearing of B from A?
questions.answerHtml:
The north lines at A and B are parallel. The line AB crosses them both. The direction from B back to A points exactly the opposite way to the direction from A to B.

Turning to face the opposite way is a turn of 180°, so the back bearing is the bearing ± 180°. Use + if the first bearing is under 180°, − if it is over.

questions.promptHtml: For the largest angle of a triangle with sides 8, 10 and 14, why is it enough to find one angle, and which one?
questions.answerHtml:
In any triangle, the largest angle is opposite the longest side. So the angle opposite 14 is the only one needed.

cos θ = (82 + 102 − 142)/(2 × 8 × 10) = −32/160 = −0.2, giving θ = 101.5°. The negative cosine confirms it is obtuse, and a triangle can have only one obtuse angle.

modules.title: Vectors and Transformations
modules.standfirst: Two topics that share one idea: movement described precisely. Column vectors and the "show by a vector method" proof sit near the end of Paper 1H, worth five marks each time. Transformations come earlier and are nearly free, as long as you say every detail and describe one transformation, not two.

subsections.html:
A vector is a movement: how far, and which way. Once you can add movements, you can find any route through a diagram, and proofs about parallel lines and straight lines become algebra. Transformations are the second half: four ways to move a shape, each with a fixed list of details the examiner is waiting for.

Notation in this module: AB→ is the vector from A to B (in the exam it is written with an arrow over it, as here). A bold lower-case letter such as a is a vector (handwritten with a wavy line underneath). 3−2 is a column vector: 3 right, 2 down.

subsections.heading: What a vector is and how it is written
subsections.html:
Spec 5.1A, 5.1B · 2018 Edexcel May 1H Q17

A vector has both a size (magnitude) and a direction; a column vector gives the movement across on top and the movement up underneath.

  1. Top number: x-movement. Positive is right, negative is left.
  2. Bottom number: y-movement. Positive is up, negative is down.
  3. To get the vector from A to B, subtract coordinates: AB→ = B − A (end minus start).
  4. Going the opposite way flips every sign: BA→ = −AB→.

Worked example: A(2, −1) and B(7, 3)

1. AB→ = end − start = 7−23−(−1) = 54 1

2. BA→ = −AB→ = −5−4

A number without direction, such as a length or a scale factor, is a scalar.

✗ AB→ = A − B, giving −5−4: start minus end reverses the direction.
✗ Writing a column vector as coordinates, (5, 4), or with a fraction line between the numbers.
✓ AB→ = B − A = 54, written as a column with no line.

subsections.heading: Adding, subtracting and multiplying by a number
subsections.html:
Spec 5.1C, 5.1D

Column vectors are added, subtracted and multiplied by a scalar one row at a time.

  1. Multiply first: every number in the vector is multiplied by the scalar.
  2. Then add or subtract the tops, and separately the bottoms.
  3. Take extra care with "minus a negative".

Worked example: a = 3−2, b = −14. Find 2a − 3b

1. 2a = 6−4 and 3b = −312 M1

2. Tops: 6 − (−3) = 9. Bottoms: −4 − 12 = −16.

3. 2a − 3b = 9−16 A1

A scalar multiple points the same way (or exactly the opposite way, if negative). That single fact is behind every parallel-line proof later on.

✗ 6 − (−3) = 3.
✓ 6 − (−3) = 6 + 3 = 9. Write the subtraction with brackets before you simplify it.

subsections.heading: Magnitude (modulus) of a vector
subsections.html:
Spec 5.1E

The magnitude of a vector is its length, found by Pythagoras on its two components.

Magnitude of a column vector|xy| = √(x2 + y2)x and y are the components · the answer is a length, so it is never negative
  1. Simplify the vector into a single column first.
  2. Square each component. A negative squared is positive.
  3. Add, square root, and round only at the end.

Worked example: a = 31, b = −25. Find |2a − b|

1. 2a − b = 6−(−2)2−5 = 8−3 M1

2. √(82 + (−3)2) = √(64 + 9) = √73 M1

3. = 8.544… = 8.54 (3 s.f.) A1

✗ |a| + |b| for |a + b|. Two separate lengths do not add unless the vectors point the same way.
✗ √(82 − 32): the minus sign disappears when you square.
✓ Combine the vectors first, then use √(x2 + y2).

subsections.heading: Using vectors to find coordinates
subsections.html:
Spec 5.1B, 5.1F · 2018 Edexcel May 1H Q17(a)

A position plus a vector gives a new position: start point + movement = end point.

  1. Write down what you know as a chain of points, e.g. B, then A, then C.
  2. To go backwards along a vector, subtract it. To go forwards, add it.
  3. In a parallelogram ABCD, opposite sides are equal vectors: AB→ = DC→ and AD→ = BC→.

Worked example: AB→ = 35, AC→ = 98, B is (4, 6). Find C.

1. A = B − AB→ = (4 − 3, 6 − 5) = (1, 1) M1

2. C = A + AC→ = (1 + 9, 1 + 8) M1

3. C = (10, 9) A1

Or in one step: BC→ = BA→ + AC→ = −3+9−5+8 = 63, and (4 + 6, 6 + 3) = (10, 9).

subsections.heading: Routes through a diagram (resultant vectors)
subsections.html:
Spec 5.1F · 2016 Edexcel SAM 1H Q22

To find a vector between two points, travel there along any route made of vectors you already know.

  1. Write the route as a sum of letters: OC→ = OA→ + AB→ + BC→. The inner letters must chain (A to A, B to B).
  2. Replace each piece with its vector. Going against an arrow, use the negative.
  3. Collect the a terms and the b terms and simplify.

Worked example: OA→ = 3a, AB→ = 2b, BC→ = c

1. OC→ = OA→ + AB→ + BC→ = 3a + 2b + c

2. CA→ = CB→ + BA→ = −c − 2b

The most-used route of all: if OA→ = a and OB→ = b, then AB→ = AO→ + OB→ = −a + b = b − a.

✗ AB→ = a − b when OA→ = a and OB→ = b.
✓ AB→ = b − a. "End minus start" works for position vectors too.

subsections.heading: Points that divide a line in a ratio
subsections.html:
Spec 5.1F, 5.1G · 2016 Edexcel SAM 1H Q22 · 2016 Edexcel Jan 3HR Q19

If P divides AB in the ratio m : n, then AP→ is m/(m + n) of AB→.

  1. Add the ratio parts to get the denominator: AP : PB = 2 : 3 means AP is 2/5 of AB, not 2/3.
  2. Find the whole vector AB→ first, as a route.
  3. AP→ = (fraction) × AB→, then OP→ = OA→ + AP→.
  4. The midpoint is the ratio 1 : 1, so its fraction is 1/2.

Worked example: OA→ = a, OB→ = b, P on AB with AP : PB = 1 : 3. Find OP→.

1. AB→ = b − a B1

2. AP→ = 1/4(b − a), because 1 + 3 = 4 parts M1

3. OP→ = a + 1/4(b − a) = 3/4 a + 1/4 b A1

Check: the coefficients add up to 1 (3/4 + 1/4). For a point on the line AB they always do.

✗ AP : PB = 1 : 3, so AP→ = 1/3 AB→.
✓ 1 : 3 is 4 parts in total, so AP→ = 1/4 AB→ and PB→ = 3/4 AB→.

subsections.heading: Proving two lines are parallel
subsections.html:
Spec 5.1G · 2016 Edexcel SAM 1H Q22 · 2014 Edexcel Jan 3H Q21

Two vectors are parallel if one is a scalar multiple of the other, so the proof is: find both vectors, then show one equals a number times the other.

  1. Find the first vector by a route, in terms of a and b. Simplify fully.
  2. Find the second vector the same way.
  3. Factorise each so the same bracket appears, e.g. 2(b + 2a) and 3(b + 2a).
  4. Write the conclusion: "AE→ = 2/3 BC→, so AE is parallel to BC."

Worked example: trapezium ABCD, AB→ = 6a, AD→ = 2b, DC→ = 9a. E is on DB with DE : EB = 1 : 2. Show that AE is parallel to BC.

1. AE→ = AD→ + DE→ (a route) M1

2. DB→ = DA→ + AB→ = −2b + 6a, so DE→ = 1/3(6a − 2b) = 2a − 2/3b M1

3. AE→ = 2b + 2a − 2/3b = 2a + 4/3b A1

4. BC→ = BA→ + AD→ + DC→ = −6a + 2b + 9a = 3a + 2b M1

5. AE→ = 2/3(3a + 2b) = 2/3 BC→, so AE is parallel to BC A1

From the same mark scheme: "NB Correct expressions for BC and AE must be given".

✗ Finding both vectors and stopping. The last A1 needs the link and the word parallel.
✓ "AE→ = 2/3 BC→, a multiple, so AE is parallel to BC."

subsections.heading: Proving three points lie on a straight line
subsections.html:
Spec 5.1G · 2018 Edexcel May 1H Q17(b) · 2012 Edexcel Jan 4H Q22

Three points are on a straight line (collinear) if two of the vectors between them are parallel and share a point.

  1. Pick a point common to both vectors, e.g. AB→ and AE→ both start at A.
  2. Find both vectors, as columns or in terms of a and b.
  3. Show one is a multiple of the other.
  4. Conclude: "parallel and they share the point A, so A, B and E are on a straight line".

Worked example: A is (1, 1), AB→ = 35, E is (31, 51). Prove that ABE is a straight line.

1. AE→ = 31−151−1 = 3050 M1

2. 3050 = 1035, so AE→ = 10AB→. The lines are parallel and both pass through A, so ABE is a straight line A1

The 2018 scheme also accepted comparing ratios: 50 ÷ 30 = 5 ÷ 3, so the gradients match.

✗ "AE→ = 10AB→ so they are parallel." Parallel lines can be side by side.
✓ "…parallel, and share the point A, so A, B and E are collinear."

subsections.heading: The four transformations and what each one needs
subsections.html:
Spec 5.2I, 5.2K, 5.2M · 2016 Edexcel SAM 2H Q6

"Describe fully" means the name of the transformation plus every detail that fixes it. Each detail is a separate B1.

TransformationDetails to stateShape after
Translationthe column vectorcongruent, same way round
Reflectionthe equation of the mirror linecongruent, flipped
Rotationcentre, angle, direction (clockwise or anticlockwise)congruent, turned
Enlargementcentre and scale factorsimilar: same angles, lengths × scale factor

Translations, reflections and rotations keep lengths and angles, so the image is congruent. Enlargements keep the angles but change the lengths.

✗ "It moved 4 right and 3 up." / "It turned 90°." / "It got bigger."
✓ "Translation by 43." / "Rotation 90° clockwise about (0, 0)." / "Enlargement, scale factor 2, centre (1, 3)."

subsections.heading: Translations and reflections
subsections.html:
Spec 5.2D–5.2H · 2016 Edexcel SAM 2H Q6(a)

A translation slides every point by the same column vector; a reflection puts every image point the same perpendicular distance from the mirror line on the other side.

  1. Translate: move every vertex by the vector, e.g. 52 is 5 right and 2 up. Then join up.
  2. Reflect: for each vertex, measure straight across (at 90°) to the mirror line, and go the same distance out the other side.
  3. Find a mirror line: it runs halfway between each point and its image. Give its equation.
Mirror lineWhat it looks likePoint (3, 1) goes to
x = 2vertical, through 2 on the x-axis(1, 1)
y = −1horizontal, through −1 on the y-axis(3, −3)
y = xdiagonal, up to the right(1, 3): swap the coordinates
y = −xdiagonal, down to the right(−1, −3): swap and change both signs

✗ "Reflection in the y-axis line" or "reflection in x = 0 … I mean y = 0". The x-axis is y = 0 and the y-axis is x = 0.
✓ Write the equation: "Reflection in the line x = 0 (the y-axis)."

subsections.heading: Rotations
subsections.html:
Spec 5.2A–5.2C · 2016 Edexcel SAM 2H Q6(b)

A rotation turns a shape about a fixed centre through an angle; anticlockwise counts as positive and clockwise as negative.

  1. Find the angle by comparing one side before and after (a vertical side that becomes horizontal has turned 90°).
  2. Find the direction: clockwise or anticlockwise. For 180° the direction does not matter.
  3. Find the centre with tracing paper, or where the perpendicular bisectors of point-to-image lines meet.
  4. Write all three: "Rotation, 90° anticlockwise, centre (−3, 0)."
About (0, 0)(x, y) goes to(4, 1) goes to
90° anticlockwise(−y, x)(−1, 4)
90° clockwise(y, −x)(1, −4)
180°(−x, −y)(−4, −1)

Worked example: rotate (4, 1) through 90° anticlockwise about (1, 2)

1. Position relative to the centre: (4 − 1, 1 − 2) = (3, −1).

2. Rotate that 90° anticlockwise: (3, −1) goes to (1, 3).

3. Add the centre back on: (1 + 1, 3 + 2) = (2, 5).

In the exam, use the tracing paper you are allowed: trace the shape, pin the centre with your pencil, turn 90°.

The SAM scheme accepted "+90°, 270° clockwise, −270°" for 90° anticlockwise. What it will not accept is an angle with no direction.

✗ "Rotation 90° about (−3, 0)."
✓ "Rotation 90° anticlockwise about (−3, 0)."

subsections.heading: Enlargements, including fractional scale factors
subsections.html:
Spec 5.2J–5.2L · 2014 Edexcel Jan 3H Q9 · 2016 Edexcel Jan 3HR Q3

An enlargement multiplies every distance from the centre by the scale factor; a scale factor between 0 and 1 makes the shape smaller but it is still called an enlargement.

Scale factorscale factor = image length ÷ object lengthgreater than 1 → bigger · between 0 and 1 → smaller · angles never change
  1. For each vertex, find the vector from the centre to it.
  2. Multiply that vector by the scale factor.
  3. Add the result to the centre to get the image vertex.
  4. To find the centre of a given enlargement: draw straight lines through each vertex and its image. They meet at the centre.

Worked example: enlarge (6, 4) with scale factor 1/2, centre (−2, 0)

1. From the centre to the point: (6 − (−2), 4 − 0) = (8, 4).

2. × 1/2: (4, 2).

3. Image = (−2 + 4, 0 + 2) = (2, 2).

Scale factor 3, centre (1, 1), point (2, 3): from the centre (1, 2), × 3 gives (3, 6), image (4, 7).

Going back the other way undoes the scale factor: if P to Q is scale factor 3, then Q to P is scale factor 1/3 with the same centre.

Negative scale factors are not on 4MA1. The spec says enlargements are "positive scale factor only (including fractions)", so you will not be asked for one.

✗ "Enlargement scale factor 1/3" with no centre: one mark of three.
✗ Calling scale factor 1/3 a "reduction" or "shrink". The mark scheme word is enlargement.
✓ "Enlargement, scale factor 1/3, centre (4, 3)."

equations.name: Scale factor
equations.formula: scale factor = image length ÷ object length

subsections.heading: Combining transformations into one
subsections.html:
Spec 5.2M · 2014 Edexcel Jan 3H Q9(c)

When a question gives two transformations one after the other, find the single transformation by tracking a few vertices from the start to the end.

  1. Pick two or three vertices and apply the first transformation, then the second.
  2. Compare the start and end shapes: same size or not? Same way round or flipped? Turned?
  3. Name the single transformation and give all its details.

Useful results: reflect in the x-axis then the y-axis = rotation 180° about (0, 0). Two translations = one translation by the sum of the vectors.

The facts behind most of the marks

AB→ = B − A (end minus start). BA→ = −AB→. If OA→ = a and OB→ = b, then AB→ = b − a.

Magnitude: |xy| = √(x2 + y2).

Ratio m : n along AB: AP→ = m/(m + n) × AB→.

Parallel: one vector = a number × the other. Straight line: parallel and a shared point.

Describe fully: translation + vector · reflection + mirror line equation · rotation + centre + angle + direction · enlargement + centre + scale factor.

About (0, 0): 90° anticlockwise (x, y) → (−y, x) · 90° clockwise (x, y) → (y, −x) · 180° (x, y) → (−x, −y) · in y = x, swap.

questions.promptHtml: Why is AB→ = b − a, and not a − b, when OA→ = a and OB→ = b?
questions.answerHtml:
To get from A to B you can go A → O → B. A to O is backwards along a, so it is −a. O to B is b. The total is −a + b = b − a.

It is the same "end minus start" rule as for coordinates. a − b is BA→, the same length but pointing the other way.

questions.promptHtml: You have shown PQ→ = 3PR→. Why does that prove P, Q and R are on a straight line, but PQ→ = 3ST→ would not prove P, Q, S and T are?
questions.answerHtml:
A multiple only proves the two lines point the same direction: they are parallel.

PQ and PR both pass through P, and two parallel lines through the same point must be the same line. So P, Q and R are collinear. PQ and ST share no point, so they could be two separate parallel lines, like the opposite sides of a parallelogram.

questions.promptHtml: P is on AB with AP : PB = 2 : 3. Why is AP→ = 2/5 AB→, not 2/3 AB→?
questions.answerHtml:
The ratio splits the whole line into 2 + 3 = 5 equal parts. AP is 2 of those 5 parts, so it is 2/5 of AB.

2/3 compares AP with PB, not with the whole line. Check: 2/5 + 3/5 = 1, the whole of AB. With 2/3 and 3/3 you would get more than the whole line.

questions.promptHtml: Why does reflecting in the line y = x just swap the coordinates?
questions.answerHtml:
The line y = x is at 45°, so it treats the two axes symmetrically. Reflecting in it swaps the x-axis and the y-axis over.

A point 3 across and 1 up becomes 1 across and 3 up: (3, 1) → (1, 3). Points on the line, like (2, 2), stay where they are, which is what you would expect of a mirror line.

questions.promptHtml: A shape is enlarged with scale factor 1/2. Why is this still called an enlargement, and what happens to its angles and its lengths?
questions.answerHtml:
"Enlargement" is the name of the transformation type: every distance from the centre is multiplied by the same number. The number can be less than 1.

Lengths are all halved. Angles are unchanged, so the image is similar to the object. The position also moves, towards the centre, because each distance from the centre is halved too.

questions.promptHtml: Why does "rotation 90° clockwise about (0, 0), then translation by 20" score no marks, even if it does map A onto B?
questions.answerHtml:
The question asks for the single transformation. The mark scheme says that if more than one transformation is given, no marks can be awarded.

A rotation followed by a translation is always equal to one rotation about a different centre. Find that centre (tracing paper, or perpendicular bisectors) and describe just the one rotation.

questions.promptHtml: a = 30 and b = 04. Why is |a + b| = 5 and not 7?
questions.answerHtml:
a + b = 34, and its length is √(32 + 42) = 5.

Walking 3 east then 4 north covers 7, but you end up only 5 from where you started, in a straight line. Magnitudes only add when the vectors point the same way.

questions.promptHtml: Why do the perpendicular bisectors of the lines joining each point to its image meet at the centre of rotation?
questions.answerHtml:
A rotation keeps each point the same distance from the centre. So the centre is equidistant from a point and its image.

All points equidistant from two points lie on their perpendicular bisector. The centre must be on every one of these bisectors, so it is where they cross. In the exam, tracing paper and trial and error is usually quicker.

modules.title: Statistics
modules.standfirst: Some of the most reliable marks on the course. Every dated 4MA1 paper here opens or nearly opens with an estimated mean from a grouped table, and a cumulative frequency graph or a histogram is never far behind. The methods are fixed routines. The marks go to people who use midpoints, divide by the right total, and read the graph at the right height.

subsections.html: Statistics on 4MA1 is about three things: a typical value (an average), how spread out the data are, and pictures that show both. The Higher tier adds cumulative frequency graphs, quartiles and histograms with unequal class widths. Box plots are not on the 4MA1 specification, so you will not be asked to draw one.

subsections.heading: Mean, median, mode and range from a list
subsections.html:
Spec 6.2A–B (Foundation) · 2016 Edexcel SAM 2H Q7

The mean shares the total out equally, the median is the middle value once the data are in order, the mode is the most common value, and the range is largest minus smallest.

  1. Order the data first. Count how many values there are, n.
  2. Median: the value in position (n + 1)/2. If that is a half, take the mean of the two middle values.
  3. Mean: add them all, divide by n.
  4. Range: largest − smallest. It is a single number, not "3 to 12".
Meanmean = total of the values ÷ number of valuesso total = mean × number of values, which is the key to every reverse-mean question

Worked example: 4, 9, 2, 7, 7, 5, 10, 3, 8, 6, 11

1. In order: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11. There are 11 values.

2. Median: position (11 + 1)/2 = 6th, so the median is 7.

3. Mode 7. Range 11 − 2 = 9. Mean 72 ÷ 11 = 6.55 (3 s.f.).

equations.name: Mean
equations.formula: mean = total of the values ÷ number of values

subsections.heading: Working backwards from a mean, and combining groups
subsections.html:
Spec 6.2B (Foundation) · 2018 Edexcel May 2H Q7 · 2016 Edexcel SAM 2H Q7

Means cannot be added or averaged directly, but totals can: convert every mean to a total first.

  1. Total for each group = mean × number in the group.
  2. Add or subtract totals, and numbers of people, as the question needs.
  3. Divide the new total by the new number of people.

Worked example: 24 students have a mean of 68; 16 other students have a mean of 73. Find the mean of all 40.

1. Totals: 24 × 68 = 1632 and 16 × 73 = 1168 M1

2. Combined total 1632 + 1168 = 2800 M1

3. Mean = 2800 ÷ 40 = 70 A1

Backwards: a class of 30 has mean 71.5. The 18 boys have mean 69. Girls' total = 30 × 71.5 − 18 × 69 = 2145 − 1242 = 903, so the 12 girls' mean is 903 ÷ 12 = 75.25.

✗ (68 + 73) ÷ 2 = 70.5. That only works when the groups are the same size.
✓ Weight each mean by its group size: total ÷ total number.

subsections.heading: Frequency tables for ungrouped data
subsections.html:
Spec 6.2A–B (Foundation) · 2014 Edexcel Jan 4H Q4

In a frequency table each value appears "frequency" times, so the total of the data is the sum of value × frequency.

  1. Add a column for x × f.
  2. Mean = (total of the x × f column) ÷ (total of the f column).
  3. Median: find the position (n + 1)/2, then run down a cumulative total of f until you pass it.
  4. Mode: the value with the highest frequency, not the highest frequency itself.

Worked example: number of pets x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 with frequencies 3, 7, 9, 4, 2

1. x × f: 3, 14, 27, 16, 10. Total = 70 M1

2. Total frequency = 25, so mean = 70 ÷ 25 = 2.8 A1

3. Median position (25 + 1)/2 = 13th. Running totals 3, 10, 19: the 13th value is in the "3" row, so the median is 3. The mode is 3 (frequency 9).

✗ Mean = 70 ÷ 5, dividing by the number of rows.
✗ "Mode = 9", giving the frequency.
✓ Divide by the total frequency, 25. The mode is the value, 3.

subsections.heading: Grouped data: modal class and the estimated mean
subsections.html:
Spec 6.2C–D (Foundation) · 2018 Edexcel May 1H Q1 · 2016 Edexcel SAM 1H Q3 · 2016 Edexcel Jan 4HR Q7

With grouped data you do not know the exact values, so you use each class midpoint as a stand-in, which is why the mean is only an estimate.

  1. Find the midpoint of each class: (lower bound + upper bound) ÷ 2.
  2. Multiply each midpoint by its frequency.
  3. Add those products, and divide by the total frequency.
  4. Modal class: the class with the highest frequency. Write it as the class, e.g. 20 < m ≤ 30.

Worked example: masses 0–10 (5), 10–20 (12), 20–30 (18), 30–50 (10), 50–80 (5)

1. Midpoints 5, 15, 25, 40, 65. Products 25, 180, 450, 400, 325 M1 M1

2. Total 1380; total frequency 50 M1

3. Estimated mean = 1380 ÷ 50 = 27.6 A1

This is how the 4-mark estimated mean is scored: M2 for frequency × midpoint (M1 if you use a consistent value in each class that is not the midpoint), M1 for dividing by the total frequency, A1.

From the SAM 1H scheme: "M1 for frequency × consistent value within interval". Using the class ends instead of midpoints loses a method mark straight away.

✗ Dividing by 5, the number of classes, or by the sum of the midpoints.
✓ Σ(midpoint × frequency) ÷ Σ frequency.

subsections.heading: Quartiles and interquartile range from a list
subsections.html:
Spec 6.2B–C (Higher) · 2016 Edexcel SAM 1H Q12 · 2015 Edexcel Jan 3HR Q12

The quartiles cut ordered data into four equal parts, and the interquartile range (upper quartile − lower quartile) is the spread of the middle half.

  1. Put the data in order.
  2. Lower quartile: position (n + 1)/4. Median: (n + 1)/2. Upper quartile: 3(n + 1)/4.
  3. IQR = UQ − LQ.

Worked example: the 11 values 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11

1. In order already; (11 + 1)/4 = 3, so the LQ is the 3rd value, 4 M1

2. UQ is the 3 × 3 = 9th value, 9 M1

3. IQR = 9 − 4 = 5 A1

The IQR ignores the top and bottom quarters, so a single very large or very small value (an outlier) does not affect it. The range uses exactly those extreme values.

subsections.heading: Cumulative frequency tables and graphs
subsections.html:
Spec 6.1B–C (Higher) · 2016 Edexcel SAM 2H Q12 · 2014 Edexcel Jan 3H Q8

Cumulative frequency is a running total, and each running total is plotted at the upper end of its class.

  1. Running totals: add each frequency on to the one before. The last one must equal the total.
  2. Plot each total at the upper class boundary: 0 < m ≤ 10 is plotted at 10, not 5.
  3. Join the points with a smooth curve or straight line segments. You may start at (lowest boundary, 0).

Worked example: frequencies 8, 17, 25, 40, 22, 8 for 0–10, 10–20, …, 50–60

1. Cumulative frequencies: 8, 25, 50, 90, 112, 120 B1

2. Points: (10, 8), (20, 25), (30, 50), (40, 90), (50, 112), (60, 120) M1

3. Join with a curve or line segments A1

SAM 2H scheme: "NB A bar chart, unless it has a curve going consistently through a point in each bar, scores no points."

✗ Plotting at the midpoints (5, 15, 25…).
✓ Plotting at the upper bounds (10, 20, 30…).

subsections.heading: Reading a cumulative frequency graph
subsections.html:
Spec 6.2A, 6.2D (Higher) · 2018 Edexcel May 1H Q10

Go across from a cumulative frequency to find a value, or up from a value to find how many are below it.

  1. Median: go across from n/2 on the cumulative frequency axis to the curve, then down.
  2. Quartiles: go across from n/4 (LQ) and 3n/4 (UQ). IQR = UQ − LQ.
  3. "How many more than x?": go up from x, read the cumulative frequency, and subtract it from the total.
  4. Show the reading lines on the graph: they carry the method mark.

Worked example (based on 2018 1H Q10): 80 films

1. IQR: read across at 80 ÷ 4 = 20 and 3 × 80 ÷ 4 = 60. The 2018 readings were 103 and 123 minutes M1

2. IQR = 123 − 103 = 20 minutes (the scheme accepted 19 to 21) A1

3. "More than 35% are over 120 minutes." Up from 120: cf = 55. Over 120 = 80 − 55 = 25 M1

4. 25 ÷ 80 × 100 = 31.25% M1

5. 31.25% is less than 35%, so no, she is not correct A1

✗ Reading 55 and saying "55 films are over 120 minutes". The graph gives how many are up to 120.
✓ Subtract from the total: 80 − 55 = 25 are over 120.

subsections.heading: Histograms: frequency density
subsections.html:
Spec 6.1A (Higher) · 2016 Edexcel Jan 4HR Q18

In a histogram the area of each bar shows the frequency, so the height is frequency density, not frequency.

Frequency densityfrequency density = frequency ÷ class widthso frequency = frequency density × class width = area of the bar
  1. Work out each class width from the table (upper bound − lower bound).
  2. Frequency density = frequency ÷ width, for every class.
  3. Draw bars with no gaps, width = class width, height = frequency density. Label the vertical axis "Frequency density".

Worked example: 0–10 (10), 10–30 (24), 30–40 (30), 40–80 (18)

1. Widths 10, 20, 10, 40 M1

2. Frequency densities 10 ÷ 10 = 1, 24 ÷ 20 = 1.2, 30 ÷ 10 = 3, 18 ÷ 40 = 0.45 A1

The tallest bar (30–40) is not just the biggest frequency: it is the most densely packed class.

✗ Bar heights equal to the frequencies. With unequal widths that makes wide classes look far too big.
✓ Height = frequency ÷ class width.

subsections.heading: Reading a histogram when there is no scale
subsections.html:
Spec 6.1A (Higher) · 2016 Edexcel SAM 1H Q14 · 2018 Edexcel May 2H Q20

If the axis has no numbers, use the one frequency you are given to find what one unit of area is worth.

  1. Count the area of the bar(s) you know the frequency of, in small squares or as width × height.
  2. Work out how many people one unit of area stands for.
  3. Find the area of the bars you need and convert with the same rate.

Worked example (based on SAM 1H Q14): 26 plants are under 20 cm

1. The 0–20 bar gives frequency density 26 ÷ 20 = 1.3, which fixes the scale for the others M1

2. The other bars then give 3.6 × 10, 3.3 × 10 and 1 × 30, so the total = 26 + 36 + 33 + 30 M1

3. = 125 plants A1

The 2018 version gave the frequency of the two end bars together (6 babies) and asked for the middle ones. Same idea: area of end bars ↔ 6, then scale up.

subsections.heading: Estimating from part of a bar
subsections.html:
Spec 6.1A (Higher) · 2012 Edexcel Jan 3H (old spec)

To estimate how many are in part of a class, take the same fraction of that bar's area, assuming the values are spread evenly across the class.

  1. Find the frequency density of each bar involved.
  2. Multiply by the width of the part you need, not the whole class.
  3. Add the pieces. Say it is an estimate.

Worked example: the 20–40 bar has frequency 24. Estimate how many are between 25 and 35.

1. Frequency density = 24 ÷ 20 = 1.2 M1

2. 25 to 35 is a width of 10, so 1.2 × 10 = 12 (an estimate) A1

subsections.heading: Comparing two distributions
subsections.html:
Spec 6.2B (Higher) · 2016 Edexcel SAM 1H Q12(b) · 2015 Edexcel Jan 3HR Q12

A full comparison makes two points: one about an average and one about the spread, each in the context of the question.

  1. Average: compare medians (or means). "Group A's median is higher, so on average A took longer."
  2. Spread: compare IQRs (or ranges). "Group A's IQR is smaller, so A's times were more consistent."
  3. Quote the numbers you are comparing.

✗ "A is higher and more spread." Higher what? More spread how?
✓ "A has a higher median (34 compared with 29), so on average A scored more. A has a lower IQR (8 compared with 15), so A's scores were more consistent."

subsections.heading: Pie charts and two-way tables
subsections.html:
Spec 6.1A–C (Foundation)

A pie chart shares 360° in proportion to the frequencies; a two-way table splits the same people two ways at once.

  1. Angle = frequency ÷ total × 360°.
  2. Frequency from an angle = angle ÷ 360 × total.
  3. Two-way table: every row and every column must add up to its total. Fill in the cells you can, then use the totals to find the rest.

Worked example: 72 students, 110° for football

1. 110 ÷ 360 × 72 = 22 students M1 A1

2. 18 students would need 18 ÷ 72 × 360 = 90°.

The facts behind most of the marks

Total = mean × number. Combine groups with totals, never by averaging the means.

Frequency table mean: Σxf ÷ Σf. Grouped: use midpoints, and call it an estimate.

Median at (n + 1)/2 for a list. LQ at (n + 1)/4, UQ at 3(n + 1)/4. IQR = UQ − LQ.

Cumulative frequency graph: plot at upper bounds; read at n/4, n/2, 3n/4; "more than" means subtract from the total.

Histogram: frequency density = frequency ÷ class width; frequency = area.

Compare: an average and a spread, with numbers, in context.

subsections.html:

questions.promptHtml: Why is the mean from a grouped frequency table only an estimate?
questions.answerHtml:
The table only says how many values are in each class, not what they are. Using the midpoint assumes the values in each class average out to the middle of it.

If most values in a class were near the top, the true mean would be higher than the estimate. The raw data would give the exact mean.

questions.promptHtml: Class A (20 students) has a mean of 60. Class B (30 students) has a mean of 70. Why is the overall mean not 65?
questions.answerHtml:
65 treats the two classes as equally important, but B has more students. The totals are 1200 and 2100, so the overall mean is 3300 ÷ 50 = 66.

The combined mean is pulled towards the bigger group. It only equals the midpoint of the two means when the groups are the same size.

questions.promptHtml: Why are cumulative frequencies plotted at the upper class boundary and not the midpoint?
questions.answerHtml:
A cumulative frequency of 25 for 10 < m ≤ 20 means 25 values are 20 or less. You only know that all of them are in by the end of the class, at 20.

At the midpoint, 15, some of the class's values would not have been reached yet, so plotting 25 there would overstate how many are below 15.

questions.promptHtml: One player's scores include a single very high score. Why is the IQR a better measure of consistency than the range here?
questions.answerHtml:
The range uses only the largest and smallest values, so one unusual score makes it large even if every other score is close together.

The IQR uses the middle 50% of the data, so it ignores the extremes. It reflects how the player usually performs.

questions.promptHtml: A histogram has classes 0–10 and 10–40. Both have a frequency of 30. Why are the bars different heights?
questions.answerHtml:
The area shows the frequency. The 10–40 bar is three times as wide, so it only needs a third of the height to have the same area.

Frequency densities: 30 ÷ 10 = 3 and 30 ÷ 30 = 1. If the heights were equal, the wider class would look as if it had three times as many values.

questions.promptHtml: A cumulative frequency graph for 60 people shows a reading of 42 at 30 minutes. What does 42 mean, and how many took more than 30 minutes?
questions.answerHtml:
42 people took 30 minutes or less. The graph always counts from the bottom up.

So 60 − 42 = 18 people took more than 30 minutes. The most common error is to give 42 as the answer.

questions.promptHtml: For 11 values, why is the lower quartile the 3rd value, while for 80 values on a cumulative frequency graph you read across at 20, not 20.25?
questions.answerHtml:
With a short list you need an exact position: (11 + 1)/4 = 3, so the 3rd value.

A cumulative frequency graph is a smooth estimate for grouped data, so the quarter-of-the-way point is simply 80 ÷ 4 = 20. The 2018 scheme used readings at cf 20 and cf 60. With large n the difference is too small to see on the graph anyway.

questions.promptHtml: Why does a comparison need both an average and a measure of spread?
questions.answerHtml:
They answer different questions. The average says which group is typically higher. The spread says which group is more consistent.

Two groups can have the same median but very different spreads, like a steady player and an unreliable one with the same typical score. Exam comparisons usually give a mark for each, and each needs context: "on average the girls scored higher", not just "the median is higher".

modules.title: Probability and Sets
modules.standfirst: Set notation and Venn diagrams, then probability from the basics up to tree diagrams without replacement and "given that" questions. A Venn diagram question and a two-stage probability question appear on almost every paper. The marks go to people who fill Venn diagrams from the middle out, change the second-branch fractions when nothing is replaced, and write probabilities as fractions, never as ratios.
